**The container runs as the engine's own user, and the mount is proved before the box is used.** Under a **rootful** Docker or Podman the container's root is the host's root, so directories the box creates in the mount would be root-owned and the engine could neither write into them nor reclaim the disk at teardown. Crewlet therefore passes `--user <uid>:<gid>` on a rootful runtime and **not** on a rootless one, where the user namespace already maps container root onto the invoking user and `--user` would map it into the subuid range. The runtime is asked which it is (`docker info` / `podman info`); an unanswerable probe is treated as rootful, because that mistake fails loudly at creation and the other is silent.

If your image needs its own user (one that installs packages at run time, say), put `--user 0:0` in `run_args`. Operator flags are spliced last and both runtimes take the final occurrence of a repeated flag, so yours wins, and you take back the ownership problem above.

Every container box is proved once, at creation, before anything runs in it: the engine writes a token the box reads back, and the box creates a directory the engine writes into and removes. That catches the ownership case and another invisible one: a `runtime` pointed at a daemon on **another host** (`DOCKER_HOST`, a forwarded socket) bind-mounts *that* machine's filesystem, so the agent finds no brief, credentials or tools. A box that fails the proof is torn down and the error names the cause; point the runtime at a daemon on this host.

**A box reaches the engine host by the runtime's name for it.** The engine hands a box addresses written in its own network: the [tool bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box) (`CREWLET_MCP_BRIDGE_URL`), the telemetry receiver (`CREWLET_SANDBOX_OTEL_RECEIVER_URL`), the URL of every HTTP [MCP server](#mcp-inside-the-sandbox) the seat scopes into the box, the run's [notes route](#notes-to-a-running-run) on the bridge, which OpenCode's plugin polls, [Gitlet's base](#repositories-on-gitlet) (`CREWLET_BOX_GIT_URL`, handed as `CREWLET_GIT_URL` with the run's credential helper scoped to it), and a [check's](gitlet.md#check-boxes) reads of its commit (`CREWLET_CHECK_API`). A single-host install sets those to loopback (`http://127.0.0.1:8000`, `http://localhost:8000/box/git`), which inside a container is the container itself. So where a URL handed to a `container` box names the engine host's loopback (`127.0.0.1`, any `127.x` address, `::1` or `localhost`), the box gets the same URL with the host replaced by the runtime's name for the engine host:

- Docker: `host.docker.internal`, which the engine defines for every box it starts (`--add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway`, needed by Docker Engine on Linux and answered the same way by Docker Desktop).
- Podman: `host.containers.internal`, which Podman defines itself.

Any other host is handed on as written, and so is every value you declare for the box (`role.sandbox.env`, a setup step's `env`), which is already in the box's network: a box reaching a service on the host names `host.docker.internal` there. `direct` shares the host's network and gets every address as written (for the bridge it needs none on a node that serves the API, which dials its own listener on loopback, derived from the socket it binds), so one company runs `direct` and `container` entries side by side with one loopback `CREWLET_MCP_BRIDGE_URL` and one loopback `CREWLET_BOX_GIT_URL`, each read under the alias by the containers alone. Docker Desktop, and Podman's machine on macOS and Windows, deliver that name over the host's loopback, where a loopback bind hears it and the [tool bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box) and Gitlet's box routes serve a box under any name. Docker Engine and Podman on Linux deliver it from the container's bridge network, so the engine's API must listen there too: `api.host` empty (every interface) or the bridge's address, never `127.0.0.1`. `crewlet validate`, given both files, and every apply on a Linux `ingress` node that starts container boxes (one with the `seats` role, whose executors dial the bridge and the receiver, or one with the `gitlet` role in a company that runs [checks](gitlet.md#check-boxes), whose boxes dial Gitlet; a node with neither starts no box here) warn (`config_advisory` at `api.host`, or `api.public.host` when the public listener serves the box routes) when a company that reaches the `container` cell meets a loopback bind.

**Setup commands get a provisioning budget, not a control one.** Each command may run for `timeout_seconds` (default 600), since a dependency install, cold image pull or large clone takes minutes. Raise it for a slow step; lower it for one that should be instant, so a hung command surfaces as a named setup failure rather than eating the turn. A failure names the step and what failed (the file it could not write, or the command's position and the status it exited with or that it reported none), never the command text: the engine resolves nothing in a command, but a recipe may spell a credential out literally, and the failure is logged and handed back to the agent.

**Setup steps and the cells.** Neither cell writes a setup step's *file* outside the box's home. `direct` has no filesystem virtualisation, so a file elsewhere would be the engine host's own (its real `/usr/local/bin`) and is refused with an error naming the mode; its home is minted per box, so no absolute path a document can write is inside it. `container` writes on the host side of its one mount, the home at `/home/user`, and refuses any other path. A relative path is under the home in either cell, as is a path starting `~/`, which names the home in either cell; a path that climbs out of the home with `..`, names the home itself, names another account's home (`~name/…`), or puts a backslash after its leading `~` (`~\.npmrc`: a backslash is a character of a file name, not a separator) is refused. So name a step's file relative to the home (`.npmrc`, `.local/bin/tool`, or `~/.npmrc`), the one form every cell writes in the same place. File paths in a setup step are **not** shell-expanded, so `$HOME` does not work there; a step that needs a file's absolute path has a `commands` entry, which runs in a shell and expands `"$HOME"` (the [git-auth recipe](#the-git-auth-recipe) writes its helper that way, because git is given the helper's absolute path).

**A step whose file a box would refuse is refused when the document is written**, by `crewlet validate` and every write path, not at the seat's first box. The check is the boxes' own rule (the function both cells call before touching a path), applied to every box a seat actually runs in: each box its executor runs in, placed by the `run_in` of each entry its launch can pick (or `default_run_in`). The refusal sits at the file in the step, names the step, the path and the first seat whose box it fails (and how many more), and is an admission rule: a stored revision that keeps such a step still applies, reported as a warning, so a rolling upgrade never takes a node off the fleet's revision. It cannot see a link an existing directory on the engine host holds; the box refuses that itself when it writes.

**A setup command is not confined the way a file is.** It runs in the box's shell; under `direct` that is the engine host, as the engine's user, so a step installing a system package installs it on the host or fails for want of rights. Under `container` it runs inside the container, as the engine's own uid on a rootful runtime (which an image's system directories usually refuse too) and as container root on a rootless one. Have such a step check for the tool it needs and name what to install where, and provision a box's system toolchain deliberately: on the host for `direct`, in the image for `container`.

**Credentials.** The local backend seeds the credential files of the [`providers.llm` entry](llm-backends.md) the launch picked (the first member of the seat's executor chain whose harness has a runner and is not sitting out), or for OpenCode the login document its export printed, which the run imports and exports again ([OpenCode](#opencode)), into the box before the run, and writes one the run **refreshed** back afterwards. OAuth access tokens expire in hours and most vendors rotate the refresh token with them, so discarding the rewritten file would log the fleet out at the next expiry.

- **Seeding.** The box is seeded with what the login holds, **read whole** under the shared credential directory's lock ([one login](llm-backends.md#a-login-of-several-files-is-written-whole), never one sign-in's token beside another's `config.toml`), and given every file of it or none. A **mixed** file, one the harness also reads its own settings from ([`login_keys`](llm-backends.md)), is given whole, its settings with its login, as a person's own home holds it, and held to its login's fields alone. A login it cannot be given whole (a credential path that would leave the box's home) is not seeded at all, with a `local_sandbox_credential_seed_failed` warning, so the harness answers its own "not authenticated" rather than failing on half a login.
- **Write-back is a compare-and-swap against the seed**, recorded in the box's records at creation (a SHA-256 of the login the box was given, a mixed file's login fields, and every file of the login it was not given). Refreshed files are written back only where the box's copy differs from its seed **and** the shared login, as a whole (every file, every absence), still holds that seed; then as **one write** of the whole login, so a teardown killed part way never leaves half of it. A file is compared on its login, and written back as its **token fields alone** ([`refresh_keys`](llm-backends.md)): the shared copy keeps every other byte, an endpoint, a provider choice, a setting the run wrote, so none of it reaches the shared login or any seat, and a file naming no token fields is never written back. A file the box's copy holds that does not read in its format writes nothing back, logged with `shared=unreadable`; so does a file with no rule in the box's records.
- **An idle box writes nothing** (an OpenCode box's export reproduces its import byte for byte, so it would otherwise put a stale seed back over a login the host refreshed meanwhile).
- **A superseded refresh is dropped.** If the shared login also moved (another seat's refresh, a new `crewlet llm login`, or a file the login gained because the host signed in again), the shared one is newer and stays; `local_sandbox_credential_superseded` is logged with `shared=changed`, naming the file and its path, never a value. A credential the shared directory did not hold at seeding is never created from a box, nor is one since removed with `crewlet llm logout`: such a refresh is dropped and logged with `shared=removed`.
- **A copy whose account fields or named token name another account is not written back.** Where the harness's profile names the keys that say which login it is (`identity_keys`), every file of the box's copy, changed or not, must hold the shared login's value at each, absent from both included. A token is compared by the account its claims name: the ID token for Codex and Gemini CLI, the access token for Qwen Code, Cursor Agent, Grok, Muse Code, Kimi Code, Hermes and Pi. The check does not bind the refresh token, or any token it does not name: a copy that keeps the named fields and token passes. A copy that dropped a file holding them is not written back either. The shared one stays, and `local_sandbox_credential_superseded` is logged with `shared=other_account`, naming the file, never a value.
- **Locking.** The comparison and write are one step under the shared credential directory's lock (`<state_dir>/<harness>/credentials.lock`, beside it), which the [harness backend's](llm-backends.md) seats and `crewlet llm` commands take for their own writes; a teardown waits at most 10 s for a writer holding it.

**Pause / resume works.** A run blocked on a human answer is suspended: `direct` SIGSTOPs the job's process group, `container` issues `docker pause`. Both hold memory and the box's directory on its node, which the `default_pause_ttl_seconds` reaper bounds.

**A box goes before its engine when memory runs out.** On Linux every process a box runs stands ahead of the engine for the kernel's OOM killer: raised, before it runs anything, to the engine's own `oom_score_adj` plus 1000, held to the kernel's ceiling of 1000. A `direct` box's first process raises itself and then becomes the command, so every setup command, exec and the detached job start there, with everything they start; a `container` box is started with the runtime's `--oom-score-adj`, which Docker and Podman give every `exec` into the container too. A box a whole thousand ahead is taken before the engine whatever the two hold. The run the kernel kills is collected as the failed run it is, partial output and exit status with it, where the engine killed would take every seat on the node down at once. The lead is counted from the engine's own value, because that is its deployment's decision: a Kubernetes Guaranteed pod runs at -997 so its node's kernel takes it last, and its boxes at 3 go before its engine without going before every other pod's work. An engine already above 0 leaves its boxes at the ceiling. An operator's own `--oom-score-adj` in `run_args` wins for a `container` box. It is an order for the kernel, not a boundary (a box may lower its own value again), and on macOS, which gives an unprivileged process no such priority, a box and the engine compete on size alone. What an OOM kill takes beside the box is up to whatever supervises the engine; a systemd unit's and a Kubernetes container's defaults both take the engine with it: see [When the host runs out of memory](../guides/deployment.md#when-the-host-runs-out-of-memory).

**What the cells do not give you:** provider-enforced network egress policy (use `network:` plus your own firewall), and a fresh machine per run (a `direct` box shares the host's installed toolchain, which is usually the point).

### Bring your own image

The engine ships no image for `local.image`: use one built for your repositories, kept as current as they are. The engine runs it as

```text
docker run -d --init -v <box home>:/home/user -w /home/user/workspace -e HOME=/home/user \
  --user <engine uid>:<gid> --add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway <run_args> IMAGE sleep infinity
```

(`--user` only on a rootful runtime, `--add-host` only under Docker), and runs every job and setup command in it with `docker exec`, its run environment in an `--env-file`. So the image needs:

- **the harness on the login `PATH`**: the harness is started under `sh -lc`, and a Debian or Ubuntu image's `/etc/profile` resets `PATH` to the standard directories, so a harness in `/usr/local/bin` is found and one only on an `ENV PATH` entry is not;
- **`git`**, and **`gh`** where seats open GitHub pull requests;
- **a POSIX `sh`** and no `ENTRYPOINT`, since the engine supplies the command;
- **a writable `$HOME`** and nothing it relies on under `/home/user`, which the box's own home is mounted over;
- **no assumption about the user**: it must work as a uid it has no account for (the engine's own, on Docker Desktop for a Mac user `501:20`);
- **`tar` and `gzip`**, which a run packs its harness's session with when the harness exits and restores a session carried in from another box with ([Claude Code](#claude-code), [Codex](#codex), [OpenCode](#opencode), [GitHub Copilot CLI](#github-copilot-cli), [Grok Build](#a-grok-build-runs-session), [Muse Code](#muse-code), [Kimi Code](#a-kimi-code-runs-session), [Hermes Agent](#a-hermes-agent-runs-session), [Pi](#pi)). A box without them runs as any other, and its error stream says the session was not packed. The same holds for the engine host of a `direct` cell; the published image has both.
- **`find`**, which a run that resumes a Claude Code session cuts back the session's subagents' threads with ([A Claude Code run's session](#a-claude-code-runs-session)). A box without it still resumes the session, its threads as they were left, and the error stream says no thread was cut back. The same holds for the engine host of a `direct` cell.
- **a POSIX userland**, which a run's script and the engine's own commands in the box are written for: `find`, `ls`, `wc`, `sed`, `grep`, `head`, `tail`, `cksum` and `touch` among its tools, and a **`sleep` that takes a tenth of a second**, as GNU's, busybox's and BSD's do (a run's end gives its harness its grace, and the engine's kill of a job its processes theirs, counted in tenths). A Claude Code session packed while its harness still works ([below](#each-launchs-session-kept)) is refused by a box that lacks any of these tools but `tail`, or whose `sleep` takes no tenth, naming which.
- **Kimi Code 2.7.2 and `node` 22.19 or newer**, where seats run Kimi Code ([its box image](#kimi-code));
- **an OpenCode of the set the engine judges**, where seats run it: 2.3.2, the one release supported, and the same release from one image to the next while a turn runs. A continuation's first request is judged in its box only where that box runs exactly the release that wrote the session ([What a continued session is told](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)); another release runs, and every continuation of its sessions is told as one that may be a summary.

A box reaches the engine host by the runtime's name for it, as [above](#local-sandboxes), and on Linux `api.host` must not be loopback.

**Recipe 1: a stock image and a setup step.** No image to build: a step installs Claude Code and `gh` into the box's home, each at a pinned version, `gh` checked against the checksums file GitHub publishes with the release.

```yaml
providers:
  sandbox:
    local:
      image: node:22-bookworm       # has git, curl and sha256sum
    default_run_in: container
    setup:
      - name: coding-tools
        files:
          .profile: |              # the login shell the harness starts in reads it
            export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
        commands:
          - |
            err=$(mktemp)
            npm install --global --prefix "$HOME/.npm-global" --no-audit --no-fund \
              @anthropic-ai/claude-code@2.1.310 2>"$err" && exit 0
            s=$?; cat "$err" >&2
            grep -Eq 'code E(408|429|5[0-9][0-9])$' "$err" && exit 75
            exit "$s"
          - |
            set -eu
            v=2.103.3; a=$(dpkg --print-architecture); t="gh_${v}_linux_${a}.tar.gz"
            cd "$(mktemp -d)"
            fetch() {
              code=$(curl -fsSL --retry 5 --retry-delay 2 --retry-all-errors -o "$2" -w '%{http_code}' "$1") && return
              s=$?
              case $code in 408|429|5??) exit 75 ;; esac
              exit "$s"
            }
            fetch "https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/download/v${v}/${t}" "$t"
            fetch "https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/download/v${v}/gh_${v}_checksums.txt" sums.txt
            grep " ${t}\$" sums.txt | sha256sum -c -
            tar -xzf "$t"
            mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" && mv "gh_${v}_linux_${a}/bin/gh" "$HOME/.local/bin/gh"
        timeout_seconds: 600
```

Setup steps run after the box is created and before the harness starts, as the box's own uid, which is why both install under `$HOME` rather than the image's system directories. The trade-off against recipe 2: **every new box downloads and installs both again** (a reused box keeps them), costing time on each run and needing egress to the npm registry and GitHub.

**Each download says what its failure means.** npm retries a failed fetch twice itself, and `curl` here retries every failure five times, two seconds apart (`--retry-all-errors`, since `--retry` alone gives up at once on a reset or refused connection), so a blip of a few seconds never fails the step. A registry or download server still failing on its side after that, answering a 408, a 429 or a 5xx, ends the command with 75: a download that failed for now, which a wait clears (`setup_unavailable`). Every other failure keeps its own status, a setup an administrator has to fix (`configuration`): a pin that names no release (npm's `E404` or `ETARGET`, a 404 from GitHub), a 401 or a 403, a checksum that doesn't match, and a connection refused or reset, a name that doesn't resolve or a timeout, which from inside the box look the same as blocked egress (see [Setup steps](#setup-steps--provisioning-the-box)).

**Recipe 2: your own image from Claude Code's dev container.** Build Anthropic's [reference dev container](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/devcontainer) (`.devcontainer/` in `anthropics/claude-code`) with the harness pinned, `--build-arg CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION=<version>`, then put `claude` where a login shell finds it, since that image adds its npm prefix to `PATH` with `ENV` alone:

```dockerfile
FROM claude-devcontainer:<version>
USER root
RUN ln -s /usr/local/share/npm-global/bin/claude /usr/local/bin/claude
USER node
```

Add your repositories' toolchains to the same Dockerfile and name the result in `local.image`. Its egress firewall (`init-firewall.sh`) is not started by a plain `docker run`; restrict a box's network with `local.network` and your own firewall instead.

A seat on a [plan's login](llm-backends.md#authentication) needs nothing more in either recipe: a box is seeded with the login and writes a refreshed one back.

---

## Harnesses

Eleven runners ship behind the `sandbox.Runner` interface, one per harness that can run an executor: `claude-code`, `codex`, `gemini-cli`, `qwen-code`, `opencode`, `copilot`, `grok`, `muse-code`, `kimi-code`, `hermes` and `pi`, each listed by its built-in profile's `executor` block (`config.ExecutorHarnesses`, held to the runners that exist by a test). A run's runner is the harness of the `providers.llm` entry its launch picked, with no setting beside it, and a launch passes over a member of the seat's executor chain on any other harness. Every runner gets the same two texts, the **brief** (the prompt the harness runs) and the run's **standing instructions** (added to the harness's own system prompt, [What a harness is told](#what-a-harness-is-told)), and returns the same structured result. The entry names its model in its own harness's grammar and signs in the way that harness does, so a run goes only to that harness's runner (see [One entry, one runner](#claude-code) below).

### What a harness is told

A run is handed two texts, kept apart from the launch all the way to the harness:

- **The brief** is the whole prompt the harness runs. For a run that starts a session of its own it holds, in order:
  - The turn's own ask (the user message a phase on this host sends), with the ledger of its earlier rounds where a reviewer sent it back.
  - **Every answer that carried the turn's work on** (a person's answer to a question, a withdrawal, a refused reply, a call held for approval), and every account the engine carried a run on with (the calls it parked on, the run it waited for), from this round or one a review sent back, oldest first, each naming its round, under a header saying the session holds none of them and naming which kinds they are, the later of two answers that differ standing. An account is never introduced as an answer to a question the run asked. The ledger carries none of a person's replies and a run of its own holds no earlier brief, so an instruction a person gave would otherwise be lost at the first fresh start.
    - A call approved in a round the ledger lists is pointed to there.
    - A call approved in a round the turn's park folded into an entry standing for dropped rounds (it counts their calls by tool and lists none), or in a round whose record may count calls by tool (as a park does for a round whose calls it condensed), is told with what became of it, as one of the calls that entry counts.
  - For a round carried on, what became of the run before it: the question it asked and the answer (see [Answering a parked run](#answering-a-parked-run)); or how it was cut off, with where its work is and that what it did through the seat's tools did happen, to be checked before any is redone; or that the model's provider refused every request of the session it continued, so it did nothing.
  - **Every call the round's runs made through the seat's tools so far**, held to the [prior-work ledger](turn-engine.md#prior-work-ledger-across-self_iterate-rounds)'s budgets, since a run of its own remembers none ([A relaunch continues the turn's session](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)).

  A relaunch that **continues the turn's session**, in any box, is prompted with what that session lacks rather than its task again, and carries the fresh brief beside it for its script to hand over where the box cannot take the session up ([A relaunch continues the turn's session](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)).

  **A fresh brief names the kept session its run does not continue** under `## A kept session this run does not continue`: the turn's own session kept by an earlier launch, or else the session its conversation's last turn left (a relaunch names it only where the turn's row was read holding it). It says whose it is (on a schedule's fire, in the schedule's words: its last fire's, or this fire's earlier launches'), and to read what it did with `read_session` under its turn id, `match` finding a word in it. Of the turn's own it says it is kept only until this run first saves its own, which takes its place on the turn's row. A round lost a second time, which continues no session, is told it too: its kept session is then the only record of what the round's jobs did in their boxes. It never says why the session is not continued (the log does, quoting what said no). It appears only where the run's surface carries `read_session` ([A seat reads its own](#a-seat-reads-its-own)); no standing sentence about the session tools rides every request.
- **The standing instructions** say how to work, in this order:
  1. The seat's executor system prompt (identity, policies, roster, memory, exactly as a phase on this host sends them as its system message), opened by one constant note that these, not the coding tool's own prompt, are the role (Claude Code's opens with "You are Claude Code", and no flag removes it).
  2. `## Your environment`: the box, each [setup step's](#setup-steps--provisioning-the-box) `brief`, and the connected MCP servers.
  3. `## When you need a person's answer` ([how to ask a person](#mid-run-clarification-ask_and_wait)), on every launch.
  4. The [report to write before stopping](#what-ends-a-run-each-launch-is-published-as-its-own-record), addressed at the box's own path. For a run given repositories it may push to on Gitlet, it names them and says its pushes there are [reported for it](#what-a-run-pushed-is-reported-for-it), so its report names only what it delivered elsewhere.
  5. Last, for a harness that takes a person's notes between steps: what a note is, how it opens, the heading the harness puts it under (Claude Code: a system message, or on some models a system reminder at the end of the last tool result; OpenCode: a message from the user; Gemini CLI: a message from the user as the run is about to finish; Grok Build: a system reminder after a step's results, and the stop hook's feedback as the run is about to finish), and that text a tool produced (file contents, command output, a fetched page) is never a note ([Notes to a running run](#notes-to-a-running-run)).

The standing instructions are **appended to the harness's own system prompt**, never put in its place and never in the prompt it runs. Replacing the vendor's prompt would strip what an executor exists to use (how to drive its shell and editor), and instructions in front of the task reach the model as part of the user's request, making a seat's identity and policies something it is asked rather than who it is. Each runner uses its harness's own channel:

- **Claude Code**: `--append-system-prompt-file`, which puts the file's text after the default system prompt and leaves that prompt whole (measured on 2.1.310).
- **Muse Code**: `run.system_prompt_append` in the settings the run writes ([Muse Code](#muse-code)), which Muse adds at the very end of its own system prompt and reads afresh on every resume (measured on 1.4.25).
- **Grok Build**: the body of an agent file the run writes (`<home>/.crewlet/grok-agent.md`, [Grok Build](#grok-build)), which Grok adds at the very end of its own system prompt; a continuing run's script writes it into the session's record, which Grok resumes on (measured on 1.0.92).
- **OpenCode**: an absolute `instructions` entry in the [configuration the run writes](#opencode) (`<home>/.crewlet/opencode.json`), which OpenCode adds after its default agent's prompt as `Instructions from: <path>` and the file's text (measured on 2.3.2). An entry rather than a global `AGENTS.md`, because the entries of every configuration OpenCode reads are added together (the home's, an image's, the repository's and a managed configuration's instructions survive, where a written `AGENTS.md` would replace the home's) and the run's configuration is rewritten every run (a reused box never carries a previous entry). Absolute, because a relative entry is matched by walking up from the checkout.
- **Gemini CLI**: none of its own, so the run's script builds one: it has Gemini CLI write its prompt out and names that prompt with the instructions after it as `GEMINI_SYSTEM_MD` ([Gemini CLI](#gemini-cli)).

Each reads the text from **a file** in the box, never argv (Muse Code's settings file in the box home, the others' in its work directory, `<home>/.crewlet`): the text carries a seat's org chart, policies and memory, and a command line is readable by every process that can list it (on a `direct` box, every account on the engine host) and bounded by `ARG_MAX`. OpenCode's `instructions` entry names `system.md`. A Claude Code launch writes `system.md` (the instructions as they stand) and, for a run wired to its turn's notes (every seat's executor run), `system-notes.md` beside it (the same text with what a note is after it). The script names `system-notes.md` on a release that reads notes ([Claude Code's hooks](#claude-codes-hooks)) and `system.md` on an older one; a run not wired to notes uses `system.md`. Each file is written afresh every run at the mode a box writes every file with (`0600`) even where a reused box left one wider, and outside the checkout, so a `git clean` cannot remove it and a commit cannot carry it into a repository. A run with no standing instructions writes no `system.md` and passes no flag; a runner always has at least the report instruction.

Neither text is recorded where the engine reads back: the run's record holds the task and the turn's parked state, which a resumed turn reads instead. The brief lives on only in the harness's own session, [kept](#each-launchs-session-kept) for a relaunch to continue.

**A continued run is told how to work by its own launch, never an earlier one's.** A harness keeps a session's standing instructions its own way, so each runner takes one of three routes (a test holds every registered runner to its row): the harness **reloads** them from what this launch hands it, the runner **rewrites** what the session stored before the resume (OpenCode's by re-importing the session), or the harness **supersedes** the stored text with this launch's, in its own words.

| Runner | Where the standing instructions go | On a resume |
|---|---|---|
| `claude-code` | `--append-system-prompt-file` | **reloaded**: the resume runs with `--system-prompt-snapshot off` (2.1.267 or later), [below](#a-claude-code-runs-session) |
| `codex` | `developer_instructions` in the run's `config.toml` | **rewritten**: Codex replays the developer message its session's first turn recorded, and nothing of a resumed thread's configuration reaches the model, neither `config.toml` nor `thread/resume`'s `developerInstructions` (measured on 0.171.0). So the box's note helper rewrites that message in the rollout to the run's text first. A box with no helper for its machine, or a rollout recording none, starts a session of its own |
| `gemini-cli` | `GEMINI_SYSTEM_MD`: Gemini's prompt with the text after it | **reloaded**: a resumed chat's system instruction is built afresh |
| `qwen-code` | `QWEN_SYSTEM_IDENTITY_MD` | **reloaded** as the session loads |
| `copilot` | `copilot-instructions.md` in the run's Copilot home | **reloaded** on every resume (measured on 1.0.114) |
| `muse-code` | `run.system_prompt_append` | **reloaded** on every resume (measured on 1.4.25) |
| `kimi-code` | the run's agent profile | **rewritten**: Kimi renders a profile once, as it creates the session, and restores it on a resume, so the run's driver renews the session's record from this launch's profile first (measured on 2.7.2) |
| `grok` | the run's agent file, between `<crewlet_seat_instructions>` bounds | **rewritten**: Grok Build resumes on the system message its record's first line holds, whatever the agent file says, so the gate replaces that line's instructions with this launch's first (measured on 1.0.92). A record without them starts a session of its own |
| `opencode` | an `instructions` entry | **rewritten (re-import)**: OpenCode leads a session's requests with the instructions it first rendered and tells it a later launch's only as a message that they changed, for a longer file a diff against the earlier text (measured on 2.3.2). An import writes no instruction state, so before the run's server starts the gate exports the box's own copy, deletes it once the export passed a carried import's checks, and imports the export: the resumed request leads with this launch's text whole (measured). It costs about 3 seconds, three standalone starts, a continuation; the copy's child sessions are not imported, as on the carried path. A copy it cannot re-import starts a session of its own, saying why. A session carried into another box is imported anyway, [An OpenCode run's session](#an-opencode-runs-session) |
| `hermes` | `HERMES_EPHEMERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT`, read from the run's file | **rewritten**: Hermes freezes the value with the session as it creates it (its local policy's client environment) and a resume keeps it, so the gate writes the run's text there first, the gateway stopped (measured on 0.23.3, [below](#hermes-agent)). A session with no launch frozen starts a session of its own |
| `pi` | the `crewlet` prompt section | **superseded**: Pi keeps the session's first system message and adds `Updated system prompt section "crewlet"` with the whole new text (measured on 1.6.0). A model without mid-conversation system messages folds them all into one current prompt, which holds only the new text |

### Claude Code

Runs headless:

`claude -p --output-format stream-json --verbose --permission-mode bypassPermissions --settings <home>/.crewlet/claude-settings-notes-pinned.json --append-system-prompt-file <home>/.crewlet/system-notes.md`

- That is the [settings every run has](#a-claude-code-runs-session) with the run's [hooks](#claude-codes-hooks), and its [standing instructions](#what-a-harness-is-told) told of notes: every seat's executor run on Claude Code 2.1.163 or later.
- Older release, or a run not wired to notes: `--settings <home>/.crewlet/claude-settings.json` (the settings every run has, nothing else) and `--append-system-prompt-file <home>/.crewlet/system.md`, a run that starts [its own skills](#a-runs-own-skills)' hook among them.
- From 2.1.310 each settings file is handed as its pinned copy, its name ending `-pinned.json`, which adds [the pin of its compaction point and of what a resume loads](#a-claude-code-runs-session).
- `--model` from the entry; `--max-turns` from the run's turn cap.
- `--mcp-config <file>` names the bridge (the engine's own tools and each of the seat's MCP servers), the seat's in-box servers, and every server its own configuration declares ([MCP inside the sandbox](#mcp-inside-the-sandbox)).
- `--plugin-dir <home>/.crewlet/claude-skills` carries the seat's [own skills](#a-runs-own-skills) on Claude Code 2.1.118 or later.
- The session: `--session-id <id>` for one it starts, `--resume <id>` for one it continues ([below](#a-claude-code-runs-session)).
- The brief is on standard input.

It prints every message as it happens, one JSON object a line, into its own **event stream** (`stream.jsonl` in the box's work directory), which is what a person watching sees and the transcript is built from. (`--output-format json` printed one object at the end and nothing before, and print mode writes nothing to stderr. `--verbose` is not optional: print mode refuses stream-json without it.)

The stream's **last line is the result message**, which the wrapper copies to `result.json` after the harness exits, never through a pipe beside it (its exit status would be the copy's, not the harness's). It maps directly onto the result: final text, session id, token usage, cost; an error subtype such as `error_max_turns` and its `errors` are the failure. A stream ending on anything else is a run that stopped before saying how it ended, and reads as one, not as a success. If the wrapper never made the copy (process group killed by an OOM or host restart, so the poll ended it on the wrapper's liveness), or the box refuses the result file (one that is [not a regular file](#what-ends-a-run-each-launch-is-published-as-its-own-record); the refusal is still said), the stream's last line is read instead: the result if the harness printed one, otherwise what it was saying when it stopped. A harness that exited before printing anything (not installed, a bad flag) leaves both empty, and reads as what it is.

**The bridge's own server is always loaded.** In the file `--mcp-config` names, the engine's `crewlet` server is marked `alwaysLoad`, exempting it from Claude Code's tool search, so what the run reports and asks a person through is in front of its model on every request. Every other server (the seat's over the [bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box), and those in the box) is left to the tool search, which keeps a server's tools out of a request until the model looks for them (Claude Opus 4, Sonnet 4, Haiku 4.5 and later; an earlier model is sent every tool every request).

**A run loads what a person's session of Claude Code loads**, beside the run's own: the box home's `.claude/` (its settings and their hooks, `CLAUDE.md`, rules, skills, agents, commands and installed plugins), the home's `~/.claude.json` (its user and local MCP servers, [linked](#a-claude-code-runs-session) into the pinned configuration directory), and the start directory's `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/` and `.mcp.json`. Nothing is passed that narrows it (no `--setting-sources`, `--strict-mcp-config` or `--bare`). The run's own sit on top, by Claude Code's own precedence (measured on 2.1.330): a server the home or the repository names `crewlet` gives way to the one `--mcp-config` names. **A box that switches hooks off refuses a run that starts one of the engine's** (its notes' hooks, its skills' plugin): before Claude Code starts, the engine reads the settings Claude Code merges (`~/.claude/settings.json`, the start directory's `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json`, then the managed `/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json` and `managed-settings.d/*.json`, a later file's value winning), and where `disableAllHooks` ends up `true`, or a managed file sets `allowManagedHooksOnly: true`, the run fails naming the file and the key. Claude Code then runs no hook of the run's, without a word (measured on 2.1.330); the run never writes `disableAllHooks: false` over it, which would also run the home's and the repository's hooks where a person's session runs none. A file Claude Code ignores decides nothing: one it cannot read (a directory, mode 000, a broken link), one that is no JSON, and one holding the key as anything but a boolean (measured). It reads no `settings.local.json` in the home (measured). Claude Code has no layer that undoes a `deniedMcpServers` entry or an `allowedMcpServers` list in any settings file, the home's and the repository's included, a `permissions.deny` entry naming the server (`mcp__crewlet`), one of its tools (`mcp__crewlet__<tool>`) or a wildcard over them (`mcp__crewlet__*`, `mcp__*`, `*`; a partial name such as `mcp__crewlet__sub*` matches nothing), an `agent` setting running the main thread as an agent whose `tools:` leave the bridge's out, or a `disabledMcpServers` entry for the start directory in `~/.claude.json`, so **a run whose bridge is not there is ended as it starts**, never left to work without its notes and tools. The script reads the stream's init event, which lists each server and its status, and the tools the model is offered (measured on 2.1.330: a denied server missing, a disabled one `disabled`, one that did not answer within Claude Code's own connect wait `failed`, and one whose tools a `permissions.deny` entry takes `connected` without them), and where `crewlet` is not `connected` with every tool the bridge lists as the run starts (or still `pending`) it ends the harness and the run fails saying so on its error stream: for a missing server, each settings file holding either list (the box's managed settings, `~/.claude/settings.json`, and the start directory's `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json`); for one without some or all of its tools, the missing tools and each of those files holding an entry that can take them (the tool's own name, `mcp__crewlet`, `mcp__crewlet__*`, `mcp__*` or `*`), with the entry, and each holding an `agent` setting, with the agent's definition found under `.claude/agents` in the start directory or the home; for a disabled one, the `.claude.json` that disables it. The engine hands the runner the tools the bridge lists ([The tool bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box)); a tool it activates later is not checked. A deny naming another server's tools, `mcp__other__<tool>` included where a bridge tool has that name, is the settings' own to keep.

**Every server the bridge serves carries the bridge's wait.** Its entry's `timeout`, in milliseconds, is the longest the bridge can take to answer a call ([The tool bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box)). It is Claude Code's own tool timeout for the server, at which it cancels a call whatever progress flows (measured on 2.1.310: `"timeout": 360000` cut a call the bridge kept going at 360 seconds with `notifications/cancelled`). On 2.1.310 it is also the HTTP transport's budget for a response's first byte (measured: 360000 in place of 60000) and the check on a call that has sent nothing. A release whose configuration schema has no such key (2.1.118's) drops it and keeps its own clocks, which the bridge's progress still answers. A server in the box carries none.

**The brief is read on stdin**, from `brief.md` in the box's work directory, never argv: `-p` with no prompt reads its prompt there verbatim (measured on 2.1.263 and 2.1.310). A brief grows with every note the turn has read; one argument is capped at 128 KiB; and a command line is readable by every account on a `direct` box's host.

**The wrapper unsets `CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE` and `CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE`** before the harness starts. Bare mode drops every hook (with `CLAUDE.md`, subagents and a plan's login) and safe mode drops hooks and the `--mcp-config` bridge. Either can arrive from the seat's `role.sandbox.env`, the image or a profile the login shell sources; only the wrapper, running after all three, reaches every one, so they are removed for every run rather than refused in configuration.

**It unsets `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE` beside them, on every run.** The variable marks Anthropic's own hosted environment (Claude Code on the web), which no box is. Switched on (`1`, `true`, `yes` or `on`) it changes what a resume hands its model: a record whose parent the transcript does not hold is given an earlier record as parent, picked by timestamp, up to 16 times, so the run would continue a conversation its session never recorded (2.1.310 and 2.1.322, unless a flag Claude Code fetches turns it off), and 2.1.322 alone can also take another of the conversation's ends as the one it continues. Both releases also admit their coordinator and hermetic modes with it on, and where its value is exactly `true` put `--max-old-space-size=8192` in their `NODE_OPTIONS`. No settings file can set it, and it is unset on fresh and resumed runs alike, so a relaunch runs as the job it continues ran.

**A run a hook stopped is a failure.** Claude Code reports a loop that a hook of the repository's or image's settings stopped (exit 2 or a block) as a success subtype with an empty result and `terminal_reason: hook_stopped` (measured on 2.1.263 and 2.1.310); the runner reads it as a failed run saying so.

The run's input is its **whole** prompt: the vendor's `input_tokens` counts only the uncached remainder, so the engine adds `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` and carries both as the cache's share, as for a call on a Claude Code entry on its own host.

**A run is charged what it spent, never its session's spend.** From 2.1.277 a run that continues a session (`--resume`) starts from the totals the job before it saved, so the result's `usage` and `total_cost_usd` are the **session's**. From 2.1.310 every result also states, per model, what the calls this process made since its previous result cost (`model_usage_since_last_result`), so a run is charged the sum of those figures over every result it printed (a person's note handed to the run as it finished carries its loop on to another result). A result whose figures name more than 64 models (every result measured names one or none), or that writes them as anything but an object, null among it, is read for none of them, so the run is charged as on a release that states no such figures, never a sum that leaves calls out. Before 2.1.310, a continued run keeps the result the job before it left in the box (`base-result.json`, beside the run's other artefacts) and is charged its result less that one, where the release its script recorded (below) restores the totals. Before 2.1.277, and for a run that started a session in place of one its box could not give it, the result is the run's own.

The run's model and sign-in come from the `providers.llm` entry the launch picks: the first member of the seat's executor chain (its `llm`, else the company's fallback entry) whose harness has a runner and is not [sitting out](llm-backends.md). For this runner that is a Claude Code entry (`harness: claude-code`, or no `harness`). Its model goes to `--model` exactly as the entry's calls on the engine host pass it, an alias (`sonnet`) or an id, and the entry's `env` goes into the run environment, so an entry reaching its model through a gateway (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, and the `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` it takes) or a cloud provider (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` and its region) runs its executor the same way ([Credentials and the run environment](#credentials-and-the-run-environment)). A seat may sign Claude Code in itself in `role.sandbox.env` (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` for a Pro/Max plan, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, or a platform switch: `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK`, `_VERTEX`, `_FOUNDRY`, `_ANTHROPIC_AWS`, `_ANTHROPIC_GOOGLE_CLOUD`, `_MANTLE` or `_GATEWAY`); a variable it names there wins over the entry's.

**One entry, one runner.** An entry's model is written in its harness's grammar and its sign-in is that harness's, so a `claude-code` entry runs under Claude Code, a `codex` entry under Codex, a `gemini-cli` entry under Gemini CLI, a `qwen-code` entry under Qwen Code, an `opencode` entry under OpenCode, a `copilot` entry under Copilot, a `grok` entry under Grok Build, a `muse-code` entry under Muse Code, a `kimi-code` entry under Kimi Code, a `hermes` entry under Hermes Agent and a `pi` entry under Pi. There is no runner setting beside the entry: the runner *is* the entry's harness. A harness with no runner (`cursor-agent`, ...) cannot be an executor: a launch passes over it in the seat's chain, a seat whose chain has no member that can run is [refused on the write](#failure-modes), and a `run_in` on such an entry is refused. It still serves the seat's reviewer, workers and side passes (`llm_review`, `llm_subagent`, `llm_auxiliary`, `llm_judge`, `llm_triage`).

At launch the entry's environment is exported into the box:
- its whole `env` (a gateway's address and token, a cloud provider's switch and region, a proxy, and for `opencode`, which reads its model provider's key from its own environment, [that key](llm-backends.md#6-a-provider-key-in-env-opencode-hermes-pi));
- what signs that harness in: the headless subscription token (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, minted by `crewlet llm login <key> -capture-token`, so Claude Code there bills your Pro/Max plan with no API key anywhere), the key of an `auth.mode: api-key` entry, and the variables `inherit-env` forwards.

Each is a scoped, revocable variable, and none is required: a box in either cell is seeded with the entry's login itself (Claude Code's credential files, OpenCode's exported login) and writes a refreshed one back ([Local sandboxes](#local-sandboxes)), so a token or key is an alternative to the login.

#### A Claude Code run's session

**Where the session is kept is pinned.** After it unsets the variables above, and over whatever the seat's `role.sandbox.env`, the image or a login-shell profile set, the wrapper exports:
- `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` as the box home's `.claude` (the default, named explicitly; the login stays where a box is seeded with it and writes it back from, `.claude/.credentials.json`). Set, it also moves the harness's state file `.claude.json` from the home into `.claude/`, so the script links `.claude/.claude.json` to the home's own `~/.claude.json` before the harness starts, and the run reads and writes the file a person's session does, the home's user and local MCP servers with it (measured on 2.1.330, which creates the home's file through the link where there is none). A `.claude/.claude.json` the box already holds as a file of its own, as an image that sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` there writes it, is left and read instead.
- `CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME=crewlet`, so a transcript is `.claude/projects/crewlet/<session>.jsonl` whatever the box's working directory (a `direct` box's holds its own id; from 2.1.234).
- `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`, so no notes the harness wrote for itself ride a session into a later run unseen (the rule a call on the engine host keeps too, [LLM Backends](llm-backends.md#the-executors-run-in-a-box)).
- `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` as the context window of the model the run works under ([What a continued launch costs](#what-a-continued-launch-costs)), whatever the seat or image set.
- `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1`, so the release in a box never changes under a session it holds ([A relaunch continues the turn's session](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)).

It unsets `DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT` and `DISABLE_COMPACT` (either switches compaction off) and `CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE` and `CLAUDE_CODE_BLOCKING_LIMIT_OVERRIDE` (either moves the point it compacts at).

A repository's own Claude Code settings could set any of these again once the harness has started (Claude Code applies a settings file's `env` block to its own environment). So from 2.1.310 the run is started with its settings file's pinned copy (name ending `-pinned.json`), whose `env` block sets `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` to the same window, both overrides to nothing, the two switches a resume is started without (below) to nothing, and `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` to `1`; Claude Code applies it after the repository's. A managed settings file in the image or on the host still wins, as its operator's policy.

An agent definition's own `autoCompactWindow` (a repository's `.claude/agents/<name>.md`, say) can lower its subagent's window, from 2.1.312, never raise it; nothing caps the main conversation's. A repository can still switch compaction off (`autoCompactEnabled: false`, or `DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT` or `DISABLE_COMPACT` in its settings' `env`), and that run's requests then grow to its model's own window ([What a continued launch costs](#what-a-continued-launch-costs)).

The script turns `CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC` on from 2.1.304: a `-p` run then trims a transcript of 5 MiB or more that holds a compaction, after each compaction and once 20 MiB has been appended since its last trim, keeping only history from its last compaction on (which a resume restores either way), by writing a new file and renaming it over the transcript. It is unset on an older release, whose trim could lose messages.

**Every run names its session before the harness starts.** A run that starts one gets `--session-id` and a UUID the runner minted, which the launch records, so a run killed before its result line still names its session. A run that continues one (a relaunch, [below](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)) gets `--resume <id>`, never both (the harness refuses `--session-id` beside `--resume` unless forked), and **`--system-prompt-snapshot off`** from 2.1.267 (2.1.263 refuses the option). By default a conversation records the system prompt its first request rendered (the first launch's standing instructions and the box's report path among them) and every later request and resume sends that record until compaction, so a resumed run would be told what an earlier launch said.

The script continues the copy of the session the box **holds** (its transcript under any project directory of `.claude/projects`) unless an archive of it was carried in that the copy does not hold (below). Where the box holds none it restores the session carried in from another box. Where it can do neither it starts the session the runner minted, saying why on the run's error stream and in what the run reports back (asked to resume a session it does not hold, the harness would fail), and hands the harness the **fresh brief** the run carried beside its continuation, so a new session never answers a brief written for one that remembers. Before the harness starts, the script records the session it took up, whether it is the one asked for, why not where it could not, and the harness's `--version` (`session`, in the box's work directory), which the collection reports as what the run did.

**A resume leaves the session as it stands.** The script unsets `CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN` and `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_PRECOMPACT_SKIP` on every resume, whatever the seat's environment set. The first, set, has a resume rerun the turn its last process was cut off in before it reads the brief, repeating a call that may already have run (the brief tells the run to check instead). The second, set, has the resume of a transcript past 5 MiB read the whole file and prune it by a rule of its own, and the two readers can hand the model different records (read in 2.1.310 and 2.1.322). A repository's settings could switch either on again (Claude Code applies a settings file's `env` block before it resumes), so from 2.1.310 the pinned settings copy (above) sets both to nothing, which Claude Code reads as off. A managed settings file still wins and can switch either on.

A tool call the previous process died in is kept: 2.1.310's resume records an error result for it, saying its outcome is unknown and to check whether it took effect, then "No response requested.", before it reads the brief.

A transcript whose last line was cut (its harness killed mid-write, or a pack read it while the harness wrote: a line with no newline, which no JSON-lines reader can use and onto which the next record would be written, losing that too) is cut back to its last whole record before the harness resumes it. This covers **the session's transcript and every subagent's thread under its sidecar directory**, at any depth, since 2.1.310's resume takes a thread cut back so (measured: a subagent continued through its last whole call) and loses the record it next writes to one left torn. A file with no whole line at all is left as it is (the session's own transcript, or a subagent's thread a pack read as its subagent wrote its first record, which 2.1.310 answers with "no transcript found for the agent" whether it is a fragment, empty or removed, and the run goes on), so no record is ever written onto a fragment. A box without `find` cuts no thread and says so on the run's error stream.

**The session is packed when the harness exits.** After the harness exits, whatever its status, and before the done marker, the script packs the session into one gzipped tar, written in a staging directory and moved whole over `session-capture` in the box's work directory. It holds the transcript, its sidecar directory (`<session>/`: the subagents' transcripts and spilled tool results) and its task list (`.claude/tasks/<session>/`), each named relative to `.claude`. **Never** the login (`.credentials.json`) or the harness's state (`.claude.json`), never `file-history/` (the file-edit snapshots of the files a run edited, which carry the checkout rather than the conversation and are off), and nothing else under `.claude`. A box without `tar` and `gzip` packs nothing and its error stream says so; a harness that wrote no transcript has nothing to pack. The run's status is always the harness's own. The collection is told where the archive is, which session it holds, the release that wrote it and its size, and the runner streams it out of the box; the clear before the next run removes it. The box keeps the archive's digest (below).

**A run ends on request, and packs as its own end does.** Before anything else the script traps `SIGUSR1`, and only then records its pid in the box's work directory (`job-script`, as `1 <pid>`), so a request sent through that file always meets the handler. The harness runs in the background, waited for, since a shell runs no handler while waiting on a foreground command. The read that ends a stopped or lost run, or one its turn's wall-clock cap passed while it still worked ([Each launch's session, kept](#each-launchs-session-kept)), sends `SIGUSR1` to that pid alone (on a `direct` box only while it is a living process of the job's own recorded group, since the job runs as the engine's user and could write any of that user's pids there). The script then stops the harness (`SIGTERM`, then `SIGKILL` five seconds on), packs the session as above, records that the job was ended and how (`job-ended`: `asked`, `killed` past its grace, or `before` its harness started, when the request comes while the script is still setting up and no harness starts), and exits with the harness's status, which the wrapper writes beside the done marker as on every exit. A run ended so never reads as a success, and its failure says first that it was ended. A second request once the end is under way is ignored, and a pack killed part way leaves only its staging directory, never part of an archive. `SIGTERM` to the job's group is still a teardown's, which the script does not trap: it goes with its harness.

**A session packed in another box is restored before the harness resumes it.** A run handed one has the archive streamed into its box as it starts (after the previous run's artefacts are cleared), and its script unpacks it in a staging directory and moves only the transcript (a regular file), the sidecar directory and the task list (directories, never links) under `.claude/projects/crewlet` and `.claude/tasks`, the transcript last.

**A box that already holds the session is compared by id and by the archive's digest.** It keeps the POSIX `cksum` of every archive of a session it packed or restored, for as long as it lives (`session-digests`, in its work directory, which the clear before a run leaves).
- **A pack reports its archive made only once that digest is recorded**: written before the archive is moved to where it is read, and read back. A pack whose digest the box cannot keep (disk full, no `cksum` or `grep`) fails and moves nothing.
- **A restore is continued only once its digest is recorded**, written and read back. A run whose box cannot keep the line starts a session of its own and says why; otherwise an archive carried back in later would be restored over the copy that went on past it.
- A box's own copy is never overwritten with an archive it already holds: the copy is the archive's or newer, since a run went on in the box after it whose own capture may have failed.
- **Except a session its harness was cut off in**: an archive the engine packed rather than the script at its harness's clean exit replaces the copy whatever it holds, since the copy may end in a record its harness never finished, and the run that continues it is told what came after the archive ([below](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)).
- An archive its copy does not hold comes from a box the session went on in after this one's copy, and replaces it (the box's transcript, sidecars and task list removed once the archive is known to hold a transcript).
- A box that cannot take a digest keeps its copy, and continues nothing it restored where it holds none.

A box continues a carried session only where all hold:
- its Claude Code is **2.1.310 or later** (the first whose results state each run's own spend, and above every release a carried session needs: 2.1.304's trim, 2.1.267's snapshot option, 2.1.234's project directory, and the resume fixes between);
- the session was written by **2.1.300 or later**, from which a compaction's summary survives a resume, and the box's release is not older than the writer's;
- it is the harness that wrote it, in the archive format the runner restores.

The runner checks this before starting a run in a box, by reading the box's `claude --version` with one login-shell exec, its bin directory first on its PATH as the wrapper puts it; the script holds a restore to the box's floor too.

**The box's own retention sweep is held off.** Claude Code sweeps its configuration directory about five seconds into every run, print mode included, deleting what is older than its `cleanupPeriodDays` setting (thirty days by default) by each file's modification time: a transcript past it with its sidecar directory, a living transcript's spilled tool results one by one, and a task list whole. A restored session keeps the modification times it was packed with, and a session is as old as its conversation, which the engine continues for as long as its turns come within [`retention_days`](conversation-sessions.md#configuration) of each other. So at the default a continued conversation would lose its oldest tool results and task list five seconds into a turn (measured on 2.1.310: a resumed session's forty-day-old tool result and task list deleted without the setting, kept with it).

Every Claude Code run is therefore started with a settings file of its own, `claude-settings.json` in the box's work directory, written afresh at `0600` and named with `--settings` on every release (from 2.1.310 as its pinned copy, `claude-settings-pinned.json`, which adds [the pin of its compaction point and of what a resume loads](#a-claude-code-runs-session)). It holds `cleanupPeriodDays: 36500` and nothing else; a run that starts its [notes' hooks](#claude-codes-hooks) carries the same setting in the file that holds them. The value is a hundred years because nothing the engine keeps bounds how old a session can get and the harness takes no "never": `0` is refused, and in print mode a settings file the harness cannot validate is ignored without a word. Its cutoff falls in 1926, before any file a box holds, and is a real date (a cutoff past the date range made releases before 2.1.310 delete recent files). The box is disposable, and the session is the engine's to keep and delete ([Each launch's session, kept](#each-launchs-session-kept)).
### OpenCode

Drives **OpenCode 2.3.2**, the one release supported, its newest (the `@opencode/cli` package; `opencode --version` prints `opencode v2.3.2`): a box on an older 2.x is refused by name before anything runs (`this box runs OpenCode 2.3.0; the opencode runner supports OpenCode 2.3.2, its newest …`), and one on a newer release runs, its box's own copy continuing in place: a session carried in from another box starts fresh there, and a session it writes is neither counted nor continued in another box. 1.x (npm's `opencode-ai`) cannot run it, and a box with 1.x is refused by name before anything runs (`this box runs OpenCode 1.18.35; the opencode runner drives OpenCode 2 …`). A box with no `opencode` on its PATH says so and exits 127; one whose `opencode` fails `opencode --version` says that instead, with the exit status and what it printed, which is the run's transcript when nothing else was written. Install 2.3.2 in your box image. OpenCode is **provider-agnostic**: an `opencode` entry names `<provider>/<model>` for any provider OpenCode speaks to, a local server included, so a seat on one runs its executor on the same entry, model and key, with no extra secret.

**A run is a short script around a server of its own.** `opencode run` alone attaches to a shared *background service* that outlives the run and keeps the credentials of whichever run started it. With `--standalone` it sends the brief before the MCP servers have connected, and 2.0 fixes a step's tools as the step starts, so the first step got none of the seat's bridged tools. So the run:

1. refuses a 1.x box and settles the session the run works in ([below](#an-opencode-runs-session));
2. starts `opencode serve` on a loopback port of its own and waits, at most 60 s, until it has printed where it listens and the password it minted, naming whichever it never printed. The password is always the server's own: `opencode serve` takes one from `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` or `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` and then prints none, so the run unsets both first (a seat's `role.sandbox.env` may carry either). It hands the minted password to its own client calls as `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`. The server is started without it, so nothing the agent runs inherits it. OpenCode reaches loopback directly whatever the proxy variables say: 2.3.2 adds `127.0.0.1,localhost,::1` to both spellings of NO_PROXY as it starts (measured), so a bridge on loopback needs no entry of the run's. Through that server the run then removes every login the box's OpenCode database holds and imports the box's login if it was given one (below);
3. asks it (`opencode api mcp.list`) until every MCP server the run declares has left `pending`, at most 60 s (twice the 30 s OpenCode gives one server to list its tools); past that it starts without the straggler and says so on stderr. Servers are matched by name exactly as OpenCode spells it (`&`, `<`, `>`, U+2028 and U+2029 literal), so `R&D tools` is seen when it settles. OpenCode names a server's tool `<server>_<tool>`, writing every character but letters, digits, `_` and `-` as `_`, and keeps one tool per name, so a server the image's or the repository's own OpenCode configuration declares as `crewlet_x` or `crewlet.x` would take the names of the engine's own tools (its `y` is `crewlet_x_y`, as the engine's `x_y` is). A run whose server lists one ends here, before the brief, naming the server to rename; `crewlet-x` and `crewletx` keep names of their own;
4. runs the brief against that server **on stdin** (OpenCode re-quotes an argv prompt), under a **session it names**, with a title, which stops 2.0 making a second billed model call to write one;
5. prints the session's usage report, exports the session to be carried to another box, asks the session's message list for what its newest request carried and prints its pages after the report (never on an end request), writes the box's refreshed login back, and stops the server. The run's exit status stays the harness's own.

**A call to the run's own server writes its answer to a file**, read back from there: each such call is bounded (below) and runs in the background so an end request can stop it, which inside a command substitution it never would. So do the pages of the message list, each measured before it is printed, and the session's export ([below](#an-opencode-runs-session)). The calls before the server starts (its version, the restore's `session.get`, delete and import) are read through command substitution.

**A run ends on request as a Claude Code run does** ([above](#a-claude-code-runs-session)): the script traps `SIGUSR1` before it records its pid, and runs `opencode run` in the background. On the request it first **interrupts its session through its own server** (`opencode api session.interrupt`), which settles the step in flight (running tool call marked interrupted) so the step-5 export holds it. It then ends the run's client within the same five seconds and goes on to step 5. On 2.3.2 the client is gone within 0.2 s of the `SIGTERM` (measured), so the job's end is recorded as asked. Ending the client alone leaves the server working the step, its tool call running to the end (measured on 2.3.2), so an export taken then would hold nothing of it (2.x answers `session.abort` with "Operation not found"). A request before the server listens starts no server and no run; one while the run waits for its MCP servers starts no run.

**No call to its own server waits without a bound**; a silent server must not hold the run. Each call ends past its bound:

| Bound | Calls |
|---|---|
| 10 s | the readiness check, the usage, the leftover steers' inbox, the interrupt, the login's export |
| 30 s | the session's export, a page of its message list |

Each is five to fifteen times the slowest measured on OpenCode 2 with the box's two cores busy. The run then goes on as if the server were gone: the readiness check runs to its deadline, no usage line, no more steers cancelled once their one bound is spent, the session not exported (the engine packs it itself once the job is over, so a silent server costs the bound, never the session), the login kept as last exported. A call in flight when an end request comes is ended too, and none starts after. The calls on an end request's way out, each at its bound plus the grace, add up to 2 min 5 s, inside the 2 min 15 s the engine waits for an ended job. Each call is a process of its own that the script ends `SIGTERM` first and `SIGKILL` past the grace, and waits for.

The script is plain POSIX `sh`: dash (Debian, Ubuntu), bash in POSIX mode (Fedora, RHEL, Arch) and busybox ash (Alpine, which OpenCode 2's musl builds are for).

The run's `--model` is the `opencode` entry's model exactly as written (`anthropic/claude-sonnet-5`, `openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-5`). OpenCode splits it at the first slash into its own provider and a model, signed in by that provider's key from the entry's `env` or the seat's `role.sandbox.env`, or by the entry's login.

**A login follows a run into its box as OpenCode's own export.** OpenCode 2 keeps its logins in the database it keeps its sessions in, so the entry's login travels as the document `opencode auth export` printed ([LLM Backends](llm-backends.md#1-broker-the-vendors-own-login-any-harness)). A `direct` or `container` box is seeded with it at `~/.crewlet/exported-credentials`, and the run imports it through its own server, once it has removed every login the database held (an earlier run's import, or one stored since): a database that keeps one ends the run before its client starts, so only the login the box was handed signs the run in. Both go through the run's server, so no second OpenCode process opens the database beside it. A token OpenCode refreshes mid-run lives only in that database, and every teardown of a run in flight (a seat retired mid-run, a launch settled as failed after its job started, the pause reaper) kills the job's group outright (`SIGKILL`, or `docker rm -f` for a `container` box). Only a person's stop, a lost run's ending and the collection of a run its turn's cap passed while it still worked ask the script to end the run first (above). So the run **exports the database back over the document while it works**, through its own server every 30 s and once more when it ends (30 s is the window a kill can lose a refresh in: an OAuth token lives an hour or more, so under one refresh in a hundred falls inside it). A `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT` or `SIGHUP` to the run (a teardown's, never an end request's) ends its client and exports once more, exiting 143, 130 or 129, also under an engine started with nohup, since `crewlet run` doesn't hand a hangup it ignores on to the boxes it starts ([Force stop](agent-runtime.md#graceful-shutdown)). An export replaces the document only where it differs and holds a login (a whole, non-empty JSON array, never the `[]` a database that dropped its credential prints), and nothing is exported where the box was given none. The box's teardown then writes the document back to the shared login under the rule every box's login follows ([Local sandboxes](#local-sandboxes)), carrying only the logins the box was handed ([Token refresh across seats](llm-backends.md#token-refresh-across-seats)), whatever the box's database came to hold.

The runner **writes OpenCode 2's own configuration to `<home>/.crewlet/opencode.json`**, never in the checkout, and the script hands its content to the run's server alone as **`OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`**. OpenCode takes no config flag, and `OPENCODE_CONFIG` (a file's path) ranks *below* a repository's `opencode.json` and `.opencode/`, while `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` ranks above them. 2.x reads managed policies, well-known, global, `OPENCODE_CONFIG`, the project's `opencode.json`, its `.opencode/`, `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` and managed settings in that order, a later document winning. Measured on 2.3.2, a repository whose `opencode.json` and `.opencode/opencode.json` disable the bridge and deny every permission still got the bridge connected and the shell run. So **a repository's own `opencode.json` is not written to**: it stays and loads beneath the run's configuration, as Claude Code loads a repository's `.claude/settings.json` beneath `--settings`. Every server the run declares, and the run's agent, states `disabled: false`, so a document beneath cannot switch one off under the same name, and a `plugins` entry beneath removing one of the run's plugins (`-crewlet.steer`) leaves it loaded (measured on 2.3.2). The run's own client calls and a private process's export of the login are handed none of it, and a run whose configuration is missing is refused before its server starts. For a run wired to its turn's notes, the same file names the run's [notes plugin](#opencodes-notes-plugin) and the server alone is handed the run's session as `CREWLET_STEER_SESSION`.

**A run loads what a person's OpenCode session in the checkout loads**, beneath the run's configuration: the box home's global directory (`~/.config/opencode`: its configuration, plugins, agents, instructions and skills), the skills under `~/.agents/skills` and `~/.claude/skills`, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and what OpenCode's project walk reads from the checkout up through the home. Their MCP servers, plugins and instructions load beside the run's, since documents are layered key by key and lists of instructions and plugins added together (measured on 2.3.2: a server and a plugin each of the home's, the repository's and the run's all connected and loaded). The run's servers and agent state `disabled: false` under names of their own, so none of them can switch the run's off.

**OpenCode's server exports its traces and logs to the run's [telemetry endpoint](#credentials-and-the-run-environment)** wherever it is set (2.3.2), so its run is handed Crewlet's telemetry. The server hands a copy of its environment to each command its model runs, less what the tool-environment plugin removes (`OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`, `CREWLET_STEER_SESSION`), so the model's shell holds the run's telemetry endpoint, its token in the path, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL`, the empty `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` (the turn and the seat) and `TRACEPARENT`. The token admits writes to that run's trace alone and expires with the run.

It declares **no provider**: the model names one of OpenCode's own, which reads its key from the run environment under that provider's own variable, so a credential is never written where the agent could read it back, and a provider declared beside the named one would shadow it. The same file sets:

- `permissions`: allow every action and deny only `question`. Headless runs have no human to approve a prompt (a gate at `ask` is auto-rejected), and the one tool that asks a person is replaced by `ask_and_wait` on the run's bridge. Rules of every document are added together in order, so these come last and, the last match winning, decide among them; an agent's own rules, a repository's included, are read after them (measured on 2.3.2). So the run's agent's rules end allowing every tool of the run's own servers (`crewlet_*`): a home's or a repository's agent rules (`agents.build.permissions`, `.opencode/agents/build.md`) come before the run's document's, so their deny of the bridge's tools gives way, while a deny of a seat's other server's tools stands. Measured with a model that calls `crewlet_submit_work`: under a home's or a repository's agent deny without the run's allow, the bridge's tools left the request, the call was answered `No tool named "crewlet_submit_work" is currently available`, nothing reached the bridge, and the run exited 0; with it, the call reached the bridge in each case. On an entry that denies the web, `webfetch` and `websearch` are denied here and in the run's agent's rules, and their plugins removed ([above](#code-sandbox)).
- `share: disabled`.
- `update: disable`: a self-updating harness would swap the tool under the brief while the seat's turn is suspended.
- `snapshots: false`: a per-step git snapshot is an undo a headless run never offers.
- `compaction.background: false`: near its compaction point, 2.3.2 otherwise sends a second model request beside a step's, for a summary it keeps aside and writes nowhere the export holds, so its tokens would go uncounted. Off, none goes out (measured on 2.3.2).

Each MCP server is declared under `mcp.servers`. A remote one gets **`oauth: false`** (the bridge authenticates with the run's token and a headless run cannot complete an OAuth flow). Each of the bridge's gets **`timeout.execution`**, the longest the bridge can take to answer a call ([The tool bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box)), at which OpenCode cancels the call whatever progress flows (on 2.3.2, 3000 cut a 10-second call at 3.0 seconds with `notifications/cancelled`, measured with no progress flowing).
