It unsets `GROK_HOME`, `GROK_CONFIG` and `GROK_CONFIG_PATH`, which move the settings and sessions the runner writes, packs and restores, and `GROK_AUTO_PERMISSION_MODE` and `GROK_LEADER_SOCKET`, which change who decides a call and which process runs it. Every other variable reaches Grok as the box sets it, the compatibility switches and the routing variables (`GROK_XAI_API_BASE_URL`, `GROK_MODELS_BASE_URL`, `GROK_CODE_XAI_API_KEY`, `GROK_AUTH_PROVIDER_COMMAND`) among them.
- A run uses its own entry's endpoint: the base it is handed (`GROK_XAI_API_BASE_URL`) wins over the model cache an earlier run left in the home (`~/.grok/models_cache.json`, which records the base it was fetched from), and a run handed none sends nothing to an earlier run's (each measured on 1.0.92), so the cache stays as Grok keeps it.
- **A brief that begins with `/` is handed as words.** Grok runs a `--prompt-file` brief beginning with `/`, after any white space, as one of its own commands (`/session-info`, `/compact`), so the run writes the brief without its leading slashes and the space around them, as [Gemini CLI's](#gemini-cli) is.
- **The model's shell starts as a person's does**, its sign-in included: the run sets no shell policy. The run is handed none of [Crewlet's telemetry](#credentials-and-the-run-environment), since the engine reads no span of Grok's, and an operator's own exporter in `role.sandbox.env` reaches it untouched.
- A run ends on request as a Claude Code run does ([above](#a-claude-code-runs-session)); Grok exits 143 on `SIGTERM`, its session kept.

**A Grok run loads what a person's Grok loads.** Grok runs in the box home, so the home is also its working directory and its project root, and it loads from there and from `~/.grok` what it would for a person: instruction files, rules, skills, commands, agents, hooks, plugins, memory, a project's `.mcp.json`, and Claude Code's and Cursor's files under its default compatibility settings. The boundary is the box, a per-run sandbox destroyed after each run, never a list of what the run may load. The runner lays its own tables into the box's `~/.grok/config.toml`, every other key of the box's kept as written: the file as the box holds it is kept at `<home>/.crewlet/grok-config-box.toml` while the run runs and put back once Grok exits, so no run starts from an earlier run's tables, none of a run's bridge stays in the box's settings, and an edit to them between runs stands. A run cut off before Grok exits leaves its tables in the settings, and the next run's start in the box, whichever harness it drives, takes them out of the settings as they then stand: its servers by the names it recorded (a server of the box's by such a name given back) and the hooks running its note helper, every other key kept, an edit made since included. A box file that does not read as TOML refuses the run, naming it. The run's tables are the key 1.0.92 adds on a home's first call (`[marketplace] default_skills_installs_purged`, where the box set none), so no call rewrites the file, the note hooks (below), first in their events with the box's own after them, and each of the seat's MCP servers under a name of the run's own, its name, `_` and six hex digits new every run (`crewlet_<digits>`): a repository's `.grok/config.toml` naming a server replaces the home's of that name, so a fixed name could be taken. Each carries the bridge's bound as `tool_timeout_sec` (Grok's own is 6,000 seconds) and its headers as written. Grok offers no server's tool by name: its model reaches them through `search_tool` and `use_tool`, by `<server>__<tool>`, as the run's standing instructions say. A name with `__`, or one opening with neither a letter nor `_`, is refused at launch. The run's own skills replace an earlier run's (`~/.grok/skills/crewlet:*`); every other skill in the home stays.

**A guard keeps a policy from switching the run's server or hooks off unseen.** A policy file Grok reads, the home's `~/.grok/requirements.toml` among them, ranks above every settings layer and no layer releases it: a `denied_mcp_servers` entry matching the bridge's URL, or an `allowed_mcp_servers` list leaving it out, blocks the bridge, and `allow_managed_hooks_only` (`allowManagedHooksOnly`) skips the run's note hooks (measured on 1.0.92 with `grok inspect --json`). The run's servers carry a nonce, so `disabled_mcp_servers` cannot name them. So before Grok starts, the script asks `grok inspect --json`, in the run's directory and environment, what Grok would load, and refuses a run whose server Grok reports disabled, naming the file, the key and the policy's server entries, or, for a run with note hooks, one whose hooks the pin skips, naming the file that sets it. A policy blocking another server, or an inspection that fails, starts the run. **A hook switched off in `~/.grok/disabled-hooks` refuses the run too.** Grok skips each hook whose id that file holds on a line of its own (blanks and a carriage return trimmed; case, the event's spelling and the place must match), and every hook outside managed policy where the file is there but cannot be read (a directory, mode 000), each with no word, while `grok inspect --json` still lists the hooks (measured on 1.0.92). A run's hooks are `user:post_tool_use[0].hooks[0]`, `user:post_tool_use_failure[0].hooks[0]` and `user:stop[0].hooks[0]` (only the first for a run reporting skill loads alone), so the script reads that file before Grok starts and refuses a hooked run where a line names one of them, naming the file and the line, or where the file cannot be read. A line naming another hook, an empty file and a broken link (read as no file) start the run.

**The [standing instructions](#what-a-harness-is-told) are an agent file's body**, `<home>/.crewlet/grok-agent.md`, which Grok appends to the very end of its own system prompt between `<crewlet_seat_instructions>` bounds (its default agent's browser-verification block is the one part of its prompt an agent file leaves out). Grok resumes a session on the system message its record's first line holds, whatever the launch says, so a continuing run's script replaces what that line carries from the bounds on with this launch's text before Grok starts. A record that holds no bounds, or one the script cannot rewrite, would resume on an earlier launch's instructions, which name another run's servers, so the run starts a session of its own instead and says why.

**Notes reach the run through hooks in its settings** ([Notes to a running run](#notes-to-a-running-run)): `PostToolUse` and `PostToolUseFailure` after each call, and `Stop` at the finish, each running the engine's note helper once per firing (`<home>/.crewlet/grok-notehelper`), which reads the bridge's address and the run's token from `<home>/.crewlet/grok-take.json`, calls the bridge's `steer_take` and writes the answer on the hook's stdout. Grok fires the hooks in a subagent's session too, under the child's id (measured on 1.0.92); the helper takes, and reports a skill load, only in the run's own session, which the script names in `<home>/.crewlet/grok-thread` before Grok starts, so a note waits for the main agent's next call or its finish. Grok fires `Stop` once more as it exits (reason `shutdown`), with no request after it; that firing takes nothing. A step of several calls fires its hooks once per call: the first takes the notes waiting, and a later one only a note sent since, so each note is handed once. A hook gets ten seconds; one past them is killed and hands nothing over.

- **Where a note lands.** Grok adds every answer of a step's hooks after all of that step's results, as a system reminder headed `Context from PostToolUse hook`, and a `Stop` block as `Stop hook feedback`, after which the run goes on. The note ends with the take's token in square brackets, which the run is told is no part of it.
- **What one answer carries.** Grok hands its model the first 10,000 characters of a hook's answer and `… [+N chars]`, so an answer carries notes up to that, its token included.
- **The confirm is the record.** The session's `chat_history.jsonl` keeps each answer as Grok handed it: a take is confirmed where its token ends a reminder of the run's own hook (`user:post_tool_use[0]`, `user:post_tool_use_failure[0]`) or the stop hook's feedback, and a model's answer follows it. An automatic compaction rewrites the record, and a hook's words it summarized survive only inside the summary, a line of Grok's own (`compaction_meta`) that confirms nothing, so a note left only there is told again (measured on 1.0.92).
- **Skills.** The run's own [skills](#a-runs-own-skills) are written as `~/.grok/skills/crewlet:<name>/SKILL.md`, which Grok lists by its absolute path; the model reads one with `read_file`, and the `PostToolUse` hook reports a read that returned the file whole, as the runner wrote it, to the bridge's skill route: the text Grok returned must hash to the SHA-256 of the file written, which the hook's command line carries, so a missing file, a part of the file, or a file the model rewrote reports nothing. Only a file in the run's own skills directory, which the take config names, is a load: a checkout's `.grok/skills` is not.

**Its answer is the main agent's words of its last request since the run's brief that called no tool**, read off the main session's `chat_history.jsonl`, which the script adds to the run's stream after a mark once Grok exits: the stream's lines carry no agent, so a subagent's words can stand last there. A run that left no record is answered off the stream. **Its tokens** are every request's `usage` line: the prompt without its cached part, which is counted beside it, and the reply with its reasoning inside it. Grok's session-title request, which every run makes first, states no usage and is not charged. A refusal ends the run with an `error` line; a `402` (`status 402 Payment Required`) or a `429`, a rate limit or spent credits alike (`Some resource has been exhausted: …`), sits the entry out, and the API's refusal of a request past the model's context (`… maximum prompt length is …`) ends it as `context_exhausted`. The live view shows the model's words and each call by the tool its model named through `use_tool`, with its input.

**The turn cap is `--max-turns`**, past which a run emits `max_turns_reached`, ends `max_turn_requests` and exits 1, and reads as capped.

**The image.** A box needs Grok's binary on the login `PATH`, as [Bring your own image](#bring-your-own-image) lays out, from the image's own environment, `/etc/profile` or a home profile a setup step wrote. Each release is downloadable by its version from `https://x.ai/cli/grok-<version>-linux-<arch>` (`https://x.ai/cli/stable` names the newest); xAI publishes no checksum, so an image pins the ones taken of the release it was measured on:

```dockerfile
FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git ca-certificates curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
ARG GROK_VERSION=1.0.92
RUN set -eu; \
    case "$(dpkg --print-architecture)" in \
      amd64) a=x86_64; s=add4d201dbf2c0bd6077a36feb55a76939de30bae48dbb06f16b2307d38ceacb ;; \
      arm64) a=aarch64; s=8c74f1dc6cdc1befff6b9faada06bec4cf6759d04f2a60cdc28ece5ff696b44f ;; \
    esac; \
    curl -fsSL --retry 5 --retry-all-errors -o /usr/local/bin/grok "https://x.ai/cli/grok-${GROK_VERSION}-linux-${a}"; \
    echo "$s  /usr/local/bin/grok" | sha256sum -c -; chmod 0755 /usr/local/bin/grok
```

#### A Grok Build run's session

**Its session is a directory**, `~/.grok/sessions/<key>/<id>/`, under an id the runner mints and `-s` starts or `-r` resumes; `<key>` is the box home's path with every byte but a letter, a digit, `-`, `_`, `.` and `~` written `%XX`. Grok runs a session in the directory its key names and refuses one whose directory is gone, so a carried session is restored under this box's key. It is carried as **the session's directory**, `<key>/<id>/`, its `chat_history.jsonl` first and every other file under it, its `terminal/` call logs included, but Grok's `*.lock` files and any link, then likewise each subagent's session the main one's `updates.jsonl` names (`subagent_spawned`), under the key of the directory it was started in (the home's, or a `cwd` it was handed); a resume needs nothing outside it, and a restore puts the session and each subagent's filed beside it under this box's key, and any other under its own key. It is compared by digest with the box's copy, as Claude Code's is. A run ended mid-call resumes with that call unanswered. A save beside a running run is the same pack, held to the rule of a pack beside a working harness ([A running job's session, saved as it works](#a-running-jobs-session-saved-as-it-works)). A box continues a session, the copy it holds as much as a carried one, only where it and the session's writer both run exactly 1.0.92; any other pair starts a session of its own, saying which release it found.

**A subagent is a thread of its own.** A run's `spawn_subagent` starts a child session that Grok files beside the run's. In the foreground the child's lines sit inside the main agent's call, which speaks after it; in the background Grok keeps the process alive until the child ends, then runs one more main-agent turn on its notice ("While you were idle, 1 background subagent completed"), whose words are the run's last and its answer (measured on 1.0.92). The transcript reads each child's record as a thread named by its session; Grok's notice is never read as a brief, nor a child's words as the run's answer. The child's requests ride the run's one stream untagged and are charged with the run's, each counted among its turns, since a launch's calls are the provider calls its spend covers; Grok's own end total leaves a background child out and says so (`usage_is_incomplete`), so it is not read.

### Muse Code

Drives **Muse Code 1.4.25** (`muse --version` prints `Muse Code 1.4.25 (1.4.25-R9361.1)`), the release every behaviour below was measured on, against a stand-in model and bridge. A box with an older release is refused by name before anything runs; a box with a newer one, or one whose `--version` names no bare MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (a pre-release), runs, but starts a session of its own where it was asked to continue one, the box's own copy included, saying so. Muse Code is one static binary per platform, so the box needs nothing of its own beside it. A `muse-code` entry signs in with `META_API_KEY` (a metered Model API key, `auth.mode: api-key`) or with a `muse login`: a box is seeded with `~/.config/muse/auth.json` and the file is read back after the run ([LLM Backends](llm-backends.md#supported-harnesses)).

**A run is a short script around one `muse exec`**, the brief from a file:

```text
muse exec --json --yolo --session-id <id> --disable-reminders \
  --disable-request-user-input --allow-workspace-switch [--model <m>] [--reasoning-effort <e>] \
  [--max-model-steps <n>] -c telemetry.enabled=false --prompt-file <home>/.crewlet/brief.md
```

- `--yolo` turns approvals and the OS sandbox off and trusts the workspace for this run alone (nothing is saved). 1.4.25 loads no MCP server at all, the seat's bridge included, in a workspace it does not trust. A trusted run loads the repository's hooks (`.muse/hooks.json`), `.mcp.json`, `AGENTS.md` and skills, as the repository's own code runs in the box under the model anyway.
- `--disable-reminders` drops Muse's goal-reminder agents, model requests of their own; `--disable-request-user-input` holds that a headless run has no ask-the-user tool: it asks through the bridge's `ask_and_wait`.
- `--allow-workspace-switch` lets a session carried from another box resume in this box's checkout, wherever the box that wrote it had its own.
- The run pins `MUSE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1` and unsets `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `XDG_DATA_HOME`, which would move its settings, login and sessions away from the box home's, and `TBH_EVAL_APPEND_SYSTEM_PROMPT_FILE`, which would add a file to its system prompt.
- **The model's shell holds the run environment, `META_API_KEY` and an operator's own `OTEL_*` settings included.** Muse's shell inherits Muse's environment whole. A Muse Code run is handed none of [Crewlet's telemetry](#credentials-and-the-run-environment): its own trace export is off in a box. The bridge's token is in the box home's settings file, never a variable.
- A run ends on request as a Claude Code run does ([above](#a-claude-code-runs-session)); Muse answers `SIGTERM` by flushing its session, and exits 143.

**A run loads what a person's `muse exec` loads** from the box home and the workspace: the home's `~/.config/muse/settings.json` with its MCP servers, its personal `AGENTS.md`, the skills under `~/.agents/skills` and `~/.config/muse/skills`, its installed plugins with their skills and approved hooks, and another harness's personal rules and skills (a `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`). **The run's own settings go over the home's**: `telemetry` off for that run alone with `-c`, never written to the file (two runs without it opened 26 connections to Meta's service; none with it), and the [standing instructions](#what-a-harness-is-told) set as the home settings' `run.system_prompt_append`, after the home's own append where it has one, every other setting kept as the home has it. Muse adds them at the end of its own system prompt and reads them afresh on every resume; they are no `-c`, which would put them on the command line. The home's settings file is held first (`<home>/.crewlet/muse-home-settings.json`) and put back whole once the script ends, however it ends; a run killed first leaves the run's append in it, and the next run's start in the box, whichever harness it drives, puts the home's own append back (or removes it, where the home had none), every other key kept. A settings file that is no JSON object, or an append that is no string, is refused at the launch, naming it. The script then adds the seat's MCP servers to the home's settings with `muse mcp add-json`, beside the home's own, their names recorded in `<home>/.crewlet/muse-servers-added`, and takes them out with `muse mcp remove` once Muse exits; a run killed first leaves them, and the next run's start in the box, whichever harness it drives, takes them out of the settings by those names, every other entry kept, so no run's bridge token stays in the home's file. It adds them after the notes plugin is approved, because an approval rewrites the settings and drops every server's `required` and `tool_timeout_sec`, the home's own included (measured on 1.4.25). Each is added under a name of the run's own, its name and six hex digits new every run (`crewlet-<digits>`), so the model is offered the bridge's tools as `mcp__crewlet_<digits>__<tool>` and no server a repository declares takes the place of one of the run's by its name. Muse shows the model a server's name as written up to 26 characters, so a seat's MCP server named in up to 19 keeps its name; a longer one runs as well, and Muse shows the model a hash of its name in its place. Every server is `required`, so one that cannot be reached fails the run before its first model request (`Required MCP server ... failed during startup`, exit 1), where a server not required is left out silently; each carries the bridge's own bound as `tool_timeout_sec` (Muse's own is 300 seconds), and its headers as written, so the agent can read the bridge's token in the file, as it can in Claude Code's. Muse refuses more than 65,536 bytes of `run.system_prompt_append`, so a run whose standing instructions, with the home's own append, are longer is refused at its launch, naming the setting. Calls carry `_meta.idempotencyKey`, one at a time.

**A home or a repository cannot switch the bridge off unseen.** Muse 1.4.25 leaves out every MCP server, the bridge included, saying nothing and exiting 0, where one entry under `mcpServers` in a file it reads them from is one it does not take, or the file is no JSON object or its `mcpServers` none: each `.mcp.json` from the repository's root down to the start directory, and the home's `settings.json`, where `mcp_servers` beside `mcpServers` does the same. Among 64 configurations measured, an entry it does not take is one whose `type` is other than `stdio`, `http` or `streamable-http`, an http server with no `url` (or an empty one), a server with no `command`, with both a `command` and a `url`, or with `args` on an http server, a field of the wrong kind (`args`, `env`, `headers`, `url`, `enabled`), or a `${VAR}` it cannot expand in an `env` value or a `url`; an `enabled: false` entry is still checked for its `type`. Its rules are its own, and it records no such fault. What it records is each model request's tools (the session's `model_request_configured` record), the bridge's `mcp__<name>__<tool>` among them only where it loaded it. So the script watches the session's record, and a run whose own first model request, the first written after the run started, offers no tool of its own server, under the name this run added it by, is ended there, failing with the files it reads its servers from that the box holds, and what `muse mcp list` says of the home's. A run that continues a session is judged on its own request alone: an earlier run's offer of the same server does not count, and its tool catalog, which Muse writes again only where the servers' names changed, is not read. A repository's own servers that Muse takes load beside the bridge.

**Notes reach the run through a plugin of its own** ([Notes to a running run](#notes-to-a-running-run)), `crewlet-notes`, which the script installs and approves at each launch, after removing an earlier run's: three PostToolUse hooks between the run's steps and a Stop hook at its finish. Each runs the engine's note helper once per firing (`<home>/.crewlet/muse-notehelper`, a static build written into the box at each launch, no image prerequisite), which reads the bridge's address and the run's token from `<home>/.crewlet/muse-take.json` (a hook's environment is `HOME`, `PATH` and `MUSE_*` alone), calls the bridge's `steer_take`, and writes the answer on the hook's stdout and the take's token on its stderr. A subagent's firing takes nothing.

- **Where a note lands.** A PostToolUse hook's context is a developer message after all of a step's tool results, kept in the session's history; the Stop hook blocks the finish with the note as its reason, which Muse puts in the leading developer instructions and continues the turn. A resumed session does not restore that, so a note taken at the finish is told again to a run that continues the session.
- **One item a hook.** Muse reads at most 16,384 bytes of a hook's stdout, raw UTF-8: one item of the engine's widest (4,505 UTF-16 units) fits with room to spare, two would not. So each PostToolUse hook answers one item and a step hands over up to three, while every runner's item bounds stay as they are.
- **The confirm is the hook's receipt.** The session's record keeps each hook run whole, its stderr included, which the model never sees, and the digest of the plugin package it ran from. A take is confirmed where its token is on the stderr of one of the plugin's hooks whose answer Muse took (`completed` with the effect `context`, or `blocked` at the finish), run from the package the script installed (the `package_sha256` its install reported), then that run's own context block is committed (`hook:post_tool_use:<call>:<n>`, the n-th answer to that call's hooks, or `hook:stop:stop:<n>`), then a request of the main session completes; a failed request confirms nothing. A compaction installed in between, or for the finish's a restart of the session, leaves it unconfirmed. A hook killed or timed out records no effect and no block, so its take is told again. Only the plugin's own hooks count: a repository's hook is recorded under its own file's path, and a plugin of the same name and other content records another digest.
- **Skills.** The run's own [skills](#a-runs-own-skills) are written as `~/.agents/skills/crewlet:<name>/SKILL.md`, beside the home's own, after an earlier run's `crewlet:*` are removed; Muse catalogues each under that name, and the first PostToolUse hook reports each `read_skill` load to the bridge's skill route.

**Its answer is the last `run.terminal.completed` text.** One exec may hold several runs: once a subagent's result arrives after a run ended, Muse starts another on its own. **Its tokens** are every `run.usage` of the exec (the prompt whole, its cached share inside it) and its subagents' requests: `run.usage` counts the main thread alone and the stream carries nothing of a subagent, so once Muse exits the script appends a `crewlet.child_usage` line and every `model_completed` record this process added to the session's `subagent/*/session.jsonl`. No price is reported. A failed `run.terminal.failed` whose reason names `rate_limit_error` or `billing_error` sits the entry out; a subscription's allowance (`run.usage.allowance`) was not measured. The live view shows the main thread's model words, each tool by name and its outcome: the stream carries no call's arguments and nothing of a subagent.

**The turn cap is `--max-model-steps`**, past which a run fails "model did not reach a terminal state within N step(s)" and reads as capped. It caps each of the exec's runs apart, so the script names the cap in the stream and the exec as a whole fails, saying the cap was not enforced, where its runs made more model requests than the cap between them.

**The image.** A box needs Muse Code's binary on the login `PATH`, as [Bring your own image](#bring-your-own-image) lays out; Meta's launcher script is not needed (it re-checks for updates and needs `bash`). Each release is downloadable by its version from Meta's release manifest (`https://lookaside.facebook.com/lookaside/muse/download/?channel=muse&version=<version>&file=manifest.json`, each platform's `url`, `size` and `sha256`), so an image pins one. At about 450 MB the binary belongs in the image rather than a setup step, which would download it into every new box:

```dockerfile
FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git ca-certificates curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
ARG MUSE_VERSION=1.4.25-R9361.1
RUN set -eu; \
    case "$(dpkg --print-architecture)" in \
      amd64) f=muse-x86-linux; s=c1b728fb9732503c5e1869e3ad2f2c9bdb5b2638fb4cf398d6e2c46aa6d8f94a ;; \
      arm64) f=muse-aarch64-linux; s=8fe089115ef137879fca46986d55edf18d5d3ab9cfdb6441c67e9d1807b4108a ;; \
    esac; \
    curl -fsSL --retry 5 --retry-all-errors -o /usr/local/bin/muse \
      "https://lookaside.facebook.com/lookaside/muse/download/?channel=muse&version=${MUSE_VERSION}&file=${f}"; \
    echo "$s  /usr/local/bin/muse" | sha256sum -c -; chmod 0755 /usr/local/bin/muse
```

The two checksums are 1.4.25-R9361.1's, from its manifest; a later release takes its own from that release's manifest.

#### A Muse Code run's session

**Its session is a directory**, `~/.local/share/muse/sessions/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/<id>/`, under an id the runner mints and `--session-id` starts or resumes. It is carried as **its `session.jsonl`, its subagents' records (`subagent/`) and its tool outputs (`tool-outputs/`)**, named from the day's directory down: a resume takes the conversation up whole from them, from any home and checkout, and Muse writes the rest again. Never `cron.db`, a binary file the archive's text scrub could not pass whole. A carried session is restored under the day it was filed at, so the paths its record names of its own tool outputs still hold, with every other copy of it in the box removed first; it is compared by digest with the box's copy, as Claude Code's is. A torn last line, or a lock a killed run left, resumes as it is, and a call in flight when the run was killed is answered as one whose outcome is unknown. A save beside a running run is the same pack, held to the rule of a pack beside a working harness ([A running job's session, saved as it works](#a-running-jobs-session-saved-as-it-works)); a copy made mid-call resumes whole. A box continues a carried session only where it and the session's writer both run exactly 1.4.25; any other pair starts a session of its own, naming both releases.

### Kimi Code

Drives **Kimi Code CLI 2.7.2**, Moonshot's own (`@moonshot-ai/kimi-code`; `kimi --version` prints `2.7.2`), the one release Crewlet supports and every behaviour below was measured on. A box with an older release is refused by name before anything runs; a newer one runs, in sessions of its own alone. The run drives `kimi web` and its API (KAP): print mode (`kimi -p`) takes no note, as it discards `PostToolUse`'s output and drops a `Stop` hook's continuation (measured). Kimi Code is an npm package, so the box needs `node` (22.19 or newer, Kimi's own floor) and `git` beside it; a box with no `node` is refused by name. A `kimi-code` entry signs in with a metered key (`KIMI_MODEL_API_KEY`, its model then the env model's `KIMI_MODEL_NAME`, which the run pins), or with a login, its model then an alias of `config.toml`'s, named in the session.

**Its box image** carries Kimi Code 2.7.2 and the `node` it runs on, as crewlet-operator's `images/kimi-code` recipe builds them: a build stage fetches Node.js 22.23.5, the tree's floor Node (`scripts/node-pin.env`), and checks its SHA-256; installs a `package-lock.json` that pins `@moonshot-ai/kimi-code` 2.7.2 and every dependency by its integrity with `npm ci --omit=optional --ignore-scripts` (the optional clipboard addon is unused headless, and the package's install script only migrates an older Python `kimi`); and copies `node` and the package tree into the image, `node` and `kimi` in `/usr/local/bin`, where a login shell finds them. `npm install -g` would float the dependencies the lock pins. A `container` box's own image takes the same steps ([Bring your own image](#bring-your-own-image)).

**A run is a short script around a driver of the engine's**, `<home>/.crewlet/kimi-driver.mjs`, plain JavaScript embedded in the engine that runs on the box's `node` and installs nothing. The driver, the brief on its stdin:

1. starts `kimi web --port 0 --json` and reads its one line (origin, token; the server binds 127.0.0.1) within 60 s, naming what it never printed;
2. holds the run's own MCP servers to the home's `mcp.json` (the guard, below);
3. creates the session (`POST /api/v1/sessions`, `permission_mode: auto`, the run's own agent profile, the login's model, the entry's effort as `thinking`);
4. reports the session's id once, before anything is posted ([Kimi names its session](#a-kimi-code-runs-session));
5. subscribes to the session's events and writes them to the run's stream, a line each, for the [live view](#watching-a-run-live);
6. posts the brief in a request body (`POST …/prompts`), so no argv or process table holds it;
7. waits with `:wait` until the session is idle **and holds no active or queued prompt**: between the turn a note was steered into and the turn it opens, the session reads idle for an instant, and a run ended there cancelled the note's turn (measured);
8. polls the notes route while the session works and steers each note (below); and
9. stops the server (`POST /api/v1/shutdown`, then a signal) and writes its own last line.

Every call to the server is bounded (a wait 75 s around KAP's own 60, every other 30 s), and an approval or question the session waits on is answered (approved, dismissed): a headless run has nobody to answer, and [`ask_and_wait`](#mid-run-clarification-ask_and_wait) is on the bridge. **A run ends on request** as a Claude Code run does ([above](#a-claude-code-runs-session)): `SIGTERM` reaches the driver, which cancels the turn (`:cancel`), stops the server within the grace and exits 143; a server that outlived its driver is ended by the script.

- **Standing instructions** go in an agent profile, `$KIMI_CODE_HOME/agents/crewlet/crewlet-<12 hex>.md`, its body `${base_prompt}` then the run's text, so they are **appended** to Kimi's own prompt. The name is the run's own: a repository's `.kimi-code/agents/<name>.md` of the same name shadows the home's even in an untrusted workspace (measured), and a repository cannot guess it. Kimi substitutes its template variables across the whole body with no escape, so a `${cwd}` in a seat's prompt reaches the model as the run's directory. The profile's allowlist is every default tool of 2.7.2 but `AskUserQuestion` and `ExitPlanMode`, with `WebSearch` (a login's search service registers it) and every MCP server's tools (`mcp__*`), the run's, the home's and the repository's alike; a tool a later release adds is left out until it is listed.
- **The bridge** goes in the home's `mcp.json`, beside the home's own servers (one of the home's by the bridge's name gives way), with its bearer header, `toolTimeoutMs` at the bridge's own bound (a call is cancelled at it with `notifications/cancelled`), `startupTimeoutMs` at Kimi's own default of 30 s, and `deferred: false`, so its tools are on every request. Calls carry no id and no progress token, so a call's response is silent until its answer, and Node's fetch drops it at 300 seconds whatever `toolTimeoutMs` says, then Kimi sends the call again: the runner states that ceiling, so the bridge parks the run on a call still running at 270 seconds, and a call sent again joins the one still running ([The tool bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box)). The home's own `mcp.json` is held in the run's work directory meanwhile and put back once Kimi has stopped; a home file that holds no JSON object refuses the run by name, as Kimi would. A run cut off before that leaves its servers in the home's file, and the next run's start in the box, whichever harness it drives, takes them out by the names the cut-off run recorded, giving back any of the home's own they had displaced and keeping every other entry as the file then stands, an edit made since included; once that run ends no run's server or token is left in the file.
- The run pins `KIMI_CODE_HOME` to the box home's `.kimi-code`, `KIMI_CODE_TRUST_WORKSPACE=1`, `KIMI_CODE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1`, `KIMI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` and `KIMI_LOOP_MAX_ATTEMPTS_PER_STEP=3` (ten held a 429 some two and a half minutes). It removes `KIMI_CODE_INFINITE_RETRY`, the variables that change who may reach the run's server (`KIMI_CODE_PASSWORD`, `KIMI_CODE_DISABLE_HOST_CHECK`, `KIMI_CODE_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `KIMI_CODE_CORS_ORIGINS`, `KIMI_CODE_REMOTE_CONTROL_RELAY_URL`), and `KIMI_MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT_MS`, whatever set them, and is handed none of [Crewlet's telemetry](#credentials-and-the-run-environment) (Kimi exports none); and every `KIMI_MODEL_*`, API or OAuth host and header variable, and `KIMI_WEB_SEARCH_*` and `KIMI_WEB_FETCH_*` (the web tools' services), the entry's own `env` does not set, since one from the image would swap the run's model, provider or services. A metered key signs Kimi in through its environment, and an entry's own web search or fetch key (`KIMI_WEB_SEARCH_API_KEY`, `KIMI_WEB_FETCH_API_KEY`) reaches Kimi the same way.

**The workspace is trusted, and the run loads what a person's session loads.** Trusted, Kimi loads a repository's MCP servers (its git root's `.mcp.json` and the start directory's `.kimi-code/mcp.json`), permission rules (`.kimi-code/local.toml`) and added directories, beside its `AGENTS.md` and skills, which load either way; from the home it loads the skills under `~/.kimi-code/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`, the personal `AGENTS.md` in `~/.kimi-code` and `~/.agents`, `config.toml`'s hooks and settings, and every installed plugin (measured on 2.7.2). Nothing of these is cleared or rewritten: the clear before a run removes only the run's own profile, driver and settings, and a seat's or a box's `config.toml` is the login's copy as it stands. A repository adds no hook: Kimi reads hooks from the home's `config.toml` and its plugins alone.

**A guard keeps a repository from displacing the run's own servers.** Kimi layers a repository's MCP files over the home's, a server of the same name replacing the home's, and a file it cannot read leaves no server loaded at all; it decides every deny rule before any allow, whatever its layer. It has no layer above the repository's that a run could write. So before the session is made the driver asks Kimi where each server it loads for the start directory comes from (`GET /api/v1/mcp/servers`), and **refuses the run** where one of the run's servers is a repository's or Kimi cannot load them, naming the file; and while the run works, **a call of one of its own tools that Kimi denies by a permission rule ends the run**, its turn cancelled, naming the rule's message (all measured on 2.7.2).

**Guards also cover the home's `config.toml` and plugins** (Kimi Code 2.7.2 reads `[tools]`, `[mcp]` and hooks from them, never from a repository). Each guarded key fails the run with the file and the entry, as Kimi lists them (`GET /api/v1/config`, and each plugin's manifest from `GET /api/v1/plugins/{id}`); an entry that names another server, tool or prompt, or a hook that lets the call run, leaves the run alone:

- `[tools] disabled` matching one of the run's own tools, or a non-empty `[tools] enabled` leaving one out: Kimi lists the tool inactive for the session (`GET /api/v1/tools`), and the run is refused before the brief.
- A `PreToolUse` hook, in `config.toml`'s `[[hooks]]` or a plugin's, that blocks a call of one of the run's own tools: Kimi ends the call without running it (an executed call's item is updated with its `fields` first, a vetoed one's never is), and the run ends naming each `PreToolUse` hook whose matcher matches the tool.
- A `UserPromptSubmit` hook that blocks the brief or a note: Kimi's record of the main agent's turns holds the prompt's turn ended `blocked` before any step, and the run ends as the session goes idle, naming each such hook whose matcher matches the prompt.

**A layer the run writes undoes one key:** a home's `[mcp] startup_timeout_ms`, or `KIMI_MCP_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS`, gives way to the run's own servers' `startupTimeoutMs`, which Kimi reads first (measured: 1 ms in the home's `config.toml` or in the run's environment left the run without its tools; the run's own 30000 restored them in both).

**Notes are steered into the session.** While the session works, the driver polls the notes route and posts each note to `/steer` under a prompt_id of its inbox id (`crewlet-note-<inbox>`), which KAP keeps as the message's id and answers with the prompt it already holds when it is reused, so a note admitted twice lands once. Sent while a tool runs, the note opens a turn of its own right after that tool's result; sent while the model is answering, it **cuts that request short** (its step ends `interrupted`, with no usage recorded) and the next request carries it; sent at idle, it starts a turn, so as the session goes idle the route is asked once more and a waiting note keeps the run going (all measured). The driver can read the route's URL and its token in its settings, as OpenCode's plugin can. **A note is confirmed only off the session's own record**, the main agent's `wire.jsonl`, never the driver's word: its `context.append_message` (a user message under its prompt_id), then a `usage.record` of `usageScope: turn` — a request of the agent's loop answered — with no `context.apply_compaction`, `context.undo` or `context.clear` between. The line is on disk before the request that carries it; a run killed between the two holds the line and no record, and its note is not confirmed. A compaction between them read the note in its own request (`usageScope: session`) and kept it verbatim, but its record (`keptUserMessageCount`) names no message, so a request past it may have carried the note only inside its summary ([ADR-0177](../../adr/0177-an-in-box-runners-note-take-meets-one-contract.md)): such a note is not confirmed, and is told again. A note's ceiling is the engine's item bound, 4,505 UTF-16 units; Kimi carried notes of 4,505, 20,000 and 100,000 units whole (measured).

**The turn cap is each turn's** (`KIMI_LOOP_MAX_STEPS_PER_TURN`, a model request a step): a turn past it ends on `loop.max_steps_exceeded`, which reads as the cap. A note opens a turn of its own, which the cap holds afresh, as OpenCode's `steps` holds each of its prompts.

**Its answer is the last assistant message's text**, off the session's events. **Its tokens are its own session's records**: once the driver exits, the script appends a `crewlet.usage` line and every `usage.record` and `turn.ended` of every agent's `wire.jsonl` in the session it reported, the main agent's requests, its compactions' and each subagent's (KAP's turns leave a subagent's out, measured). The run is charged their sum, the prompt not served from the cache beside the cache's reads and writes, and **no price**: Kimi states none. **Its window** is the model alias's `maxContextSize`, as the session's `context` events state it (262,144 for the env model unless `KIMI_MODEL_MAX_CONTEXT_SIZE` sets it). A turn ending on `provider.rate_limit` sits the entry out, read off the record's own `turn.ended` line as the text phases read it ([LLM Backends](llm-backends.md)); a provider's "exceeded model token limit" ends the turn on `compaction.failed` with `APIContextOverflowError`'s words, which reads as the context exhausted.

#### A Kimi Code run's session

**Kimi names its session as it creates it** (`session_<uuid>`; neither the CLI nor KAP takes one from a caller), so a fresh run's start names no session, and the driver reports the id KAP's create answered with to `<home>/.crewlet/session-report`, written beside and moved over it, before the brief, and the engine binds it ([A session its harness names as it runs](#a-session-its-harness-names-as-it-runs)): a run killed earlier is sessionless. A run that continues a session reports nothing, as it works in exactly the session it was started on. The session is `$KIMI_CODE_HOME/sessions/wd_<directory>_<hash>/session_<uuid>/`, its record `agents/<agent>/wire.jsonl`, one file an agent.

**It is carried as its `state.json`, `agents/` and `notify/`**, packed relative to the sessions directory once the driver exits; never `logs/`, and nothing outside the session (`credentials/`, `config.toml` and `device_id` stay in the box). A run that continues a session takes the box's own copy, or a carried archive where the box holds none or one the archive goes past, as a Claude Code run does ([above](#a-claude-code-runs-session)); an archive holding a link anywhere is not restored. **Kimi runs a continued session in the cwd its `state.json` names**, and a box's path differs from the one it was written in, so before the run the driver files the session under the run's own directory, as Kimi files one it creates there (`wd_<name>_<12 hex of the path's SHA-256>`), and writes the run's cwd into its `state.json` (measured: unfiled, a resumed tool ran in the writer's directory). A session neither held nor restored nor filed is **not continued**: the run starts a session of its own and its error stream says why. **A session is continued only from 2.7.2 to 2.7.2**: a box or a writer on any other release, or one whose release cannot be read, starts a session of its own, saying so and naming 2.7.2.

**Its standing instructions are renewed on a resume.** Kimi renders the system prompt once, as it creates a session, and restores that rendering on a resume (`profile.bind` in the record; a profile changed in place is refused, measured). The driver creates a throwaway session with the run's profile in the run's directory, appends its `profile.bind` to the continued session's record and deletes the throwaway: the resume renders from the record's last bind, the run's own instructions and directory (measured).

A continued run is charged its own records alone: before its driver starts, the script counts each agent's record's lines, and reads past them once it exits.

**Gaps against Claude Code:**

- A repository's server by one of the run's own servers' names, an MCP file Kimi cannot read, or a rule denying the run's own tools fails the run: Kimi has no layer above the repository's that would keep the run's servers. So does a home's `[tools]` list leaving the run's tools inactive, or a hook blocking the run's tools, brief or notes.
- No event after a batch of tool calls: a note reaches the model after the result of the tool that was running when it came, and a note that arrives while the model answers cuts that request short.
- The turn cap is each turn's, and a note opens a turn.
- No price: the record has tokens alone.

**Not measured against Moonshot's service** (measured against a stand-in model through `KIMI_MODEL_*`; each value below is the one that holds whatever the service says):

- Real models calling the bridge's tools: the calls were a stand-in model's.
- A real 2.7.2 plan limit: the `provider.rate_limit` turn end is the stand-in's 429; the service's own words are kept in the line shown.
- A copied OAuth login refreshing in a box: the box's copy is written back as every box's login is.
- The managed models' windows: the run reads whatever the session states.

### Hermes Agent

Drives Nous Research's **Hermes Agent 0.23.3** (`hermes --version` prints `Hermes Agent v0.23.3 (…)`), the one release Crewlet supports and every behaviour below was measured on. A box with an older release, or one whose `--version` names no bare MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, is refused by name before anything is written into its Hermes home; a newer one runs, in sessions of its own alone. `crewlet llm doctor` holds a `direct` cell's `hermes` to the same release and checks `hermes chat --help`.

**The box image.** Hermes is a Python application with its own interpreter and virtual environment, and PyPI's `hermes-agent` is not current. Nous Research's `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v0.23.3` image installs it as root under `/opt/hermes`, out of the box user's reach, and runs offline, on a read-only root, as any user with a home of its own (measured); crewlet-operator's `images/hermes` recipe copies that install, with the links to its bundled runtimes in `/usr/local/bin`, into the engine image. Hermes's own `scripts/install.sh` serves only the account that ran it: run under another account's home, the first launch prepares that home's own dependency environment, about 490 MB fetched from the network, and fails offline or on a read-only install (measured). Neither puts a `python3` on `PATH`, so whatever the runner runs in Python runs under Hermes's own interpreter, through its launcher's `hermes --run-module`.

**A run is a short script around Hermes's own client.** The run:

1. refuses a release below 0.23.3, then installs the runner's plugin and the run's skills into the Hermes home and settles the session it works in;
2. stops any gateway an earlier run left in the home, so the run's own starts with the run's environment;
3. runs `hermes chat --query-file <brief> --format stream-json -c <session> [--create-if-missing] [--max-turns N] [-m <model>] [--reasoning <effort>]` under the end protocol, the brief kept in `<home>/.crewlet/hermes-brief.md` and its stream on stdout;
4. once the client exits, stops the gateway, appends the plugin's record of each response to its stream, packs the session to be carried, and exits with the client's status.

**Every turn runs in a gateway** Hermes starts per home in a session of its own (`hermes gateway run --idle-exit`), which outlives the client: killing the client mid-turn left the turn and its tool running in it, and `hermes gateway stop` refuses while a turn is live (measured). So the script stops the gateway itself at the run's end, on its exit however it ends, and **first** on an end request, before the client: `SIGTERM` to the gateway's process group (the pid in `gateway.pid`, checked against the start time it records), which interrupts the turn, ends its tools and closes the session store (at most 5.5 s measured, on a 2-core box with three busy processes a core), and `SIGKILL` after 10 s. A gateway killed outright leaves its turn unsettled, and Hermes then refuses the next resume until the lost turn is discarded: the script runs `hermes sessions discard <id> --yes` once and sends the brief again, since Hermes had not sent it.

**A run loads what a person's Hermes loads.** It is pinned to `HERMES_HOME=<home>/.hermes`, Hermes's own default, and nothing in the home or the working directory is removed or rewritten. Hermes reads, measured and read off 0.23.3's source:

- from its home: `config.yaml`, `.env` (loaded into the environment, so the model's shell sees it), `SOUL.md`, `memories/`, `skills/` (with the bundled skills it syncs there), `plugins/` (each one `plugins.enabled` names), `hooks/`, `cron/` (whose ticker runs in the gateway), `kanban.db` and `bin/` (its managed `uv`, appended to the tool shell's `PATH`);
- from the working directory: `AGENTS.override.md`, `AGENTS.md` or `agents.md` (each directory from the repository root down, the working directory alone outside one), the nearest `.hermes.md` or `HERMES.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursorrules` and `.cursor/rules/*.mdc`, `./.hermes/skills` (in a trusted root) and `./.hermes/plugins` (with `HERMES_ENABLE_PROJECT_PLUGINS`);
- from a checkout below the working directory (one `code_checkout` places, say): the first of `AGENTS.override.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `agents.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `claude.md` and `.cursorrules` in each directory the model touches through a tool's path or a command, and in each between it and the working directory, added to the tool result that first touches it (its subdirectory hints, measured); none of a checkout's `.hermes.md`, `.cursor` rules, skills, plugins or configuration, which Hermes reads from the working directory alone. So the runner hands a checkout nothing;
- its launcher's bytecode cache, `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/hermes-pycache`, which Hermes's own processes load from;
- for the tool shell, a login shell's `/etc/profile`, `~/.profile`, `~/.bash_profile` and `~/.bashrc`, with Hermes's own runtimes appended after the system directories.

**The run's own settings ride an overlay**, never the box's configuration: `HERMES_MANAGED_DIR=<home>/.crewlet/hermes-managed`, whose `config.yaml` Hermes merges over the box's per leaf (its other MCP servers stay). That variable hides the box's own managed scope (`/etc/hermes`: an administrator's `config.yaml` and `.env`), so the script writes the overlay over that scope, read through Hermes's own loader, and copies its `.env` beside it (both mode `0600`). The overlay names the run's MCP servers (the bridge with its bearer header, written as a literal and never in argv or an environment; a value holding `${` is refused, since Hermes would expand it) and, for an entry that denies web tools, `agent.disabled_toolsets`: the box's own list (its configuration under its managed scope) and then `web`, `browser` and `x_search`, since a list is one leaf. Measured, the request then offers none of the box's disabled tools and no `web_search`, `web_extract` or `browser_*` tool, on a session created allowing them too. Otherwise the run offers Hermes's own default toolsets, `browser` among them, which installs a browser on first use.

**Hermes's tool search is off** (`tools.tool_search.enabled: off`): it defers every MCP server's tools and exempts none by server (0.23.3), and the bridge's own server is always loaded. Measured, the request then offers the bridge's tools directly, beside every other tool; with it on, it offers `tool_search`, `tool_call` and `tool_describe` and no MCP tool at all. So on Hermes Agent 0.23.3 the box's own MCP servers are offered on every request too: the bridge's tools must be, and that release has no way to exempt one server.

**The runner's plugin** (`<home>/.hermes/plugins/crewlet-runner`, plain Python the engine embeds, written over whatever the home held under that name at every launch and enabled once per box with `hermes plugins enable crewlet-runner`, which adds that one line and keeps the box's list, its other keys and its comments, measured) loads in the gateway. It records every response, takes the run's notes ([Hermes Agent's notes](#hermes-agents-notes)) and reports skill loads, each from a file under `<home>/.crewlet` that its settings (`CREWLET_HERMES_PLUGIN`, paths and digests alone) name.

**A box adds to the run; it cannot switch Crewlet's own off.** The overlay states every leaf of the bridge's entry that a home's or `/etc/hermes`'s entry of that name could switch it off with, so `enabled: false` or `disabled: true`, a `tools.include` or `tools.exclude` list, `transport: sse`, `auth`, a `connect_timeout` below the 60 seconds Hermes defaults to, a `command` with `args` beside the URL (which Hermes skips as suspicious), a `tool_costs`, `spend_limit` or `cost_unit` that is not a table, number or label, and an `ssl_verify` path, `client_cert` or `client_key` (an `ssl_verify` or `client_cert` naming a missing file left the bridge unreached and the run hung until it was cut off, over HTTP and HTTPS alike) all give way (measured on 0.23.3: the run reaches the bridge with its tools under each, and its calls answer). The bridge's own `headers` stand alone: where the run sends none, the overlay states them as an empty list, which replaces the box's mapping whole and which Hermes reads as no headers; otherwise a home's or `/etc`'s `authorization`, `Host` or `MCP-Protocol-Version` header reached the bridge, the last two in place of Hermes's own (measured). What no leaf of the run's can undo without overriding the box's own entries, the script judges after the overlay is installed and before Hermes starts, through Hermes's own loader and gates under the run's managed scope (the carry script's `guard`), and **refuses the run, naming the file, the key and the entry**, where:

- `agent.disabled_toolsets` in the home's `config.yaml` or `/etc/hermes/config.yaml` names the bridge's server as `crewlet` or `mcp-crewlet`, on a web-denied run too, whose list holds the box's;
- `platform_toolsets.cli` lists `no_mcp`, or names MCP servers and leaves `crewlet` out;
- `HERMES_SAFE_MODE` (no MCP servers, no plugins) or `HERMES_IGNORE_USER_CONFIG` (none of the run's settings, no plugins) is set in the run's environment, the home's `.env` or `/etc/hermes/.env`, where either starts Hermes with exit status 0;
- the home's `active_profile` names a profile, whose home Hermes would run in instead;
- the bridge's entry holds an `env` Hermes skips the server for, or a `tool_costs` table it finds malformed;
- the run's bridge sends headers of its own and the box's entry adds another, a different spelling of one of the run's included;
- the plugin is gated off once its enabling has run: `plugins.disabled` names `crewlet-runner`, or a `plugins.enabled` list leaves it out.

An `env` or `headers` mapping is named by its keys alone, never its values. An entry naming another server, toolset or plugin, a switch set to a false value, and the `default` profile start the run; so does a guard that cannot read the box's configuration, Hermes's own load deciding then. `plugins.disabled` naming the plugin before its first run is undone by its enabling.

**The run's own routes stay direct past a home's `NO_PROXY`.** Hermes 0.23.3 never sends a loopback host (`localhost`, `127.x.x.x`, `::1`) through a proxy, and matches `NO_PROXY` in either spelling by host for its MCP connections, a `host:port` entry too (measured; its source reads CIDR, `.domain` and `*.domain` entries as well). It loads the home's `.env` over the process's environment and the managed `.env` last, so a home `.env`'s `NO_PROXY` replaced the list the wrapper extends with the run's own hosts, and behind the home's proxy the bridge went unreached while the run hung (measured). So the run's managed `.env` states `NO_PROXY` and `no_proxy` as one list: the process's entries (both spellings), the home `.env`'s and `/etc/hermes/.env`'s, in that order, then the hosts of Crewlet's own routes, duplicates dropped (measured: the bridge connects and its calls answer).

**Standing instructions** ride `HERMES_EPHEMERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT`, the client's alone, which Hermes appends to its own system prompt at each request without caching it, so they are **appended**. Hermes freezes the value with the session as it creates it (its local policy's client environment), so before a run continues a session the script writes the run's own there, the gateway stopped; measured on 0.23.3, the resumed request's system message then ends with the run's text. One environment variable holds at most 128 KiB, so longer instructions are refused at launch, saying so.

**The round cap is Hermes's own** (`--max-turns`): after N tool-calling responses Hermes asks once more for a final answer and exits 1, ending its answer with "the maximum tool-iteration limit was reached before a final answer" (or answering "I reached the iteration limit and couldn't generate a summary." where that request called a tool); a run whose Nth response is its answer completes. The run reads the cap only where Hermes said so **and** the plugin's record of the last turn holds the cap's tool rounds.

**Its answer is the `result` event's text**, its transcript the stream's text, `tool_use` and `tool_result` events. A failure is Hermes's own words (its `error`, else its answer), where the profile's sign-in and limit markers read them. **Its tokens and window are the plugin's record**: one line per response (`post_api_request`), the prompt without its cached part beside its cache reads and writes, and the window Hermes held the model to; the `result` event's counts are the gateway's running total and are not read. Hermes keeps no plan limits on disk, so a run reports none; a spent plan is read from Hermes's failure sentence.

**A Hermes run's own skills** are installed as `<home>/.hermes/skills/crewlet:<name>/SKILL.md` beside the box's, the last run's removed first, and the plugin reports a load when `skill_view` returns that file as the runner wrote it (by its SHA-256), never a file the model rewrote.

**Signing in.** A provider key travels in the entry's `env`, or a login in the home's `.env`, `auth.json` and `shared/nous_auth.json`, seeded into a `direct` or `container` box and written back when the box closes, under the rule every local login follows. The model's shell sees what a person's Hermes would show it, the sign-in included: a Hermes run keeps no sign-in variable out of its tool shell, as Kimi Code's does not.

#### A Hermes Agent run's session

**The runner names the session**, as its title: `-c <id> --create-if-missing` creates a session titled with the runner's id, and `-c <id>` continues it, through its compaction lineage (a compaction child of a session that ended `compression`; a delegated subagent's session names its parent too, and is none of the run's). Measured, Hermes compacts a session in place, under the same id and title, so the lineage is one session; on a box whose `compression.in_place` is `false` it rotates instead, ending the session `compression` and moving its title to a child that names it and holds a copy of the kept tail, so the carry starts at the titled session and walks back through the sessions it continues. Hermes's own stored id, which the client prints, is indexed beside it in `<home>/.crewlet/hermes-sessions`.

**It is carried as text.** The session is rows of Hermes's SQLite store, so a pack dumps the store's schema and the session's rows (its messages, usage, admissions and system prompt, its own launch and admission results, and the store's own bookkeeping rows, all read in one transaction) as JSON lines with the runner's `hermes-carry.py`, standard-library Python run under Hermes's own interpreter (`hermes --run-module cProfile -o /dev/null hermes-carry.py …`, the launcher running modules alone), one `session.jsonl` member, which the scrub rewrites as any transcript; a restore builds a new store from it, holding that session alone, the full-text index refilled by the store's own triggers. A restored store resumed its session with its whole history in another home (measured). A run that continues a session takes the box's own copy, or a carried archive where the box holds none or one the archive goes past, as a Claude Code run does.

**A session continues only under the launch it was created with.** Hermes freezes a session's model, effort, round cap and working directory as it creates it: a resume repeating them is taken, one naming others is refused (exit 2), and a resumed session's tools run in its first working directory, or nothing runs where that directory is gone (exit 1, all measured). It freezes the model route too (provider, base URL and model, its gateway runtime) and keeps a resumed session on it whatever the box's configuration then says, so a continued session would keep the route its entry no longer names: the gate compares its provider and base URL with the route Hermes itself resolves for this launch, `-m`'s provider first (`anthropic:m` names anthropic whatever the box configures, measured), and, for a run naming no model, the configured model with the frozen configuration's, each over Hermes's defaults as its loader reads them (a named model is held to the kept launch, since `-m`'s words are not its frozen form: `openrouter:m` freezes `m`); the bridge's URL and bearer header are not frozen, and each job's new ones reach the resumed session (measured). So the box keeps each session's launch beside it from the moment that launch starts, and a run whose launch or route differs, or whose session has no launch or route kept, starts a session of its own, saying why.

**Gaps against Claude Code:**

- A session continues only under the model, effort, round cap and working directory it was created with.
- No plan limits: Hermes keeps none on disk.
- No price: the record has tokens alone.

**Not measured against Nous Research's service or a real provider** (measured against a stand-in model behind `model.base_url`): real models calling the bridge's tools, a real plan limit, and a login refreshing in another box.

### Pi

Drives the **Pi Coding Agent 1.6.0** (`@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`; `pi --version` prints `1.6.0`), the one release this build supports. A box with an older release, or one whose `pi --version` names no release (a pre-release included), is refused before anything runs, saying what it printed and naming 1.6.0; a newer one runs, starting a new session every time. Pi is a Node program, so the box needs Node 22 or later beside it; an image of your own installs it with `npm install -g @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@1.6.0` ([Bring your own image](#bring-your-own-image)). A `pi` entry signs in with its provider's key in its `env`, under the provider's own variable (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, ...); a login pi keeps (Claude Pro/Max, ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot, in `.pi/agent/auth.json`, refreshed in place) is seeded into the box, which writes a refreshed one back ([Local sandboxes](#local-sandboxes)).

**A run is a short script around one `pi` call**, the brief on stdin:

```text
pi --mode json -p --approve -e builtin:mcp \
  --model <provider/id> [--thinking <effort>] -e <home>/.pi/crewlet/extension.mjs \
  [--skill <home>/.pi/crewlet/skills] --session <home>/.pi/sessions/<id>.jsonl
```

- Pi asks no approval before a tool, so the run is fully permissioned as it stands. `--approve` trusts the working directory, as a person answering pi's trust prompt does, so a repository's `AGENTS.md` and its `.pi` settings, MCP servers, extensions, skills, prompt templates and system-prompt files load; pi only creates the directory a `sessionDir` setting names, as the run's session is its own file.
- **A Pi executor uses the provider and model its entry names** (`model: <provider>/<id>`), with the provider's key from the entry's `env` or pi's own login, and reads no custom provider from the box.
- **A run loads what a person's pi session loads.** Pi's agent directory keeps its own settings, MCP servers, extensions (pi's hooks are their handlers), skills, prompt templates, themes, context and system-prompt files and provider definitions, and they load beside the run's own extension and skills, which the launch names with pi's MCP support (`-e builtin:mcp`, so no setting turns it off). Before every run only the run's own directory, `.pi/crewlet`, and the agent directory's `bin` are removed: pi puts `bin` first on the model's shell `PATH`, so a program an earlier command left there would run in place of the box's own. Pi runs without it, and with `PI_OFFLINE=1` never downloads its `rg` and `fd` into it again.
- **A repository or the home adds to the run; it cannot stand in for Crewlet's own.** The extensions the launch names load first, so the run's shell tool and servers win over a same-named one another extension registers. An `mcp.json` entry, the home's or the repository's `.pi/mcp.json`, wins over a registered server in pi, so a run whose server name (`-` and `_` alike) such an entry also defines stops at its first turn, before any request, naming the entry and its file: rename that entry.
- **A home or a repository cannot switch the seat's tools off unseen** (measured on 1.6.0):
  - `codemode.mode: "only"` in the home's `.pi/agent/settings.json` or the repository's `.pi/settings.json` (the repository's wins) has pi declare only its `codemode` tool while codemode is active (a `defaultTools` entry turns it on, as does any `mcp.json` server of codemode exposure), so the seat's tools leave the model's requests; the run stops before any request, naming the file, the key and the entry. A mode of `on`, codemode inactive, or `codemode.inlineBudget` alone leaves the tools declared, and the run goes on.
  - A `defaultTools` in either settings file that leaves both `read` and `bash` out of pi's tools (a repository's plain list replaces the home's, a list of `+name` and `-name` entries changes it) has pi list no skill at all, the run's own included; either one kept keeps the listing. A run handing skills of its own stops before any request, naming each file that sets the key and its value; a run with no skills of its own runs.
  - `extensions: ["-builtin:mcp"]` in either settings file is undone: the launch names `-e builtin:mcp`.
  - An `httpProxy` in the home's settings that cannot reach the bridge, or an extension that takes over pi's `/mcp` command, leaves the bridge without a tool, which fails the run as below.
- The run pins `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` to the box home's `.pi/agent`, and `PI_OFFLINE=1`, `PI_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1` and `PI_TELEMETRY=0`: no catalogue refresh, version check or telemetry at start.
- **Everything the run adds is one extension**, embedded in the engine and written with the run's settings, so the agent can read the bridge's URL and token in the file, as it can in the other runners' configuration. It registers every engine server over streamable HTTP with its headers, its tools declared to the model by name (`mcp__crewlet__<tool>`), with the bridge's own wait as the call timeout; it adds the seat's standing instructions as a prompt section of their own, which pi renders after its own prompt, its tools and the repository's `AGENTS.md`; it holds the turn cap; it hands over notes; and it reports skill loads.
- **The model's shell holds the run environment**, the sign-in, a seat's own tool credentials and an operator's own `OTEL_*` settings included, as set. A pi run is handed none of [Crewlet's telemetry](#credentials-and-the-run-environment): pi reads no `OTEL_*` variable.
- **A bridge that offers no tool fails the run.** Pi starts a run whose server is unreachable or refuses its token silently, the tools just absent. So at the first turn, once pi has connected its servers, the extension checks that the bridge's own server offered a tool, and otherwise stops the run before any request, recorded on the stream and said on the error stream; the run fails naming the server.
- **The run's own skills** are a directory each under `.pi/crewlet/skills`, named `crewlet:<name>` (pi warns of the colon and loads it), named with `--skill`. Pi lists them and the model loads one by reading its `SKILL.md`; the extension posts each such read to the bridge's skill route, before the model sees the file.
- **The turn cap is the extension's**: Pi has no native one. Every turn is one model request, and the turn past the cap is aborted as it starts, before its request, with the entry `crewlet-cap`. A run with a cap whose extension never ran, or whose requests number more than its cap, fails.
- A run ends on request as a Claude Code run does ([above](#a-claude-code-runs-session)). Pi answers `SIGTERM` by recording an abort and ending its shell tool's process group, which runs in a session of its own; a pi killed past the grace leaves that group until the box goes.

**Notes reach the run at pi's own step boundaries.** The extension polls the notes route while the agent works (each poll held ten seconds by the route, a failure waiting a second doubling to thirty, a refused route ending the polling) and keeps each note it admits. At the end of every turn that completed, after the turn's tool results and before the next request, and as the run is about to finish (`agent_before_settle`), it hands every admitted note over as a custom message of its own: pi sends it to the model whole, as a user message, never inside a tool's result, and the run goes on to answer one handed over at the finish. One note carries up to **4,505 UTF-16 units**, the shared item bound: pi bounds no message (93,000 units reached the request whole, measured). Nothing is handed over once the cap is spent. A note admitted and not yet handed over lives in the extension's memory only, so a killed run loses it, and the route serves it again to the next run, as an unconfirmed note always is.

**A note is confirmed by pi's own record**, never the extension's word: the custom message carries the note's inbox id, which pi records and never sends to the model. A note is held only where, on the session's active branch, an answer of the model's (a message that stopped as `stop`, `toolUse` or `length`) follows it with no compaction between them, which would have left the note only inside its summary, and no edit taking it out. A run killed after the hand-over, or answered only by an error or an abort, holds nothing, and the note is told again.

**Its answer is the last assistant message's text**, read off the stream: **pi exits 0 when a request fails in JSON mode**, so a failed run is its last assistant message's `error`, the provider's status and words (`429 {"type":"error","error":{"type":"rate_limit_error",...}}`), which are all the profile's limit and sign-in markers are matched against. **Its tokens and price are its own requests'**: every assistant message's usage and every compaction's, the stream carrying this process's messages alone, a resumed run's included. The window is the one pi reports at each turn's end, from its own model catalogue.

**Its session is one file, `.pi/sessions/<id>.jsonl`, at the same path in every box.** The run's script writes its header (the id the runner minted, and the working directory) and pi continues it with `--session`. Pi continues a session only in the directory its header names, and a `direct` box's working directory differs from any other box's, so a carried session is restored with its header written again naming the box's own; the rest is as carried, and pi patches its prompt's working directory itself. It is carried whole, saved beside the working run under the rule a Claude Code save is held to (the file is append-only), and continued only between boxes on exactly 1.6.0, the writer's and the box's, a box's own copy as much as a carried one. A newer box, or a session another release wrote or whose writer's release cannot be read, starts a new session, saying so and naming 1.6.0; a box whose own release cannot be read, or is older, runs nothing ([above](#pi)). Pi skips a torn line and repairs the file's end itself, so no line is cut. `auth.json` never travels.

**Gaps against Claude Code:**

- No native turn cap: the extension enforces it.
- Notes arrive at a turn's end, after the whole turn's tool calls, not after each call.
- Not measured against a provider's service through a login: the wording of a spent Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot plan is the provider's, matched by the profile's markers as a key's error is.
- How a relaunch judges a continued session: as one whose compaction point only its box could say, with no point read and no count, so it is always told the summarized telling; no reading of its calls thins a telling; and its brief counts a token a byte. A relaunch so never under-counts the next request.

### What ends a run; each launch is published as its own record

A run is **never stopped on a clock of its box's**. The waiter stamps the box's keepalive every poll tick; the stamp only lets the orphan reaper take a box nothing runs in and nothing has touched for `host_grace_seconds`. A run ends when it finishes, or when you set a limit:

- A **round cap**: `role.sandbox.max_turns`, else `providers.sandbox.default_max_turns`, uncapped unless one is set. It is handed to every runner as its own turn cap (Claude Code's `--max-turns`, Gemini CLI's and Qwen Code's `model.maxSessionTurns`, OpenCode's agent `steps`, Copilot's extension, which aborts the run past it, Grok Build's `--max-turns`, Muse Code's `--max-model-steps`, Kimi Code's `KIMI_LOOP_MAX_STEPS_PER_TURN`, Pi's extension, which aborts the turn past it, and a Codex run's note helper's count of each turn's model responses).
- A **wall-clock cap**: a turn whose trigger carries one (a schedule's `timeout_seconds`) ends its run at that deadline. The collection ends its job as a stop does and records what the run did up to then.
- A **person's stop** ends it at once ([Pausing a seat](agent-runtime.md#pausing-a-seat)): the harness is told to stop, its session is packed as its own end packs it, and the job is killed where it will not go ([A Claude Code run's session](#a-claude-code-runs-session)).

Completion is detected by tracking the job itself: see [Durability and completion](#durability-completion-and-observability).

The harness's standing instructions tell it that it is *not* the last step, so it writes a structured **findings report** to a known file before stopping. `collect` prefers that file for the result text: it survives a run whose process group died before it printed its final message, and a tool-only run that streamed no final message. **A report is a success only beside the harness's own end**: a clean exit, and the stream (or Claude Code's result line) holding the harness's account of how its run ended, its terminal result whether a success or a failure. A harness that exited 0 without one, having printed nothing or only lines that end nothing, failed whatever it left, a report included: an earlier run in the same box could leave a launcher that starts no harness at all.

**The report names what the run delivered**: a line of its own for each branch it pushed and each pull or merge request it opened, such as `Delivered: fix/retry-backoff` or `Delivered: https://git.example.com/acme/api/pull/42`. Those lines are the run's **delivered refs**, in the report's order, on any host and any scheme. The engine keeps no list of code hosts, because which hosts a box can push to is set by the seat's own [environment and setup steps](#credentials-and-the-run-environment), which it never names.

- A line counts when what follows the label, alone on the line, is a URL carrying no credentials or a name git accepts for a branch (valid UTF-8, at most 244 bytes, as a parked run's branch is: [below](#mid-run-clarification-ask_and_wait)). A list marker, emphasis or backticks around it are fine. `Delivered: the fix for the flake` is a sentence, not a ref.
- A report that names none is read for pull and merge request URLs by their **shape**, on any host and port (`/pull/N`, `/pulls/N`, `/-/merge_requests/N`, `/pull-requests/N`, `/pullrequest/N`). That is a guess, since a pull request the run only read looks like one it opened; so a named ref always wins over a scraped one, and the report's over the harness's final message.
- The refs ride the run's phase record and the collected executor's record, which the reviewer reads under `## What the agent delivered`; nothing else judges the turn on them. Both are JSON, where a non-UTF-8 byte is replaced, so a URL (named or scraped) is listed only if valid UTF-8; listed otherwise, it would be a URL the run never delivered. It is counted instead, with the refs past the record's bound (*the delivered refs*, below).

The runner also reconstructs an **activity transcript** from each harness's event stream (OpenCode's line-flushed `--format json` events, Claude Code's `stream-json` messages) in one shape, the grammar `internal/activityline` declares:

- what the agent said, untagged;
- each tool call numbered in its run with its tool and a preview of its subject (`[tool 3] Bash: go test ./...`); where the preview cuts the subject, the whole of it follows a line at a time (`[input 3] ...`, redacted with the preview and held to 8 KiB in whole lines); a tool with no subject field of its own, an MCP server's, is named by its arguments as compact JSON;
- its result (`[ok 3 2400ms]`, or `[failed 3 35ms]` with the first line of its error), timed where the harness's stream says when the call began and ended;
- a person's note as the run's hook handed it over (`[steer]`);
- the engine's own notes (`[note]`, lines not read or a middle left out);
- how a run that did not succeed ended (`[error]`).

The dashboard draws it as rows of calls, results and narration. It holds **never a tool's output** (a successful result's body is a whole file or everything a command printed; the transcript summarises it), nor the model's thinking, nor a message type the build does not know. The error stream is the transcript only where the event stream says nothing, such as a harness that failed before it could stream.

**Each collected launch is a record of its own.** When the completion is claimed and the result read back, the coordinator publishes one `executor_collected`, the launch's own record beside the executor's. It is **no phase**: the executor's phase is the round's own `agent_phase_completed` with `phase: execute`, which states the launch and its answer as one round and carries no tokens. A round can take more than one launch (a person's answer carries a parked run on in a second launch, or a launch lost with its host is relaunched). Every spend reader files a launch under `execute`, its calls its harness's own turns:

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `turn_id`, `iteration`, `launch_id` | The identity. `iteration` is the executor round that launched it, written onto the run's record beside the turn's parked state; `launch_id` tells a round's launches apart |
| `started_at`, `duration_ms` | From the launch, dated by the store when it named the job, to the collection on the node that read the result, so the completion poll's interval is inside it |
| `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `total_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`, `cache_write_tokens` | What the run spent, as its harness reported it (for OpenCode, its session's totals) |
| `cost_usd` | What the launch's harness said it billed, where it says so. On this record only: it is the launch's fact, and the collected executor's record is one a run that parked on a question does not get until it is answered |
