| `provider_key`, `model`, `harness`, `sandbox_id` | The `providers.llm` entry the launch picked, the model it pointed the agent at (empty when it named none), the harness and the box |
| `harness_turns` | The harness's own count of the turns the launch took, where it reports one (Claude Code's `num_turns`; OpenCode reports none): what every spend figure's `calls` counts the launch as, one where it reports none |
| `response`, `delivered_refs`, `activity_transcript` | The findings report, what it delivered, and the transcript |
| `delivered_refs_elided`, `activity_transcript_elided_lines`, `activity_transcript_elided_bytes` | What the record's bounds left out: refs it does not list (past its bound, or not UTF-8), and the lines and bytes of the transcript's middle. Absent when nothing was left out |
| `pushed_refs`, `pushed_refs_elided`, `pushed_refs_unread` | What the run's push record says it moved on Gitlet, for a run given a repository there to push to: each ref `{repo, ref, old, new, pushes, change}` as it ended, with the change its branch heads, how many more the record names than are listed, and why the record could not be read where it could not ([What a run pushed is reported for it](#what-a-run-pushed-is-reported-for-it)). On the collected executor's record too |
| `failed`, `error`, `error_kind`, `notes` | `failed` and `error` are set when the launch did not succeed, a failure of its turn as a failed phase's is. `error_kind`: `context_exhausted` where its harness said the conversation no longer fits its model's context; `request_refused` where the model's provider refused the request its harness made as built (`error` is the provider's message; see [A session its provider refuses is retired too](conversation-sessions.md#a-session-its-provider-refuses-is-retired-too)); `out_of_memory` where the kernel killed its harness for memory; `max_turns` where it ended on its [round cap](#what-ends-a-run-each-launch-is-published-as-its-own-record) before it finished (Claude Code's `error_max_turns`, Gemini CLI's `FatalTurnLimitedError`, Qwen Code's `max_turn_requests`, Copilot's abort by its extension at the cap ([GitHub Copilot CLI](#github-copilot-cli)), Grok Build's `max_turns_reached`, Muse Code's "model did not reach a terminal state" failure ([Muse Code](#muse-code)), Kimi Code's `loop.max_steps_exceeded`; an OpenCode run at its `steps` answers in text and ends as one that finished); `launch_failed` for every other cause. A launch that stopped to ask a question, one a person stopped and one its host cut off are **not** failed; their `notes` say which |
| `memory_kills`, `memory_bytes` | How many processes the kernel killed for memory in the job's memory domain while its harness ran, and that domain's ceiling (the smaller of its cgroup's limit and the machine's), on any ending; absent where it killed none. The job's script reads the domain (its cgroup, else the machine where the box is a machine of its own) before the harness starts and after it exits, so a kill is counted for this job alone and never guessed from an exit status: a harness ended by SIGKILL with no kill counted is not `out_of_memory`, and a run that survived a killed command still says the kill. A `direct` box shares the engine host's domain, so its kills are recorded and never make its run `out_of_memory` |
| `work_item`, `work_key`, `conversation_key` | As on the turn's phase records |
| `harness_session`, `harness_version` | The harness's own session the launch **ran**, as its script recorded it (so a launch asked to continue a session its box could not is named by the new one it started), and the harness's release, as its `--version` gave it. Each is absent where the box named none of the shape a harness gives it: an id of letters, digits, `-` and `_`, at most 128 of them, and a release of at most 64 bytes |
| `brief`, `harness_session_continued`, `session_not_continued` | Which brief the launch handed its run: `continued` (the turn's session, in the box it was last worked in), `continued_new_box` (the turn's session, restored into another box), `continued_conversation` (the session the turn's conversation's last turn left, restored into a box of its own; [A conversation's next turn continues its last turn's session](#a-conversations-next-turn-continues-its-last-turns-session)) or `fresh` (a session of its own). Then whether the run did take up the session it was asked to continue, and the launch's final verdict on the newest session it did not continue: its loss, what it did instead, the turns either side and the engine's detail ([When a run does not continue its session](conversation-sessions.md#when-a-run-does-not-continue-its-session)). A run whose script started a session of its own in place of the one it was handed is `restore_failed`, its detail the script's reason, one sentence, redacted and cut to **1 KiB**, marked `…`. `brief` is absent where the launch recorded none, `session_not_continued` where it lost nothing |
| `session_taken_bytes`, `session_not_kept`, `session_not_kept_loss` | What the read that collected the launch [took of its session](#each-launchs-session-kept): the size of the sealed session taken out of the box to be kept, or why none was taken, redacted and cut to **1 KiB**, marked `…`, and that why's loss ([When a run does not continue its session](conversation-sessions.md#when-a-run-does-not-continue-its-session)). Whether it then landed is said after the read, by `executor_session_kept` or `executor_session_not_kept` in the log and on the run's record. Both absent where nothing was taken (a harness that carries no session, or `turn_engine.conversation_session.enabled` off) |

It is published **once per launch**, however often the tail is retried: a resume that fails hands the completion back and the retry collects the same job again, so the run's coordination record says the launch's record already went out, in the same write that hands the claim back, exactly as the [charge](#budgets) is recorded. A publish the broker refused is not recorded and is offered again by a retry, if one comes; telemetry never fails the resume. Every spend reader folds these records (the spend rollup, each data node's daily usage and the turn list), so the executor run's tokens are counted where every phase's are, in the Execute band.

**The whole record fits its event**: the broker refuses one over 8 MiB, and this record is the launch's only spend record, so a refusal would lose its tokens, cost, report and refs. Every piece of text a box wrote that rides it has a bound, in bytes, measured redacted (a redaction can lengthen a text: a password's value written in pieces between escaped breaks becomes a marker a piece, seven times its bytes):

- the report, the failure's detail and the transcript: **256 KiB** each (`sandbox.MaxRunTextBytes`);
- the question in `notes`: one sentence of at most 300 bytes;
- the delivered refs and the refs its push record names: **16 KiB** together (`sandbox.MaxDeliveredRefBytes`);
- the reason the push record could not be read, where it could not: **64 KiB**;
- the two reasons, why the run started a session of its own and why its session was not kept: **1 KiB** each (`sandbox.MaxFellBackBytes`, and the bound the executor log holds the second to);
- each listed pushed ref carries its two whole object ids, under 140 KiB for the most a record lists, less than the push record's reason's worst, which it never rides beside;
- the session and the release the box names are held to the shapes a harness gives them, at most 128 and 64 bytes, where the box is read and again as the record is published.

JSON can grow text six-fold (a control byte becomes `\u00XX`, `<` and its kin `\u003c`, an invalid byte `\ufffd`), so the worst case is (3 × 256 + 16 + 64 + 1 + 2) KiB × 6, about 5.0 MiB, inside the ceiling. What happens past a bound depends on who reads the piece:

- **The report and the failure** are what the collected executor's record carries and the reviewer judges, so one past the bound is **condensed by the seat's auxiliary model** (`llm_auxiliary`, falling back to `llm`) and labelled as condensed, never cut: a report's opening read as the whole would seem to say less than the run did. Both are redacted before they are measured, and so is the model's rewrite: a rewrite the redaction puts past the bound is refused as one that came back too long is.
  - The failure's detail is any piece the engine could not read, the exit status, the harness's own error and the **end** of its stderr, in that order (the unread start said by size; see *What is read whole, and what is read as a stream* below). The whole is held to what one condensation reads (`sandbox.MaxCondenseBytes`, 2 MiB) less 1 KiB the engine keeps for a sentence of its own it may put in front. The engine's sentences are taken as they are, and the stderr gets what is left. Kept from its end alone, a failure with a long stderr would lose every one of the engine's own sentences. Output the harness printed that is no result is its error, whole up to half what the failure may be (just under 1 MiB), and past that only its end, redacted before it is cut, after its size; an end that is one line begun before it shows nothing of it.
  - A failure still past what a condensation reads (a harness error as long as the file it came from) keeps whole lines from its start and its end up to that, with the lines between counted, and that is what the model is shown.
  - Where no model can condense one, it keeps **whole lines** up to the bound and says how many it left out: a report from its start; a failure from both ends, its first 32 KiB, an eighth of the bound, where the engine states the exit status, the harness's own error and any piece it could not read, and its end for the rest, because the line naming what broke is the last one printed.
- **The question** a run parked on is never condensed: the run asks it through `ask_and_wait`, which refuses one past its bounds (a one-sentence question of at most 300 bytes, a context of at most 16 KiB, the decision's own caps) before anything is recorded, so the run rewrites it while it can, and what the person reads is what the run wrote.
- **The delivered refs** are read from the whole report with no count to them (every `Delivered:` line, or every pull-request URL its prose holds where it names none), redacted, deduplicated and listed up to 16 KiB (over a hundred and sixty pull-request URLs of the usual length; the bound is shared with the refs its push record names, [below](#what-a-run-pushed-is-reported-for-it)). The rest is counted (`delivered_refs_elided`) and said where the reviewer reads the refs, never dropped unsaid. A ref that is not valid UTF-8 is counted with them and never listed, whichever runner read it: JSON would replace its bytes, so the record would name a ref the run never delivered, and two refs that differ only there as one.
- **The two reasons** (`session_not_continued`'s detail, `session_not_kept`) are a sentence each, so one past its kibibyte keeps its opening, where it says what happened, cut on a character and marked `…`. Each is redacted whole before it is cut, so a credential across the cut is never left as an unrecognisable fragment, and is held again as the record is published, after the publish's own redaction. The first is read off one line of the run's session record, a file its script writes and the box's own agent can rewrite at any length, so it is held too where the runner builds the run's result, which carries no more of it, to a node that asked for the read as well; its whole is on the run's error stream, where the script prints it. The record is read where it lies, a line at a time and only as far as its four keys, and the line saying where a continued OpenCode run began, which its script writes before the release, on every collection and every take of the box's session, so a record the box's agent made long costs the engine nothing past its own bytes.
- **The session and the release** the box names are identifiers, so neither is ever cut: a session id the harness reports that is not one a harness mints (letters, digits, `-` and `_`, at most 128) gives way to the session record's, and one the record holds that is not is none; a release longer than the 64 bytes the executor log records is none, which every reader takes for a current release, as it takes one it cannot read. The record holds both to those shapes again as it is published, whatever runner or host of another build read the box.
- **The transcript** is read by a person, no model and no prompt, so it is not condensed: a long one keeps **whole lines from its start, up to 64 KiB, and from its end, up to 191 KiB**, with one note line where its middle was, naming how many lines and KiB were left out; the note counts inside the 256 KiB. The end gets the larger share because the run's conclusion and what broke sit there; the start is kept because it is the run's plan and its first look at the code (some 320 calls at their longest, since a call's header is the tool's name and at most 160 bytes of what it ran, its result a line, and only a cut subject adds its whole, never its output), which a log cut to its end loses. A single line longer than its half keeps its own start (or end), on a character, marked `…`. The counts also ride the record as `activity_transcript_elided_lines` and `activity_transcript_elided_bytes`, so the dashboard's Activity fold says the record is not the whole log. A runner holds a transcript as it is up to the 256 KiB the record keeps, so a box read never holds a longer one only to cut it; past that it redacts the transcript as it reads it and keeps only what the record keeps, with its counts, and a transcript the redaction cannot read in one pass is not kept at all, a note naming its lines and size in its place. The coordinator bounds whatever a runner sent, after redacting it again, and adds its counts to the runner's, so a runner that forgot the bound cannot publish an unbounded transcript.

Everything read out of the box is **secret-redacted whole, before anything is bounded** (a secret straddling a cut would otherwise survive as a fragment the pattern no longer recognises) and again at the publish. That includes the preview a transcript line shows of what a tool call ran, why it failed and how a run ended: each is redacted whole before it is cut to its 160 bytes, because a token whose start fell just before the cut kept most of its body, too little for any later pass to recognise and enough to identify it. Redacting twice reads as once: the coordinator, redacting again a transcript the runner redacted, changes nothing, save the key's piece beside an END line that goes on to a password's key (below).

**Private keys.** A private key (PEM's armour, or OpenPGP's `-----BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK-----`) is the one shape that spans lines, so it is redacted as a block, **read by its structure** whether or not its END line was written: its headers (RFC 1421's `Proc-Type:`/`DEK-Info:`, OpenPGP's `Version:`/`Comment:`), its base64 lines at the encoder's width and one shorter last line, then its END when it has one. Any number of blank lines may lie among them (a key printed double-spaced is one key), and at most one other line between two of its own (a log line another process wrote in the middle of it).

- **Direction.** A key is read **forward from its BEGIN, and back from an END** that no BEGIN's block reached: a body cut off from its BEGIN by two such lines in a row, or whose BEGIN is not in the text (a stream's end read from inside a key). Read back, a full line also has to read like a key's, carrying upper and lower case letters as base64 of random bytes does, digit or none (random base64 lacks a digit about once in fifty thousand lines, and lines a key's encoding fixes in part, such as an EC key's second line or a last line of forty-odd characters, far more often). So a few lines of CamelCase identifiers or mixed-case paths directly above a bare END line are read as its body and redacted with it. The END's own line is read both ways where what comes before its armour ends in base64 (a diff's `+` is a prefix and a line of base64 both), and the block reaches as far back as either reading does.
- **Reading back across two lines.** Two lines in a row end a block, and an END after them reads back **across them** to a line of the key exactly as wide as an encoder writes one (64 characters: PEM as OpenSSL and Go write it, PKCS#8, OpenPGP; 70: OpenSSH; 76: MIME's base64, which Java's, Python's and .NET's encoders write; one more under a diff's `+`), from a full line of the same width, from the body's last line or from the END itself, with the body's last line and one more line another process wrote above the two. OpenPGP's checksum line (`=` and a CRC-24, after the body) is read back from as its END is.
- **Password prompts.** A password prompt (a line ending in a password's key and its separator: `Password:`, `hunter2 Retype password:`, `pwd=x password:`; that key is neither the value of a key before it, as in `pwd= password:`, nor part of a token run into it, as in `sk-…Pwd:`) is not one of the two lines: the read back passes over it, so another process asking for a password three times between a key's lines and its END no longer publishes the key above, and the prompt is redacted with the key.
- **What is published.** What no read reaches is published: three lines in a row; two whose nearest full line of the key above them is at no encoder's width (a key wrapped at some other width); or two and two more with only the body's short last line between them. A key read from inside, its BEGIN not in the text, is redacted whole when another process broke it with two lines wherever they fell, and with two and one more. Such a split publishes the part above when its BEGIN is not in the text, and the part below when it holds no full line (the short last line alone, BEGIN or none).
- **Prefixed lines.** Read back, a blank line under a wrapping that marks every line (a line number, a grep's context mark) counts as a line between two of the key's, so a key printed double-spaced under one and broken by one line as well is broken by three.
- **BEGIN in the text.** Where the key's BEGIN is in the text, the block read forward and the one read back across the two lines are one, and so is their marker: the two lines are redacted with the key, as a single line another process wrote into it is. A line that is not a key's straight after a BEGIN ends its block before it has a body, so an END after it closes nothing: a BEGIN line with no key under it, such as a grep's match for the armour line, is left as it is and takes nothing after it, even when a later grep matches the END; read back from that END, the same prose is where the read stops.
- **Wrappings.** Every wrapping a key reaches a transcript in is read the same way: a JSON string with its line breaks escaped (once or twice), a line number, timestamp, grep prefix or diff `+` on every line (shaped like the armour line's own), a string concatenated across lines, a line `echo`ed at a time, or the whole key on one line, its encrypted headers too. Two whole keys flattened onto one line (`echo $A $B`, an env dump with the breaks stripped) are two keys, each closed at its own END. Read forward, the body's short last line that ends in the text around it (the quote closing the string the key was written into) ends the block at its base64 unless it reads like a piece of a key (below); what follows a full line on its line ends nothing, since only the last line is short.
- **Cuts.** A cut is read wherever it lands. A tool that bounds what it shows keeps a key's line up to a point (`MIIEow…[...truncated]`, or `MIIEow…` before a bare ellipsis), from a point (`[… 812 bytes truncated]q3O4Ou…`, a window's first line) or both, with its mark between (`MIIEow…[… 2,345 characters truncated …]…Xyz`), on one line, on every line, or every line cut short with no mark at all.
  - What is read is the piece of the key such a line still holds where a key's line would stand (the base64 run that opens the line after its prefix, or ends it before its suffix: eight characters or more in upper and lower case with a digit), never the mark, which no two tools spell alike. Once a piece has said a cut wrote into the line, the run at its other end is the key's too when it reads like one, digit or none, since the first sixteen characters of an RSA key's line (`MIIEogIBAAKCAQEA`) hold none.
  - Read forward, such a line is a line of the body and the block goes on from it; so is a short piece straight after the BEGIN or with text after it, a short piece with another below it (a body has one last line; two in a row are a key cut short on every line), and the tail a cut kept between a BEGIN's armour and its line break.
  - Read back, every line a cut wrote into is a line of the body, however narrow and whichever end the cut kept, and so is a short piece, so a key cut on every line is read back from its END whole. The cut hid the line's width, so a read across two lines another process wrote lands on it from a line at an encoder's width below and goes on to one above.
  - A key written on one line is read back from its END as it is read forward from its BEGIN, across one cut in it, to the key's runs beyond the mark when they hold one at a full line's width, or, where nothing up to the END reads as the key's, one exactly as wide as an encoder writes or wider than any (a path in mixed case before a grep's match for the END is forty characters too).
  - Nothing another rule redacts is a piece of a key: a password's key, its separator and its value, and a token, are left to their own rules.
  - Published, because it reads like no key's: a piece shorter than eight characters, or with no digit or in one case alone, where it is all a line holds of the key (straight after the BEGIN it ends the block before it has a body, and two together end a block anywhere, the key's lines below published unless an END reads back to them); a piece between two marks, at neither end of its line; on a one-line key, what lies across a second cut or across a cut beyond which no run of the key is that wide; with no END below, the tail a mark on a line of its own kept after a head cut short, and the key's lines after it; and, read from inside, the lines above two another process wrote into a key cut short on every line.
  - A line of prose beside a key that opens or ends in such a run (`=== RUN   TestSHA256Sum` above an END) is read as one a cut wrote into and redacted with the key; so are lines of prose that each open or end in one, straight above an END, as far up as they go. Such a run anywhere else is not, except on an END's own line, where one before the armour, up to one shorter run after it, is read as the body a window kept, key or none (`=== RUN   TestSHA256Sum x -----END PRIVATE KEY-----`, a wrapping's gutter `[Worker1A] ` before the END).
- **No END.** After a key whose END was never written, a short line after a line a cut wrote into is read as the body's last line, as it is after any full line, so a word the tool printed next is redacted with its mark. A line another rule names is no line of the key (a token, or a password's key and its separator): under a key whose END was never written, `Password:`, or a `pwd=` whose `=` ends its line, interrupts the key rather than being its last line, so the value on the next line is redacted with the key, or by the password's rule when it cannot be the key's last line, never published with the separator left behind. The cost is a key's last line that ends in a password's key and `=`, about one key in fifty thousand, which is published when no END follows it.
- **Other armour.** Another block's armour (a certificate's) ends a key's block in either direction, on a line of its own or on the key's, and so does a key already redacted, whose marker stands where its armour stood, which is what makes text redacted twice read as it did once. A one-line key whose END was lost is redacted up to the certificate or the next key written after it, and so is one whose END comes after a word.

A password's key is read **as the text writes it**: closed by the quote or the markup it is written in (`{"password": "x"}`, `**Password**: x`, `` `password`: x ``), its quotes escaped where the object is written inside a string, once for each string around it — a quote only where it closes the key's own string, a name such as `"db_password"`, so a longer string ending in the word (`"POST /auth/password": () =>`) is no key — and separated from its value by `:`, `=` or the operator a language assigns or compares with (`:=`, `==`, `=>`) — read with a bare `:` or `=` straight after the key, a JSON object's password was no key at all, and an operator's second character was taken for the value. The markup that closes what the key's line opened before its label is the key's too (`**Root password:** x`, `| Password: | x |`, `| **Password:** | x |`), and the value is read after it — on its line, or, where nothing follows it there, on a line below as after a separator (`**Password:**` over the value, `- **Password:**` over the value indented under it); a quote is no such markup, since a logged string closes with one and what follows it is the next field. A password's value is read **where its wrapping puts it**: when what follows `password:` on its line is only the punctuation the wrapping writes after every line — the quote closing an `echo`'s string and its redirection, the `" +` of a string concatenated across lines, a table's ` |` — or nothing, the value is on the first line after it that is not blank, read past the **gutter** that line opens with — the start of what the key's line has before the key (a reader's line number, a grep's context mark, a diff's `+`, a log's timestamp, the quote opening a concatenated string), shaped so that a number moving on from line to line, or a timestamp's fraction written on one line and not the next, is still the gutter, and ending where a word of both lines does; a key's last run glued to its END on the key's line, or a space before it, is the key's, not the gutter, unless the line after the value's repeats it too, and is redacted with the key on every line that spells it — and ended before the same punctuation, or before what a list's or a concatenation's last line closes with instead, or before the `>>` that appends to a file the key's line opened with `>`, or before that punctuation without the quote it opens with where the line writes its content unquoted (`echo hunter2x9 >> key.pem` under `echo "Password:\n" >> key.pem`). Markup the value's line opens with that the key's line does not (a table's `|`, a list's `-` or number, a quote's `>`), on a line below or on the rest of a string's line after an escaped break, is read past to the first word after it that is a value, which is replaced with it: the rule leans to hide, since markup replaced costs a line its formatting and markup taken for the value shows the password. Before a key, a marker or an armour, or with no value after it on its line, the markup is the value. The wrapping's blank lines between — an empty numbered line, `echo "" >> key.pem` — are passed over; a line holding a password's key where the value would be ends the read, since its key names what is there, while a key further along the line is the line's own and the value before it is still read; a line that does not end in that punctuation says it was no wrapping's, so the punctuation is the value, as `***` is; and a word in any script, or an empty quoted string, is a value, never punctuation. The value alone is replaced, so the gutter, the punctuation and the blank lines stay. A password's key inside a logged JSON string escaped in layers (holding a `\\`, a `\"` or a `\uXXXX`), in a line's JSON value after any prefix such as a timestamp or a level, is read twice: as written, and with the string decoded once (`\\n` as the line's own `\n`, `\"` as `"`, `\u003e` as `>`), and every value either reading names is hidden; a string that is not well-formed JSON is read only as written. Taking the first word after the separator wherever it stood, the rule redacted the wrapping's own syntax — an `echo`'s closing quote, the quote that closes a concatenated string's piece, the number of a numbered line a tab follows or of a blank one — and published the value on the line after. What is still published: a value under a quoted key whose name is more than letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.` (`{"Admin Password": "x"}`); a value `printf '%s\n'` writes a line at a time (the escaped break is inside every line's own prefix); a blank numbered line that lost the tab after its number, or a log's blank line that lost the space after its timestamp, which is read as the value; a value shaped like the word the key's line opens with, a space after it on both (`pass2 next` under `pass1 Retype password:`), which is read as the gutter as one timestamp is under another; a value written over several lines — a YAML block scalar (`password: |`, `password: >-`), a YAML sequence under the key (`- hunter2`), a heredoc — of which the first word at most is read; a diff whose key is on a context line and whose value changed, of which the removed line's value is read and the added value published; a value under a gutter that holds an armour, or under a blank line of the wrapping whose gutter holds a password's key; under a wrapping's suffix, a value on a line that holds a password's key of its own (`echo "hunter2 password:" >> f` under `echo "Password:" >> f`), the key's line taking its own punctuation for its value instead, or the closing of the markup that alone ends it (`| Password: |` over `| > Retype password: |`), since redacting the value would change how that line ends once the second key's value is replaced, and a second pass would read the first key's value elsewhere; the part of a value after an escaped break inside it when that part is punctuation alone (`pwd=ab\n!!`), which reads as a string's closing quote; and a key's piece on the line of a value read below a password's key that a key's END line goes on to (`-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----|passwd:`): the keys are read with that value claimed, in the text as written, so the piece is no line of a key, while the rule reads the value in the text the keys' blocks leave, where the END's line is a marker that can join the value's line to it or take the gutter the END's line opened with, and reads another value, or none — and a second pass, the block gone, can read the piece as a key's and redact it. What it costs is a line after the key that ends as the key's did and holds no value: a prompt logged as `msg="password:"` over `msg="connected"` has `connected` redacted, where the rule used to replace the quote; a key a quote closes whose separator ends its line — a Go `case "password":` — has the next line's first word redacted, and so does a JSON key whose value is on the next line, as it should; a code span in prose, `` `Password:` and a value ``, has the word after it redacted; and a name in a string or a code span that is no key where it stands is read as one, so a choice between two strings that opens with one (`masked ? "password" : "text"`) has the other redacted, and the shell's `` `pwd` `` before a colon (`` -v `pwd`:/app ``) the path after it. What the other rules write once the keys are read leaves a second pass nothing new to read either: a password's rule replaces its value alone, so `password:` and the line break before a value on the next line stay where they were, and an escaped line break inside a value stays too, the value redacted on either side of it (`pwd=ab\ncd` becomes `pwd=[REDACTED:password]\n[REDACTED:password]`, since whether the `\n` is a break or two characters of the password the text does not say); a value or a token stops at an armour or a marker; and an armour line that holds a marker — before its armour or after it, which is what a pass leaves beside an armour it read no key from — holds no key read across its lines, and a key written on it is read back from its END no further than the marker. So the coordinator, redacting again a transcript the runner redacted, changes nothing — save the key's piece beside an END line that goes on to a password's key, above. A block is never read more than 64 KiB from its armour (`redact.MaxKeyBlockBytes`, the largest key there is more than twice over in any wrapping), so a BEGIN on a line that runs on past that — a minified bundle naming the armour — holds back nothing after that line. And the pass stays linear on a line of many armours: each one's scan stops at the armour next to it. So it does on a password's value written in pieces between escaped breaks with no space among them (`pwd=x\nx\nx…`, or a key after every break): whether the value runs on across a break is read only as far as the first letter or digit after it, never again to the end of the value, which cost the breaks times the length — days for a file of the 32 MiB the engine reads whole.
**What is read whole, and what is read as a stream.** A file meant to be read whole (the findings report, the result line, the exit status) is refused, not clipped, past **32 MiB** (`sandbox.MaxFileBytes`), because a clipped report reads as a finished one. A refusal degrades **only that piece**: it is described by its size, the run reads as not succeeded with that as the reason, and its tokens, delivered refs and transcript are still collected, charged and published.

A run's **machine streams** are never refused for size; the engine keeps a bounded share of each:
- The event stream is decoded a line at a time in bounded memory; a single line past 32 MiB is skipped and counted where it was.
- The error stream is read **from its end**, because a process's conclusion is the last thing it prints: at most what one condensation takes beside the engine's own sentences in front of it (2 MiB less 1 KiB, and less those sentences). Its unread start is said by size.
- The read takes **386.5 KiB more** before what it keeps (`redact.LookBack`) and never shows them. They hold the redaction's cross-line reads (a private key's block back to its BEGIN, a password's value back to its key and label), so what is kept is redacted with what decides it, and begins after whatever they decide. `redact.LookBack`'s doc names the password reads that reach further.
- What it keeps opens on a line. Where the end it read is one line begun before that, or every line it opens is blank, none of the stream is shown, and the transcript and failure give its size and why.

**Box files on the engine host** are all accessed through the box's home opened as a root (Go's `os.Root`), by a name relative to the home, walked a component at a time; the engine's records about a box are reached the same way, through the box's `records/`.
- A link on the way is followed only to somewhere beneath the home. One leading out (absolute, or relative climbing past the home) is refused at the access, whenever the box put it there, in the same words as a path named outside the home.
- A file is read only if it is a **regular file where it lies**: a named pipe at the done marker, on the agent's side of a `container` box's mount, would block the completion poll for good (an open cannot be cancelled). Anything else, a symbolic link included (whether it leads nowhere or was put there after the path was checked), is refused naming the path and what it is, never read as empty.
- Anything but a directory where a directory on the way was expected (a named pipe in place of `.crewlet/`, say) is refused at once, the same way.
- The poll reports the refusal. A collection degrades **only that piece**, as for the size cap (a refused result file is read from the event stream's last line, which the wrapper copies into it). It is not retried: what a path names is the box's own doing, so a retry would be refused again until the run was settled as lost.

**Writes** **replace the file whole**: a setup step's files, a harness's configuration, and the token file the completion poll rewrites under a running job. The engine writes a fresh file beside the path, syncs, and renames it over the path in one step, so a process in the box reads the old file or the new one, never an empty or half-written one (a push's credential helper must never find the token file empty).
- The rename replaces only a regular file, or puts one where nothing is. A link at the path is refused rather than followed, a named pipe rather than waited on; each is left as the box made it, and the launch fails naming the path and what it is.
- A failed write leaves nothing staged. The new file is `0600` whatever mode the replaced one had.
- A **streamed** write (a session archive carried into a box, which grows with its session) is the same replacement fed a piece at a time, copied into the staged file, never held whole. A source that fails part way fails the write and leaves the old file.

The engine's records about a box are kept beside its home rather than in it (see [Local sandboxes](#local-sandboxes)) and read and written the same way, so a record that is not a regular file answers at once instead of blocking the poll, a collection or a reaper. An unusable record of the box's logins is logged (`local_sandbox_credential_map_unreadable`) and costs only the write-back of a login the run refreshed. An unusable job record reads as not knowing whether the job runs, which keeps the box.

The dashboard renders each launch **inside the card of the round that launched it**: how it ended, what it spent, the report, and the transcript as a closed **Activity** fold. A turn reads as the executor, one card per round:
- the launch, with the prompt the run was sent: the fresh brief the started record carries and, where the launch continues a session, the continuation it handed the run, published as the round's opening frame once the launch has its box ([A relaunch continues the turn's session](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session));
- its collection, with what the run submitted, its bridged calls, and the round's launches under them;
- then the review.

A launch whose round has no record of its own (a run that parked on a question and ended before an answer resumed it) is drawn on its own, in its round's place. In the recent-phases list a launch is a row of its own, drawn as the executor's: the `execute` phase word with the harness that ran it.

Where the record's bounds left something out, the screens say so. The Activity fold counts **kept of all** lines (`412 of 4,000 lines`, or the bytes left out of a single over-long line); a run's **Delivered**, on its page and its span in the turn trace, names how many more refs its report holds than the record lists (`… (+41 more its report names)`).

---

## Each launch's session, kept

A run's harness keeps its conversation in its box — Claude Code as a transcript and its sidecars, OpenCode in its database, Codex as its rollout — and a box does not outlive its turn. So every launch's session is **taken out of its box and kept** in the fleet's [object store](object-store.md), one sealed object per capture, named by the turn's row of the `executor` state log ([ADR-0073](https://github.com/crewlet/crewlet/blob/main/adr/0073-a-seats-executor-session-is-a-sealed-object-its-turns-row-names.md)), for a launch in any box on any node to continue: what is kept is the whole session, scrubbed, and the turn's row names the newest one the turn kept.

**Where it is taken.** At every point the box can still be read, on the node whose host the box is on — a `direct` or `container` box is touched only there, and a node that holds the seat but not the box asks that host to read it — before the box is paused or reclaimed, and, for a stop, a loss or a job its turn's cap passed while it still worked, once the read has **ended the job** (below):

| Point | What is taken |
|---|---|
| A completion's collection | The archive the run's script packed when its harness exited ([Claude Code](#a-claude-code-runs-session), [OpenCode](#an-opencode-runs-session), [Codex](#a-codex-runs-session)); for a job that ended without packing — one that failed before it got there, one [lost with its engine](#failure-modes) whose box is still there — one **packed now**, by the runner's own pack, which keeps the archive's digest in the box as the script's does. A job its turn's cap passed while it still ran is **ended first**, as a stop's read ends one (below): the archive its script packed on its way out — an OpenCode run's exported through the run's own server — or one packed now where it left none, final wherever the job ended |
| A person's stop | The archive the run's script packed as the stop's read ended its job, or one packed now where it left none — final wherever the job ended — in the read that charges what the stopped job spent, after the job's bridge session is closed and before its box is reclaimed |
| A run lost with its box still there | The archive the run's script packed as the loss's read ended its job, or one packed now where it left none — final wherever the job ended — after the job's bridge session is closed and before the loss's ending reclaims the box (a launch whose engine restarted before its turn parked), on this node's host or asked of the host the box is on |
| A job still working, as its node polls its box | A **save**: the session as it stands, packed beside the working harness, cut off and not final, at most once an interval and only once the job moved ([A running job's session, saved as it works](#a-running-jobs-session-saved-as-it-works)) |
| A node's drain, for each `direct` job it launched | A save of each such job whose session moved since its last, within 30 s of the drain's start ([below](#a-running-jobs-session-saved-as-it-works)) |

A box that is **gone** — lost from its host, or with a node that left the fleet — has nothing left to read, and keeps nothing: the launch's session is lost with it, and the newest capture the turn kept stays the one its row names — and the relaunch that follows that job continues the newest capture that job kept, where it kept one (its newest save, taken as it worked or as its node drained, where one landed), and otherwise starts a session of its own — or, where the turn has kept no session at all, continues the one its first launch was handed ([below](#a-conversations-next-turn-continues-its-last-turns-session)).

**A stop, a loss or a turn's cap ends the job before it takes the session.** A job still working when its session is taken is packed as it stands — a step in flight half recorded — so the read that takes a stopped or lost job's session, and the collection of a job its turn's wall-clock cap passed while it still ran, first asks its script to end it ([A Claude Code run's session](#a-claude-code-runs-session), [OpenCode](#an-opencode-runs-session)): the harness is told to stop and the session packed as the run's own end packs it, and the take is of that archive, final. The cap is an end like a stop: the run is ended as if it had finished, and its bridge session is closed before its job is asked. Its collection asks first whether the job finished, so a job that finished by itself before the read is collected as any finished job is; one whose poll at its collection cannot say is asked to end all the same: a poll that cannot say is no reason to leave the job working past its cap. A run whose job the collection saw still working past its cap — its poll answered that it ran, or its script heard the request to end — still says it was cut off at its turn's cap, and is never parked on a question it asked on its way out; the collection records that on the run's record before it asks or kills anything, so a collection made again after one cut short as it ended the job — its node draining, the seat moving — says so too, though the kill that outlived the first may have taken the script before it recorded the request. The read waits for the job to be over for at most **2¼ minutes** — the harness's five-second grace, the pack's two minutes, and five seconds each for the script's own stops of its login exporter and its server — and then kills what is left of it (`SIGTERM`, five seconds, `SIGKILL`, five seconds more): a sweep of stray processes after a clean end, the escalation past the wait, and at once for a script that answers no request (one an older build started, one not yet at its first line), whose session is then packed by the read, final. Only a job the kill could not reach — a box whose runtime would not run it, a kernel record a `direct` box could not read, so the signal was withheld, a `container` job whose box can name no process group of the job's own — is taken as it stands, not final, and its reclaim ends it. The kill keeps the box for the take: a `direct` box kills its job's recorded group, a `container` box the job's process group in its container — recorded as the job started, or, for a job an older build started, which recorded none, read off the job's first process where an exec's own session leads it, as every runc exec's does; never the container's main process, beside which the take still runs, and never the job's first process alone, which is the runner's wrapper rather than the job, so a job whose group neither names is signalled nothing.

A job packed while it still ran — one its box would not end, the only such pack now that a turn's cap ends its job first, as a stop does — is packed as it stands, and **its capture's save point is not the calls the run's log had taken before the pack** — nor is that of any capture of a job cut off ([below](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)): a harness can make a call, and have it answered, before its own record holds it — Claude Code writes a message only once the whole of it has streamed, so one killed while a message streamed never wrote the calls it had made, and OpenCode's export leaves out a step that has not settled — so the capture is placed at the round's start and, once its take has read the session whole, raised to the save point of a capture its session is known to hold (its launch's own last capture that landed, or the capture the launch continued, which the launch records) where that capture's newest compaction is the one the take found, and a run that continues it is told every call of its round after that point, some more than once and none never, but those past the point a reading of a cut-off Claude Code session's archive finds it holding ([below](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)), which it is never told again. **A Claude Code pack made beside a harness that may still be working** (that of a job its box would not end; one of a job that is over, its harness gone, is packed as the run's own end packs it) **refuses a file its harness rewrote under it**, since Claude Code rewrites more than it appends — a task file as its task tool changes it, a subagent's metadata as the subagent ends, its own transcript renamed over by a trim or rewritten in place where it withdraws a message — and `tar` cannot be taken at its word: GNU `tar` exits 1 on a file that grew as it read it and pads one that shrank with NULs, while busybox's says nothing of the first and cuts its archive inside the second. So the pack asks the box for the tools it reads the session with (`find`, `ls`, `wc`, `sed`, `grep`, `head`, `cksum`, `touch` and `sleep`, naming one it lacks); sets every file and directory of the session stamped in the box's future to the box's present, leaving every earlier time as it is and setting none through a link, which `touch` would follow out of the session (a box cannot hold a file from its own future, and the pack's checks would read one as written until the box's clock passed it, whether a box whose clock ran ahead stamped it, the session carried here with its times, or this box before its clock stepped back; done before the marker, it leaves a file the harness writes once the marker is down read as written all the same, and one written before the marker is whole by the time `tar` reads it; and set to the present, never to an earlier time, it hides no write from another pack of the same session running beside this one, as a stop's read and a collection's of one job may each make at once, each in a staging directory of its own — which at most refuses a file this one set after its marker); writes a marker, waits until the box's own `find` reads a file written after it as newer (a second at most, where busybox compares whole seconds; a box whose `find` never does is refused after fifty sleeps of a tenth of a second, five seconds, rather than packed blind, and one whose `sleep` takes no tenth of a second is refused saying so), lists every file of the session with its inode and size — refusing at once a session whose files add up past the quarter of a gibibyte the scrub reads, which the take would refuse once packed — and runs `tar`; then, whatever `tar`'s exit 0 or 1 said, it refuses the pack, naming the file, where the archive does not read back (busybox's archive cut inside a file that shrank among them) or holds no file, a file is gone, its inode changed or it shrank, a file the list named is not in the archive, a file other than a transcript was written since the marker, the session's own transcript (read back on every pack, since Claude Code rewrites it in place and a clock stepped back as the pack ran could hide that rewrite from `find`) or a subagent's thread written since then is not, byte for byte, the start of the live file — its copy read back out of the archive — or, looked at last, a file the archive holds is gone, which a file removed while the checks ran is. No check rests on a tool's word that what it wrote landed: a tool that checks no write it makes exits 0 having written nothing, or half, to a full disk, which a harness still writing can fill under the pack. So every list and every answer a check reads reaches the shell through a pipe, each `find`'s own exit held, and the shell writes it to the pack's staging directory and reads it back, refusing the pack where the file does not hold what was written. A check that cannot be made refuses the pack as a difference would, never reading as nothing having changed: a list that cannot be made or kept, or a comparison `grep` cannot make (its exit 2, or an exit 0 that names nothing). A transcript or a subagent's thread that only grew is packed as `tar` first saw it, its last line perhaps one its harness had not finished writing, which is kept as the text it is and cut off before a later run resumes the session. A pack refused so leaves nothing behind: its staging directory goes with it. And an OpenCode export, made by the box's OpenCode itself (`--standalone`) since only the run's script can reach the run's server, leaves out the message still being written, and can find the database busy under a server still running; it is refused before its gzip where it is empty or past the quarter of a gibibyte the scrub reads, which the take would refuse once packed. **Every pack made now stages its archive in a directory of its own**, of a job still working or of one that is over, so two reads of one job at once — a stop's and a collection's — each packing it, never clear each other's files or move each other's archive, and the clear before every run removes any one a pack cut short left. **And every pack made now is its read's alone**, of a job that is over as much as of one still working: its archive is moved to a place of its own beside its staging directory, streamed from there and removed once the read is done with it — never moved over the job's capture, which only the job's own script writes, moving the job's final archive there once, the moment its harness exits. A Claude Code take reads its archive twice, opening it again by its path for its second pass, and over one capture a take was refused whenever another archive was moved there between its two passes: another read's of the same job, or the job's own end pack's, which can land while a pack still checks what it read; and the archive of a job as it stood, moved there after the final one, was taken by a read of the job once over as everything the job did. So each read streams the archive its own pack made, and one of a job that left its archive streams that archive, which nothing moves over while it reads it. The removal once the read is done is held to the take's own time, so a box that stops answering once its archive is read keeps the read no longer than the take was given, leaving its leftovers to the clear before the next run. A pack that **fails** — a box without `tar` or `gzip`, an export that would not run, an OpenCode that could not be asked whether it holds the session (its private server would not start, its database was busy, it crashed) — is a capture refused with what the pack said, never "no session"; a harness that wrote no transcript, or an OpenCode that answers it holds no such session, has nothing to take. A job read again after it was taken whole — a collection retried after a resume that failed — is not taken a second time once that take has settled; one still being kept is another read's, which this one stands by for (below).

**What is scrubbed.** Everything that leaves a box passes the engine's secret redaction, and a kept session more so — file by file, each as what it is, so what is kept is still the archive its harness restores:

1. **By value**, every secret the engine itself put in the box is taken out wherever it appears, raw and as a JSON string escapes it, whatever its shape — everything the launch handed the box from a **credential position**: every value a `${VAR}` resolved to, in the run's environment (the seat's `role.sandbox.env`, the setup steps' env), in a setup file that is one `${VAR}` whole, and in an MCP server's url; every variable of the run's environment whose name says it carries a credential (`…_TOKEN`, `…_KEY`, `…_SECRET`, `…_PASSWORD` and their kind) and the sign-in of the `providers.llm` entry the launch ran on, written or referenced alike; its MCP servers' env and headers; the run's own telemetry token and its credential on [Gitlet](gitlet.md); every string of the login the box was seeded with; and **every token the completion poll renews in the running box** (below). Each is taken out whole and, where it is a JSON document, by every string it holds, as the login is: a seat's AWS session reaches its box as the document its `credential_process` prints, and a transcript prints the session's token alone. **Every string, not only those under a credential's key**, since the engine can tell a document's credential from its settings by nothing but the names they are written under: so a JSON document you hand a box through a `${VAR}` — a Google Cloud service-account key, say — gives up every string of eight bytes or more it holds, its project ID and its client email among them, which every kept transcript of the seat loses wherever it names them. A format's own published constants are no secret, and stay: of a Google service-account key — a document whose `type` is exactly `service_account` — the values of `type`, `auth_uri`, `token_uri`, `auth_provider_x509_cert_url` and `universe_domain` are fixed by Google's format, the same in every key, so every googleapis.com URL the seat's tools print stays in its transcripts, while the key's private key and that key's ID, its client email and ID, its project ID and its client certificate's URL, which names the client email, go. Its members' names, numbers and booleans are never taken out, nor is a string under eight bytes, as no value that short is: a `true` or a `1` in the document, or the registry host a Docker config files its credentials under, stays. Keep a setting beside the secret instead, written in the document or in a variable of its own; the [Google Cloud integration](../integrations/google-cloud.md) issues a seat a bare token. **Nothing else**: not the seat's handle or email, a setting written in the document, a setup step's script or a file it writes in its own words — none is a secret, and taken out by value each was lost from every kept transcript that named it; a credential written in the document is the shapes' below. They are collected **at the launch**, from the very request the job was started with, and kept sealed under the fleet keyring **beside** the run's record, under a key of its own named for the job, written once the attach that starts the job has landed — never on the record, which every git request of a coding box and every listing reads whole, though only a capture, the next launch and the poll's record of a renewed token (below) read this — so a rotated secret or a renamed entry is the value the box was handed; a job that **continues in the box** the turn's previous job ran in carries that job's sealed set forward beside its own, since the box still holds those values and the session it resumes their lines; and the login is read again at the capture, in the box and on the engine host, since a refresh mints values the launch never saw. **A token the engine issues the seat** — its GitHub App token, its AWS session, its Google Cloud token — is renewed in the box's files while the run works ([the git-auth recipe](#the-git-auth-recipe)), and read again at the capture it would be another issue, never the one the box holds; so the poll **records each renewed value in the job's sealed set, beside the run's record, before it writes the file**, and the launch of a job that continues in its turn's kept box seals what its own refresh wrote with the job. A renewed value the store does not take is not written on that poll — the run keeps the token its files hold, said as `sandbox_token_refresh_failed` — and the next poll, fifteen seconds later, tries again, well inside the five minutes an AWS session's renewal leaves. So every capture of the run taken once its job has ended — by itself, asked or killed — is scrubbed of every token the poll put in its box; a capture of a job its box would not end, taken as it stands, reads the set before its pack, so a token the poll renews while that pack is made, printed meanwhile by the job still working, goes only by its shape. A renewed value is dropped from the set an hour past its expiry, since a lapsed token opens nothing, which keeps a day of an AWS session's renewals — one every ten minutes — to the few still near their lapse. In a fleet mid-upgrade, a node running an older version of the engine takes the renewed values out as it takes every other, and its own polls record none of the renewals they write. A capture that cannot know them — a launch whose secrets could not be sealed or whose write of them beside the record did not land, a continued box whose record keeps nothing of what the jobs before it were handed, past the 64 KiB a launch may keep, or a set the poll's renewals take past it once the lapsed ones are dropped (whose token is written all the same: the run needs a good token more than a kept session; `executor_session_scrub_incomplete`) — is **refused** rather than kept scrubbed of less; so is one whose login, read again, is past what a whole launch may hand (the box's own code can write that file), or whose values come to more than four times that in all. A value under eight bytes is left, as ordinary text, to the shapes below, and so is a PEM armour line — every key of its kind carries it, and the shapes read a key by it. The run's bridge token, which no value the launch handed holds, is caught by its shape instead (`crewlet_rt1…`), as every token the engine mints for a run is. **Never the name of an MCP server the launch declares**, whatever credential position also holds the same word: the name is in the company document and in every tool name of that server, so it is no secret, and taken out it left the kept session naming its tools outside the provider's pattern.
2. **By shape**, the denylist every surface redacts with — the vendor prefixes, a cloud session's among them (an AWS session's access key ID, `ASIA…`, and a Google access token, `ya29.…`, which a run can obtain by itself), a JSON Web Token, private keys, passwords, and an AWS session's secret access key and session token, which have no shape of their own and so are read as a password is, by the key AWS writes each under (`SecretAccessKey`, `aws_secret_access_key`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`, `X-Amz-Security-Token` and their kind), whoever issued the session — on every transcript line string by string, where a key's lines are lines again, every JSON document a token at a time, every key of every object as well as every value — a tool's structured result can name a member by a secret — a string or a number under a credential's own key (`password`, `api_key`, `token`, an AWS session's `SessionToken`, a Docker config's `auth`, `identitytoken` and `registrytoken`, and their kind) taken out whole, and every other file as text, redacted as it streams into exactly what the redaction of the whole file writes. A credential's key is read with the separators between its words dropped, so `aws_session_token`, `SessionToken` and `sessionToken` are each the session token's key, and AWS's `X-Amz-Security-Token` header is read by its own words, the security token's. An AWS session's secret access key or session token printed bare, under no key, is kept as printed where the run obtained the session by itself, though its access key ID goes by its shape wherever it is; a session the engine issued the seat, at its launch or renewed since, is taken out by value (above), whole and by each of its strings. A `.json` file that is not one JSON value — a task file a pack of a working job tore — is kept as text, and so is a transcript line that is not one JSON value: its torn last line, or a line of blanks, which is kept as written. A `.json` file of blanks alone holds no value, and is kept empty, as is an OpenCode export of them.

**A tool definition the scrub renamed is left out.** Claude Code keeps, in its transcript, the definition of every tool a session loaded through tool search, and sends each again with every request of a session it resumes. Where either pass put a marker inside such a definition's name, the name no longer matches the provider's pattern (`^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`) and every request of the restored session would be refused, so that definition is cut out of the record's line, with the comma that joined it to its list, and the session loads the tool again by search when it needs it. The calls the session made stay as rewritten. **The rest of the line stays as written**, the record's keys in their order above all, since Claude Code reads a session file past 5 MiB by where each line's keys sit (read in 2.1.310 and 2.1.322). Reading one as it does by default, 2.1.310 takes a record for a subagent's only where `"isSidechain":true` is in the line's first 256 bytes, and walks the thread back from the last record it takes for the main thread's: a subagent's record written again with its keys sorted, its list first, would be that record, and records the subagent wrote after it would be left out of its resumed thread. And under `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_PRECOMPACT_SKIP`, which a managed settings file can set whatever the launch unsets, Claude Code prunes the file to the conversation it resumes and finds a record only by its line beginning `{"parentUuid":`, so a record written in another order would be no record to it, and the records above it could be pruned from the resumed session. Whatever the scrub takes out, a transcript keeps every line, and each record every key in the order written and its `uuid`, `parentUuid` and `type` as written: the scrub changes what a string says, and cuts nothing out of a record but such a definition. It does write every key and string again, so an escape in a kept line can be spelled otherwise than its harness wrote it, and a lone surrogate's escape or a byte that is no UTF-8 comes out as U+FFFD.

**And the archive's own words.** A member's name is scrubbed by value and by shape, as the transcript's paths to it are, its header carries only its kind, name, mode, size and time — no owner, no link target, no extended record of the box's — and anything but a file or a directory (a link the box's own code made) is left out.

**No value is refused for its length.** A harness keeps no bound on one value: Claude Code writes a whole PDF it read on one line of its transcript, its base64 twice, about 56 MB at its 20 MiB file limit, and OpenCode keeps a message part of 27 MiB. So the scrub holds no line, string or stretch of text whole: it reads JSON a token at a time, hands each string's text to both passes a piece at a time, and writes exactly what the scrub of the whole string writes. A line, string or file of 256 KiB or more that a take found the redaction leaves unchanged is remembered by its digest, in the engine's process alone and never the text, so later takes on that node scrub it by value alone, every byte checked against what the first take found; a restart, a deploy or the seat's move to another node empties that memory, and the session's next take there costs at most what it would without it. What a line is, JSON or text, is known only at its end, and a tar names each file's size before its bytes, so the scrub's first reading writes the archive scrubbed into a spool of the take's own, gzipped in the engine process's spool directory ([below](#a-sessions-spools-on-its-node)), counting each file's size, and its second writes the tar from that spool, reading the box no more: a header always names the size of what follows it, whatever the box's archive does meanwhile. **A box that changes its archive while it is taken changes only its own session**: members before the point a first reading goes on from are kept as that reading read them, and the member it goes on in is checked by name, kind and length, the take refused where it changed. The first reading reads each line as JSON alone, and from the first that is no JSON on both ways at once, holding each way to 64 KiB until the line's way is known; a way past that is cut back out of the spool where it is not kept, and a line whose text was let go before its JSON failed is read once more, as text, all within the first reading. An OpenCode export is spooled as well, so an export the scrub refuses never reaches the session's spool, its checksum or the context meter with a byte.

**Within bounds, whatever the box wrote.** The archive is the box's own, and its code can write a gzip that expands a thousandfold or a value nested a million deep. So the scrub reads at most 256 MiB of plaintext, rewrites no JSON value nested past ten thousand levels as JSON, and holds at most about 132 MiB while it does, whatever the session holds: two redactions at once, each within its stages' windows, the readers and writers of the archive and of its spool, a line's two ways at 64 KiB each, and a plan between its two readings of a tar or an export: a bit for each element of a list of loaded tool definitions it cuts, and a few dozen for each file and each cut, at most a sixteenth of the plaintext whatever shape the box gave its session. A session past the plaintext's bound, one whose text the redaction refuses (a text built against a password's rule, or an AWS secret's quoted key, beside a key's armour, which its stream would have to decide before it knew what the rules claim there), or one not scrubbed within its time is **refused**, its stamp saying which. And a defect a box's text reaches in the scrub, or in the meter that reads what the session's last request carried beside it, never ends the engine: the scrub reads every byte of the archive on the take's own goroutine, and a panic there **refuses** the session with the panic's message (`session_scrub_panicked` logs its stack), while one in the meter leaves the session's context unmeasured (`session_meter_panicked`); each is [reported](../guides/engine-issue-reports.md) as `engine.panicked` under the `session_take` scope.

**Six minutes for the scrub, from its measured worst, and closed past it.** A take's scrub is given six minutes, sized on the slowest sessions a harness writes, measured on two cores of the build machine: the archive read twice out of a box at its floor pace of a mebibyte a second, 96 s for 48 MiB, and 256 MiB of plaintext of the slowest shape, a tool result's short assignments, which the redaction weighs at every `=` (a string of `pwd=` lines torn at its last line as a take finds a session mid-write, read on from that line, 183 s, as slow under the engine's [memory limit](../guides/deployment.md#the-engines-memory-limit); one string of `pwd=x ` repeated, 136 s, and 139 s at worst under the memory limit; a tool result's file of `pwd=x` lines, 123 s; `password: x` repeated, about 84 s). With the minute a take may first wait for its spool's room ([below](#a-sessions-spools-on-its-node)), that is 339 s counted apart, though the two readings overlap, which six minutes holds 1.06 times over. Only sessions a harness writes set it: lines that are no JSON, which only a corrupted or deliberately malformed transcript holds, scrub at 1.2 to 1.3 s a mebibyte. **A take past its time fails closed**: the session is not kept, its place is stamped refused, and the last kept copy stands, so a box can only cost its own session. A piece of 256 KiB or more holds the process's one large slot while the scrub's first reading redacts it, up to about 183 s, and other takes' large pieces and a collection's large read of a main thread wait behind it.

Then the archive is **sealed as it streams** under the fleet keyring, bound to the seat, the turn and its object, into a spool on the host's disk ([below](#a-sessions-spools-on-its-node)) — sealed there too, and removed once its keep is done, refused or dropped — and the box is paused or reclaimed; the **upload and the record are the keep's**, begun off the read the moment the take has spooled the session, so no read and no ending waits on the object store's pace, and no keep waits on what its read does after the take (a collection's record of how its job's harness ended, the box's pause and the pause's record). No step holds more than a piece of the archive. The scrub changes the archive's bytes, so the box records the kept archive's digest beside its own: carried back into the box it came from, it is never restored over the copy that box went on with.

**Recorded through the estate router, on every node.** The capture is recorded on the executor log through the [estate router](../guides/satellite-nodes.md), so a seats-only node records one through a data node as a data node records its own; under the operation the turn, the launch and the capture's place derive, asked again under that same operation while the log does not answer — for thirty seconds, which outlasts a broker's leader election — so it lands once however often it is asked.

**Every capture is stamped on the run's record.** Each launch of a turn is numbered (1, 2, …) in the write that opens it, and each capture takes its place — the launch's number and its own among that launch's captures — on the run's record before a byte moves, beside what the job had been answered and told when it was packed — its **save point**, how many of the round's calls the run's tool log had taken when the capture read it, where the job was over and its harness had exited cleanly by itself, a read made after its script packed it and before the take — every other capture, of a job still working or cut off, reads no log, and is placed at the round's start and raised after its take (above), so a log the store cannot read refuses none of those — and the last note read, where its harness ended its own run, stopped before the first read the record marks [unanswered](#notes-to-a-running-run) — a take whose answer never reached the harness, whose notes the session lacks while it holds the answered ones after them — or **restarted**, a note its session shows a hook took only before its last restart, and before the place of a note a hook served that no step has read (a capture cut off states none: it may lack its job's last serve of the notes, and is not known to hold its job's brief, which told the notes the session it continued lacked) — so a later launch that continues it knows what came after. The tool log numbers every call of a round as it takes it, so each call it takes after the read that placed a save point is one the session may not have been answered, wherever it sits among the calls the run made: a call still in flight at the read is taken once its tool answers. Off the same read — or off the capture whose save point it takes — the stamp also carries the highest bridged call and the places below it the log held no call at, which an older version of the engine reads its place by in a fleet mid-upgrade and this one does not, since a long round's dropped middle fills the places it keeps and hides a call in flight below them. Each stamp also says whether its harness was cut off — the engine packed it, or the run's script packed it after a harness that did not exit cleanly, killed by a signal or its memory limit — so it may end mid-record; and, once it is spooled, what its last request carried and the harness's own estimate of its next request, read off its own transcript as it was taken, kept or not, which a launch that continues it — restored, or as the job's own box holds it — is held to ([What a continued launch costs](#what-a-continued-launch-costs)). How it came out is stamped beside it: **landed** (the executor log names its object); **refused**, with why — a pack that failed, a session past its 48 MiB bound or the scrub's, secrets the scrub could not know, the store's reservation spent, the seat's [budget](../getting-started/configuration.md) its live turns already hold, a record the log will never take; or **unresolved** — uploaded, and its record sent and not answered, which the turn's end asks again under the same operation before it ends the turn, and a relaunch before it decides which session it continues, whatever its object's age: the executor log refuses a record past the twelve hours an object may be named in by its own clock, from the instant another node's clock minted the object's key, so a node whose clock stands ahead never refuses one the log would still take. A reader holds it as awaiting that answer until fourteen hours have passed on its own clock, the twelve and the two hours any two machines' clocks may stand apart. Every capture of a turn that read its conversation also carries that read as the turn's first launch froze it, which is what the turn's end absorbs ([below](#a-conversations-next-turn-continues-its-last-turns-session)). **And the turn's end carries the newest capture where it was not kept, and says where the turn went on past the session its row names** — wherever the run's record does not hold the turn's last word, the final capture of its last launch that ran a job, kept: a capture taken while its job still worked, an earlier launch's, the jobs after it keeping nothing newer, or one beside a newer capture that was not kept. The executor log's row keeps whatever session it names — a capture whose taker stopped, which the log took after a relaunch had read it as refused, among them — so the conversation's next turn continues what the turn did up to it rather than an older session or none, and the row says the turn went on past it, never that it is the turn's last; where the turn's newest capture was its last word, the end names that capture (`last_word`), and a row that holds it after all — the log took its record although the run's record held it refused — is read as the turn's last word ([Turn Engine](turn-engine.md#how-a-turn-ends-on-the-executor-log)).

**Of two reads of one job at once, one holds the place and the other stands by.** A stop's read and a collection's of one job can take its session at once, each streaming the archive its own pack made, or the job's own capture where its script left one (above), and the place both ask for is the coordination store's to give one of them. The other — its reservation refused, or never answered and its place found another's when it settled it, or the job's capture found begun by the first — takes the session all the same and **stands by** for that capture rather than walking away from it: named on the capture's stamp (`standby_taker`, `standby_taker_epoch`, `standby_at`) before it spools, its session sealed on its own node's disk, and its keep waiting to see what the capture comes to. Where it **lands**, the standby keeps nothing: the session is uploaded once. So too where the executor log took its record while no stamp of it reached the run's record: before it takes the place after a capture that has stood begun past the time a capture can take, or once its own wait has run out, the standby reads the turn's row on the log once, whatever the coordination store answers of that capture's taker lease, and keeps nothing where the row names the capture, whether or not the run's record then takes it as landed (below). Where it does not — the read holding the place had its scrub refused, its seal or its upload fail, or its node stop before it uploaded — the standby takes the place after it and keeps its own session there; and where that read's record went unanswered, the standby asks it again under its own operation, as the turn's end does, keeping nothing where the log holds it and its own where the log refuses it, so the session is never uploaded twice beside a record that landed. A read that walked away once left such a failed place to keep nothing, though it held the session whole. A loss's read does the same: it once passed the box over wherever the job's final capture was on the record, one still being kept included, and reclaimed it unread beside a keep that could still fail; it now passes over only one that has settled. **A read of the job ended beside a capture taken as the job stood** — a stop's read whose end could neither end its job nor poll it — takes the place after it instead of standing by, since its session is the more whole, and is kept whatever the other comes to. The standby waits, on its own clock, for as long as the capture it stands by for can live (its take with its reservation, its keep with that keep's two reads, every change of its record, which any node may make, so each given the thirteen minutes a change of a record at its bound takes to cross a link at the slowest pace allowed, [below](#what-a-runs-record-and-its-log-keep), and for a takeover the takeover's own changes and its read of the record back, given the four minutes a read's reply takes: about an hour and eleven minutes at the bounds), and then reads the turn's row on the executor log once, for that capture still begun, keeping nothing where the row names it, whatever its taker's lease and whether or not the run's record takes that capture's landed settle, and reads the record once more: that capture still begun or refused, it takes the place after it; landed, it keeps nothing; its record still awaiting the log's answer, it stands down.
