A key is spelled for a ref: every character outside letters, digits, `_` and `-` becomes `-`, and a key that had to be respelled (or already ends like one) takes a dash and twelve hex digits of its own digest, so keys that spell alike are two branches. A changed key starts a new branch |
| `base` | The branch, tag or commit (a whole id or its first seven or more hex digits) to start from | The branch's head where it exists, else the default branch's; an empty repository has none, and the first commit starts the branch |
| `access` | `read` (fetch only) or `write` (and push) | `write` where the box could push the branch (the seat's grant lets it; in a colleague's turn the branch is the seat's own or one the colleague could push too; in a credential's turn the seat's own), else `read`: a read-only seat naming a repository to look at is not refused |
| `paths` | A cone of directories to check out, for a large repository | The whole tree |
| `change` | A [change](gitlet.md) to work on, by number (`42`) or reference (`web!42`): the run works on its source branch from the head it holds, so pushes are the change's next revisions. Never beside `branch` or `base`. Read once, linearizable; a closed or merged change is refused | No change: the branch above |
| `open_change` | `{target, title, draft}`: open a change from the run's branch once the run is done; see [A run's changes](#a-runs-changes). Needs `write`, never beside `change` (whose branch heads one already) | No change opened |

**Whose grant judges it.** Reads are at the seat's level, judged by the seat's grant on the node that answers, and in a turn somebody woke by **that person's or colleague's grant too**: a box is never given a repository its requester could not read. A turn woken by a stranger, a person who may not act or a person without the Gitlet permission is given none: the checkout is refused, naming Gitlet for the person without it, before anything is read ([ADR-0110](../../adr/0110-reaching-a-repository-takes-the-gitlet-permission.md)).

- **Colleague seat's turn:** the record names the colleague, and Gitlet holds the box to the colleague's grant on every request: what it may fetch, and what it may push outside the seat's own `seats/<handle>/` ([Gitlet → Coding boxes](gitlet.md#coding-boxes)).
- **Credential's turn (no seat, e.g. a pipeline's token):** the record names the credential. The box fetches what it was given (the credential reads every repository itself) and pushes the seat's own work alone (its `seats/<handle>/` and the repositories it owns), since the credential pushes to no repository itself.
- Whoever the turn works for is carried on every push of the box and on the change its run opens.

A checkout is refused, before anything is written and naming the repository and why, for:

- a repository the seat may not read, or one deleted or being purged;
- `write` on an archived repository, or on a branch the box could not push: one the seat's grant does not allow (a seat outside the owning unit pushes only under its own `seats/<handle>/`), one only maintain moves (another seat's namespace), in a colleague's turn one outside the seat's namespace the colleague could not push, or in a credential's any outside the seat's own work;
- a `base` the repository does not hold; a `change` it does not hold or that is closed or merged;
- an `open_change` whose target branch does not exist or is the run's own, whose title is not one line of at most 256 bytes, or that comes to a run that could not push its branch;
- a repository where the company hosts no code (`code.backend` is not `gitlet`), where this node does not serve Gitlet yet (a restart owed), or where this node has no `CREWLET_BOX_GIT_URL`, the address a box reaches Gitlet at (logged `sandbox_git_url_unset`).

A checkout costs a few reads at the seat's level: the repository, a `change` it names, then every ref it needs (branch, a base named as a ref, default branch, an `open_change` target) in one; a base named by id takes one more read. A scratch repository the run checked out is held from expiry while the run is unended, whichever later launch replaced its grants (see [Gitlet](gitlet.md)).

**Its git is the engine's to configure.** Every run launched on a node that serves Gitlet gets its Gitlet access, minted once the job is named and never written on the run's record:

- the run's credential, a token naming the turn and THIS launch, so a job a later launch replaced is refused at once whatever its expiry. It reaches nothing until a checkout grants a repository. It is written to a file in the box before the job starts (`~/.crewlet/git-access`, readable by the box's user alone), and the environment holds only that file's path, `CREWLET_GIT_ACCESS_FILE`: the token is in no variable a model's tool shell, a harness's hook or any process the run starts could print or hand on, and it is scrubbed by value from what the run's session keeps. `CREWLET_GIT_URL` is the launching node's `CREWLET_BOX_GIT_URL` as the box dials it (a loopback one, in a `container` box, under the [runtime's name for the engine host](#local-sandboxes)), which every clone's remote names.
- git's configuration through the environment: the run environment's own entries are **kept** (a proxy or CA bundle) and the engine's are appended after them, so for the credential, identity, protocol and index its value wins. Two go in `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS`, which git reads after every `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` entry, so a harness whose shell appends count entries emptying `credential.helper` (Gemini CLI's does) still reaches Gitlet:
  - an empty `credential.<base>/.helper`, `<base>` being `CREWLET_GIT_URL`, the URL git dials, clearing every earlier credential helper for Gitlet's URL, so a `credential.helper store` from a setup step is neither asked for the token nor told to save it;
  - a helper answering git's credential request with the run's token, read from the file `CREWLET_GIT_ACCESS_FILE` names each time git asks.

  Five go in `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, `GIT_CONFIG_KEY_<n>`, `GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_<n>`, which no harness empties:
  - `user.name` and `user.email`, the seat's identity as a commit the engine builds for it names it: its role's name and `email:`, else its handle on `code.identity_domain`;
  - `protocol.version 2`, which partial clones and fetches by id need;
  - `index.version 4` with `core.untrackedCache true`, the index settings a wide checkout's `git status` was [measured](#what-a-clone-costs) faster with: what `feature.manyFiles` sets minus its `index.skipHash`, which writes an index older libgit2 builds refuse.
- A run environment whose own `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` is not a count, or names an entry it does not set, is refused naming it (git would fail every clone), and so is a `CREWLET_BOX_GIT_URL` holding `=`, which no `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` item can name in a credential key.

The identity is a **convention**, never a check: generated code can set any committer, and the push's record, never a commit header, says which run pushed what. The names the engine sets (`CREWLET_GIT_ACCESS_FILE`, `CREWLET_GIT_URL`, and what a [check's box](#check-boxes) is told of its check) are **reserved**: `role.sandbox.env`, every setup step's `env` and the company's check secrets (`code.checks.env`) are refused naming one: a value there would break a box's clones or tell a check's command another check than its own. A run launched where the company hosts no code, or on a node that does not serve Gitlet, gets none of this.

**How a box is given one.** Nothing is cloned at launch. A checkout's answer carries the commands the agent runs in its working directory, in order: a check of the box's git, then the clone. They run in the box's shell with the job's environment and credential, and cost only when the repository is asked for. An executor's clone is:

- **blobless** (`git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout`): every commit and tree, file contents fetched as git needs them (the agent rebases, logs and blames, so it needs the history, rarely every file);
- of the **default branch alone** (`--single-branch`): the history of the branch the repository's `HEAD` names, with its tags, as a local branch and `origin/<default>`, and **no other branch**. Most branches are other seats' work ([a seat's own branches](gitlet.md#who-may-read-and-push)); sending all would grow the clone with the company's work and pull every seat's next push on `git fetch`. The remote tracks the default branch alone, so `git fetch` or `git pull` moves only that; another branch is fetched by name (`git fetch origin <branch>`, which leaves it at `FETCH_HEAD`), which the environment block tells the agent. git still lists every ref name (about eighty bytes each) but the host sends no object of an unwanted branch: [measured](#what-a-clone-costs), ten thousand seats' branches add 0.8 MB of listing and no objects;
- narrowed to its **cone** where one is named (`git sparse-checkout set --cone`): only those directories and the top level's files are checked out and fetched. A directory name starting with `!` or holding a glob character is taken literally;
- at its **base**, fetched by id (a base off the default branch, such as a continued branch's tip or a deleted branch's commit, sends only what the clone lacks), on its **branch**, made there (`git checkout -B`);
- never **treeless** (it would fetch each tree a walk touches one request at a time), and never from a **bundle URI** (a filtered client still downloads it whole).

An empty repository is cloned with its branch as the unborn `HEAD`, so the first commit starts it. After the commands, the answer tells the harness what they make true: where the checkout is, its branch and starting commit, that the clone holds the default branch alone and how another is fetched, its cone, and how it pushes (or, for a read repository, that a push is refused). The environment block names no repository, as none is given at launch.

**Where the checkout is.** At `./<name>`, in the directory the box's commands and the harness start in (the box's workspace, [Local sandboxes](#local-sandboxes)), so both agree on the path without naming it.

**A reused box keeps its checkouts.** A later launch that reattaches to the box an earlier one left applies nothing to it, neither setup nor clone, so checkouts and the agent's work are as it left them. A carried-on round keeps its job's grants; checking one out again answers commands whose guard skips a repository already there. A box that lost its clone (a fresh one the round was launched in) is given it again by the same call, cloned at its branch's head, so it carries on from everything pushed before. A failing command is the run's to read: git's own words, and the version check's sentence below.

**And none of the files the job before was started with.** Before a job starts in a reused box, the box removes what the job before was handed: its brief, standing instructions, settings and MCP configuration, markers and session pieces, never the harness's session store, which the new job continues. The new job's files are then written as new ones. On a `container` box whose home is mounted across a VM (Docker Desktop), this lets the harness read them as it starts: the box keeps its entry for a file replaced from the host side for about a second, and a harness opening it then finds nothing.

**The box's git.** It must be **2.40 or newer**, Gitlet's floor for every client. The check is the first command a checkout answers; where the image, or a `direct` box's host, has no git or an older one (Apple's bundled git is 2.39) it stops the clone, naming the git found and the floor. A box image is the operator's to keep current.

### What a run pushed is reported for it

A run's report says what it delivered in its `Delivered:` lines, and a box writes it as it likes. What it pushed to **Gitlet** is not taken from the report: every push is recorded under the run that made it ([Gitlet → Coding boxes](gitlet.md#coding-boxes)), and at collection the engine reads those records and writes what each ref became on the collected executor's record, which the reviewer reads beside the run's own refs. The harness is told in its standing instructions that pushes to repositories it may push to are reported for it, and asked for `Delivered:` lines only for what it delivered elsewhere.

**What the reviewer reads.** After the run's own `Delivered:` line, one line per ref the run moved, in the order it first pushed each, every repository in the order the run was given them:

```
Pushed to Gitlet (its push record):
- web refs/heads/seats/swe/ENG-42 1a2b3c4d5e6f → 4d5e6f7a8b9c (3 pushes), change web!42
- web refs/heads/seats/swe/spike created at 9f8e7d6c5b4a
- api refs/heads/seats/swe/old deleted (it was 0a1b2c3d4e5f)
```

Each ref is **what it became**, never every step: the old value of the run's first push, the new value of its last, and how many pushes moved it (a rebase loop is fifty pushes of one branch). A branch that heads a live [change](gitlet.md) at collection names it, whether the run was launched on it, [opened it](#a-runs-changes), or anybody did. A command Gitlet refused is left out. The list shares the run's own refs' bound, 16 KiB of lines for both (the run's own first), and stops at the first ref that does not fit, the rest counted (`- and N more ref(s) its push record names, not listed here`).

**Never silence.** A run given a repository it may push to is always told something: the refs, or `nothing — no push of this run was recorded`, or, where the record could not be read, `unknown`, why, and the branches to read with `code_resolve` before reporting them. An unreadable record does **not** hold the run back: collection goes on and says so (logged `sandbox_pushes_unread`), since retrying until Gitlet answers would hold a finished run's seat while Gitlet is down. A read stopped by the collecting node itself (a drain, a seat moving) is the collection interrupted, handed back and collected again. A run given its repositories only to read is told it could push none, with no read.

**What it costs.** One read for a collected run that could push: the first page **linearizable**, so "nothing" is never stale, and later pages at `session` at the first page's position. It scans the run's own repositories' pushes since launch rather than keeping an index of every box push on every data node ([Gitlet](gitlet.md#coding-boxes)). The engine holds at most 1 024 refs (more than a record can list), counting the rest, so a looping box costs the collecting node no more memory than a record carries. Past those, a ref with no room is counted once per push that moved it.

Naming the changes costs one more read and no second barrier: one `branch_changes` read of every branch the run pushed on every repository it may push to, and of each branch of a change it asked to open (one index seek a branch, one transaction; more than a thousand branches take two), at `session` at the record's first page's position. That page's barrier already followed every push and every change they opened, so the read answers what a linearizable one would, and a collection appends one barrier to the code log however many repositories it names. A failed read names no change and holds nothing back (logged `sandbox_changes_unread`).

**Where it is recorded.** The refs ride the run's phase record and the collected executor's as `pushed_refs`, each `{repo, ref, old, new, pushes, change}`, with whole object ids and `change` the change the branch heads (`web!42`, absent for none), beside `pushed_refs_elided` (how many more the record names) and `pushed_refs_unread` (why it could not be read). A run that parks on a question has them on its own record, and the run that carries on is collected again for what it pushes since.

### A run's changes

A run works on a change when a checkout names one (a repository's `change`, by number or reference), and is given its source branch from the head it holds, so every push is the change's next revision. It **opens** one when a checkout asks (a repository's `open_change`, `{target, title, draft}`), and the engine opens it at collection, from the branch the run delivered:

| Field | What it is | Left out |
|---|---|---|
| `target` | The branch the change proposes the run's branch into, resolved at the checkout; it must exist and differ from the run's | The repository's default branch at the checkout |
| `title` | The change's title, one line of at most 256 bytes | The subject of the commit the run delivered its branch at (as `git push -o change` titles its change), else the branch's name as one line, else `commit` and the commit's short id: an ask is never left unopened for its title |
| `draft` | Open it as a draft, not yet asking to be merged | Open, asking to be merged |

**At the collection, once, by the seat.** A box could open a change itself with `git push -o change` ([Gitlet](gitlet.md)), but a harness pushes as it goes, and a change opened at its first push asks reviewers to read work in progress. So the engine opens it once the run is done, and only for a run that **finished**: it succeeded and stopped on no question.

- A run that did not succeed is told it opened none and why, so the turn decides whether half the work merits review (`code_open_change`). A run parked on a question opens none; the run that carries on after the answer keeps the ask and opens it on finishing.
- The change is opened as the seat the run is for (owner and first author), from the branch's head as the push record left it, into the resolved target, carrying the run's work item and naming the turn and run that opened it: the open a `code_open_change` of the same turn would make, decided by the repository's committer.
- It is made for whoever the turn works for, held to them as the box's pushes are. In a credential's turn it opens only the seat's own work (a branch under its namespace, or a repository it owns). In a colleague seat's turn the committer judges the open for that colleague too, from its own chart at that time, so a colleague a configuration change shut out of the repository while the run worked has no change opened for them, the seat's own work excepted, as for the tool ([Writes made for somebody else](gitlet.md#writes-made-for-somebody-else)).
- Its operation derives from the launch's id and the instant it began, so a collection retried (on this or another node, after a restart) asks the same open, opens nothing twice, and names the change as the one it opened.
- A branch that already heads a live change (the run's own `git push -o change`, or anybody's) opens no other: the run is told that change.
- Changes on several repositories are opened **at once**, so the collection, which holds the seat, waits for the slowest open rather than every open in turn.

**What the reviewer reads.** After the pushed refs, one line per ask:

```
Changes on Gitlet (opened at the run's collection):
- web!42 opened from seats/swe/ENG-42 for review
- seats/swe/ENG-7 already headed api!5, so no other was opened
- docs: no change opened from seats/swe/ENG-42 — the run pushed nothing to its branch, so there was no work to propose
- site: no change opened from seats/swe/ENG-42 — the node that answered runs a build that cannot read the request, so nothing of the open ran; the commits the run pushed are kept, and the change is the seat's to open again with code_open_change, which a node of this build answers
- app: no change opened from seats/swe/ENG-42 — no Gitlet node could take it, so nothing of the open ran; the commits the run pushed are kept, and the change is the seat's to open again with code_open_change
```

A refusal is Gitlet's own sentence (a target merged into since, a branch at its target's commit, or whom the open is made for where the committer's chart moved since checkout, such as a person's seat the company no longer has); nothing of a refused open ran and the pushed commits are kept. An open of unknown outcome says so and why: Gitlet could not be asked, or did not say. An open that ran nowhere says so, as the last two lines do: every committer asked answered that it ran nothing, and none went silent (a committer that never answered may have opened it, which makes the outcome unknown).

- During a rolling upgrade a committer of an older build cannot read whom the open is made for. Where none of the newer build took it, the line says the node that answered runs a build that cannot read the request; the open made again is answered by a newer node.
- Otherwise the line says no Gitlet node could take it: every committer was out of service, could not run it, or was behind.

Either way nothing of the open ran, the pushed commits are kept, and the change is the seat's to open again with `code_open_change`. The collection does not retry itself, since it holds the run's seat until the turn resumes and the roll or outage may outlast it. Each line is a fact, never a step (the reviewer holds no code tools); the one act it names, the open made again, it names as the seat's. None holds the collection back (logged `sandbox_change_unopened`, with the failure in its own words).

**A box's own push opens on the run's work item too.** A box's `git push -o change` opens its change in the push's own record ([Gitlet](gitlet.md)). The box's admission stamps every push with the run's work item (tracker and key, identity and project), so that change carries the item as the engine's own open does, and every notice about it names the item's project either way.

### Commit trailers

A commit the run makes as itself in a coding clone carries the trailers [Commit attribution](#commit-attribution) adds to every run's own commits (the co-author line, and the seat, run and work item its turn is charged to), unless the company set `providers.sandbox.commit_attribution` to `false`:

```text
Co-authored-by: Crewlet <noreply@crewlet.com>
Crewlet-Seat: swe
Crewlet-Run: 0190d8f0-1111-7000-8000-000000000001
Crewlet-Work-Item: native ENG-7
```

The clone writes no hook: the run's own hooks directory, which its environment points git at, adds them, so a repository's `core.hooksPath` (husky's) neither removes them nor is removed by them. `Crewlet-Run` is the turn the run belongs to, the one its page is addressed by (Live › Executors); a push's record names the same turn beside the job that made it.

The trailers are a **convention**, never a check: a box can unset the entry, delete the hook or type any trailer, and nothing in the engine reads a pushed commit's trailers. The push's **record is the provenance** (seat, run, harness, turn, work item and model, stamped from the run's record at admission, whatever its commits say). A trailer is best-effort provenance only where that record does not reach:

- in a mirror of the repository on another host, which carries commits, never push records. A mirror publishes the trailers: the seat's handle, the turn id (grants nothing) and the work item's key go wherever the commit goes;
- for a commit older than the push history's 181 days, where a trailer its box kept is the one note of the run and work item left in git itself.

A commit the engine **builds** (`code_commit_files`, a revert, a cherry-pick) carries none: its message is its caller's, its author the seat or person who acted and its committer the engine (see [Gitlet](gitlet.md)), so past the push history's horizon it names its seat but not its turn or work item.
### What a clone costs

Measured from the box's side (`internal/gitlet/host`'s `BenchmarkBoxClone`, `BenchmarkBoxWorktree` and `BenchmarkBoxDissociate`): a box launched as the engine launches it (run given the repository, token minted for the launch, requests on `/box/git/`, steps and git under the engine's environment) against a Gitlet node holding the repository warm (multi-pack-index, bitmap and commit-graph written). Setup: two E-cores of an Intel Core Ultra 7 265U, Go 1.27.2, git 2.56.0 (the node pin, which the image builds) in node and box unless a figure names the client floor's 2.40.4, the engine's in-memory object store (a warm node serves a clone from its own disk; no real bucket was measured), one count per arm: ten operations, one at a gigabyte, five for the borrowing (`make bench BENCH_PKGS=./internal/gitlet/host BENCH_PATTERN=BoxClone BENCH_TIME=10x`, likewise for each). Histories and trees are the benchmarks' seeded ones, files of 4 KiB in directories of 48.

**The two recipes**, a box cloning 100 MiB of history (44 800 commits; tip: 138 files in three directories) and 1 GiB (455 680 commits; 1 421 files), mean of the arm's clones:

| Recipe | 100 MiB, 2.56.0 (2.40.4) | What the node sent, and the box holds | 1 GiB | What the node sent, and the box holds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `coding`, the whole tree | 1.25 s (0.94 s) | 16.7 MB, 0.57 MB of it the checkout's files; 134 538 objects; 345 ms of the node's CPU | 14.6 s | 179 MB, 5.8 MB of files; 1 368 461 objects; 4.3 s of CPU |
| `coding`, one directory's cone | 1.03 s (1.19 s) | 16.3 MB, 0.20 MB of files; 134 448 objects; 295 ms | 13.3 s | 173 MB, 0.20 MB of files; 1 367 088 objects; 3.5 s |
| `single-sha`, the whole tree | 0.13 s (0.23 s) | 0.57 MB; 143 objects; 74 ms | 0.99 s | 5.9 MB; 1 453 objects; 0.83 s |
| `single-sha`, one directory's cone | 0.10 s (0.15 s) | 0.20 MB; 53 objects; 33 ms | 0.13 s | 0.23 MB; 80 objects; 52 ms |

Each recipe is two fetches: the clone's (the check's one commit) and one lazy fetch of every file the checkout writes, so a build reading the whole checkout asks git for nothing more. **A coding clone is its history's commits and trees**: a cone narrows only the files written and leaves the clone as long (13.3 s against 14.6 at a gigabyte), so `paths` is for a tree too wide to write, never for a long history. At about 14 s a gigabyte on these cores, a coding clone at the 20 GiB `repo_max_bytes` default is about five minutes, inside the ten minutes a setup step is given; at a gigabyte it is well inside a fifth of that, so a run's brief says nothing of history size and the step's timeout stays.

**Beside other seats' branches.** The coding recipe at 100 MiB on the pin, whole tree, with 0, 1 000 and 10 000 other seats' branches beside the default branch (three commits off the tip each, pushed a thousand branches a push so their packs stand beside the node's indexed one as recent pushes do), against a control that clones as git does by default, wanting every branch shown; three clones an arm (`BENCH_PATTERN=BoxClone/size=100MB/seats= BENCH_TIME=3x`):

| Other seats' branches | The recipe: the default branch alone | The control: every branch |
|---|---|---|
| none | 1.08 s; 16.7 MB sent, 0.4 KB of it the listing; 134 538 objects; 336 ms of the node's CPU | — |
| 1 000 | 1.06 s; 16.8 MB, 79 KB the listing; 134 538 objects; 344 ms | 1.19 s; 18.7 MB; 143 538 objects; 384 ms |
| 10 000 | 2.58 s; 17.5 MB, 799 KB the listing; 134 538 objects; 441 ms | 2.41 s; 26.7 MB; 224 538 objects; 1 038 ms |

**What the recipe's box receives does not grow with the company's work**: the same 134 538 objects beside ten thousand branches as beside none; only the listing grows, about 80 bytes a branch. The control grows nine objects a branch: ten thousand branches send it 90 000 objects and 9.2 MB more it has no use for, at over twice the recipe's node CPU, and its remote would bring every seat's next push into the box on the agent's own `git fetch`. At ten thousand branches both clones were slower, the recipe as much as the control, which neither objects sent nor node CPU explain; three clones an arm on two shared cores say no more.

**The box's own git in a wide tree.** Medians of ten warm runs of `git status`, of `git commit -qam` of one changed file, and of the coding clone's checkout, in a tree of 4 KiB files in directories of 48 — on git's own index settings and on the engine's (`index.version 4`, `core.untrackedCache true`):

| | 10 000 files | 100 000 files | 100 000, one directory's cone |
|---|---|---|---|
| status, git's own settings | 17.8 ms | 142 ms (140–148) | 21.6 ms |
| status, the engine's | 15.0 ms | 99.2 ms (98.0–101) | 19.0 ms |
| commit, git's own / the engine's | 26.9 / 27.2 ms | 172 / 161 ms | 55.5 / 60.9 ms |
| checkout, git's own / the engine's | 0.83 / 0.81 s | 15.4 / 15.6 s | 0.24 / 0.25 s |

A setting joins a box's git where, at 100 000 files with no cone, it cuts a warm status by at least a quarter, by more than the run spread (10th to 90th percentile, in brackets), and lengthens the checkout by at most a tenth:

- **The index settings are the engine's**, entries of its git environment: status 30 % faster (142 to 99 ms), checkout 1.5 % longer (15.4 to 15.6 s).
- **No box is given git's file-system monitor** (`core.fsmonitor`): every box's daemons would spend the engine user's inotify watches, shared with every other seat's harness and file watcher, and a monitor the kernel starves of watches costs more than none.
- **Git's automatic maintenance is left as git has it, and a long session's lazy fetches gather as packs.** A session of an agent's commands in a blobless clone (status, grep, three of a file's changes with patches, each pass over files further back, the recent log, four files changed and committed) ran 200 rounds, its lazy fetches leaving 602 packs (one count per arm, `BENCH_PATTERN=BoxWorktree/session BENCH_TIME=1x`). git 2.55.0 and 2.56.0 never repack them: their automatic maintenance, which every commit and fetch runs, behaves as `maintenance.strategy=geometric` does, whose geometric repack never fires on a blobless clone's lazy-fetch (promisor) packs, and gc is no task of it (git 2.40.4, which runs gc after a fetch, kept the same clone at 12 packs). The cost is every command's reading of them: first ten rounds to last ten, a status's CPU went from 2.4 to 10.4 ms, a `log -p`'s from 49 to 157 ms and a commit's from 11 to 32 ms, over a 20 MB history and a 100 MiB one alike (2.7 to 10.4, 49 to 150, 12 to 35 ms), in a session of 27 to 30 s of git CPU. Every bound git's own configuration offers costs the session more than the 5 % of its git CPU a box's maintenance is held to, and more the longer the history, since each repacks or rewalks what the clone holds while the packs removed do not grow with it:

  | Bound, set in the checkout | Its share of the session's git CPU, 20 MB / 100 MiB | The session's git CPU with it, against 27–30 s without |
  |---|---|---|
  | gc (`maintenance.gc.enabled`): every pack repacked into one at fifty | 12.5 % / 40 % (12 gcs, 163 and 786 ms each) | 15.7 / 23.5 s |
  | gc keeping every pack of a mebibyte or more (`gc.bigPackThreshold`) | 30 % / 67 % | 20.2 / 44.8 s |
  | the incremental repack (`maintenance.incremental-repack.enabled`): a multi-pack-index and batches | 32 % / 68 % | 20.0 / 49.1 s |

  The plain gc costs the session less in all than the packs did at both sizes, its commands' cost staying flat, and run detached as git runs it, it met no command's lock in 72 commands beside it. But its cost follows the history (five times the history, five times the gc), so past about 150 MB of history it would cost more than the packs it removes. Nothing is set; whether a box's checkout should run gc is a decision for repositories of the size a company keeps.

The million-file tree's arm runs only under `CREWLET_BENCH_LARGE` and was not measured: the in-process store would hold its 4.1 GB of packs in memory beside the fleet and the box, past the 8 GiB the benchmarks' runner gives a run.

**Borrowing the node's copy.** A box's checkout and a build reading every file, by the coding recipe, against a clone that borrows the node's copy and then copies it (`git clone --reference <the node's copy> --dissociate`, a repack of the whole history); five of each at 100 MiB, one at a gigabyte:

| | 100 MiB | 1 GiB |
|---|---|---|
| the coding recipe | 1.14 s; the box's git 1.03 s of CPU, the node's 0.36 s; 16.7 MB sent | 13.0 s; 12.2 s, 3.7 s; 179 MB |
| a borrowed copy | 2.59 s; 3.40 s, 3 ms; nothing sent | 47.8 s; 58.1 s, 3 ms; nothing sent |

Copying costs a box several times the clone it saves the node (3.7 times at a gigabyte, where borrowing would be worth designing only under half), so no box copies one. A borrow kept for a run's life and never copied is not built either: a [check's box](#check-boxes) fetches its one commit as every box does, on a Gitlet node as anywhere; lending a container that node's copy instead is [crewlet/crewlet#496](https://github.com/crewlet/crewlet/issues/496), which would measure such a borrow against the fetch first. How boxes share a node's transfer slots with people and CI is Gitlet's [fair share](gitlet.md#fair-share).

---

## Check boxes

A repository's [checks](gitlet.md#checks) run in boxes of this same catalogue, but a check's box is no executor's. It runs one command a repository defines (build, tests, linter) against one commit, and nothing of a seat's:

- **No harness.** No harness is installed, no model's sign-in is in its environment, no subscription login is seeded, and **none of `providers.sandbox.setup` is applied**: those steps provision coding boxes, their `env` and files are often credentials, and a check runs a change's own code. A box for a check that names a harness or carries a login is refused before any box exists. A check's box gets, beyond its image, its git's floor check (the [coding box's](#repositories-on-gitlet): 2.40 or newer), its checkout, and the secrets the check names.
- **Its cell** is `container`, on the Gitlet node that claimed the check, made from `providers.sandbox.local.image`. A company hosting code that sets no image runs no check: each ends errored `defs_invalid`, its reason naming that field. **A check never runs `direct`**: a `direct` box would run a change's own code as the engine's user on the engine host, reading what the engine reads, including the keyring every run's token is signed under. Unlike an executor, where `direct` is [warned about](#security-model) rather than refused: a seat's cell is its operator's choice for its own work, while a check's code is whatever was pushed. The image holds git and whatever the checks build with, and the engine builds the container backend for it as for a seat.
- **Its checkout** is its one commit, detached, on no branch, with the cone its file names (`checkout: [dirs]`) or the whole tree, or no checkout (`checkout: none`) for a check that reads its commit [through the API](gitlet.md#check-boxes). It is **fetched** as a setup step named `checkout <name>` in a failure: a repository initialised with Gitlet as its remote, the commit fetched by id at depth one, blobless, and checked out, files fetched as the checkout needs. A container on a Gitlet node is not given that node's copy to read from: its checkout is one fetch of one commit, under the same [fair share](gitlet.md#fair-share) as every box's fetch.

**Its environment** is the company's check secrets the check names in its file's `env` (each entry of `code.checks.env`, a `${VAR}` reference resolved when the box is made, and none it does not name); Gitlet's credential and base as a coding box's (the token in its file, named by `CREWLET_GIT_ACCESS_FILE`, user name `check`, and `CREWLET_GIT_URL`) but no commit identity, since a check acts as nobody; and what the check is:

| Variable | What it is |
|---|---|
| `CREWLET_CHECK_REPO` | The repository's name: the checkout is at `./<name>` |
| `CREWLET_CHECK_SHA` | The commit the check measures, the one checked out |
| `CREWLET_CHECK_BASE` | The commit it is measured against: the base its diff is read from |
| `CREWLET_CHECK_NAME` | The check's name in its file |
| `CREWLET_CHECK_ATTEMPT` | Which attempt of the check this is |
| `CREWLET_CHECK_API` | Where the box reads its commit without a clone (`/box/gitlet/<name>/…` on the listener `CREWLET_GIT_URL` names), with its own credential |
| `CREWLET_CHECK_SUMMARY` | A file the check's command may write a one-paragraph summary of its result to, read when it ends |

These names are **reserved** as Gitlet's are: `code.checks.env`, `role.sandbox.env` and every setup step's `env` are refused naming one.

**How long it runs** is its file's `timeout_seconds`, held to the company's `code.checks.max_timeout_seconds`, unset an hour: GitLab CI's and Azure Pipelines' default job timeout, and the longest one hung check holds one of its node's `gitlet.max_checks` slots. A check's box is given ten minutes past its timeout for setup. A company whose checks take longer raises it up to six hours, the most any checks file may ask ([Configuration → Code](../getting-started/configuration.md#code)).

**How many run** is bounded per Gitlet node, by its `gitlet.max_checks`. A check held back waits queued, claimed by nobody, until there is room ([What a check costs](gitlet.md#what-a-check-costs)).

**A box nothing named is still reclaimed.** A check's box records its attempt when it is made, before its runner holds a handle to it, so one the attempt's row never names (its create's answer lost, its teardown refused, or its runner gone before naming it) is reclaimed by its node's check runner once the attempt has ended ([Who runs a check](gitlet.md#who-runs-a-check)).

---

## Commit attribution

The recipe above commits as the seat, so the seat is each commit's author. Additionally, every commit a run makes as itself credits Crewlet and names the seat, run and work item:

```
Co-authored-by: Crewlet <noreply@crewlet.com>
Crewlet-Seat: swe
Crewlet-Run: 6f0c2a41-…
Crewlet-Work-Item: native ENG-7
```

- **`Co-authored-by`** is the trailer GitHub turns into a participant on the commit. The address belongs to Crewlet's own GitHub account, so the commit shows Crewlet beside the seat. It is not `Signed-off-by`: that certifies the Developer Certificate of Origin, which only whoever answers for the code can do, and credits nobody.
- **`Crewlet-Seat`** is the seat's handle, and **`Crewlet-Work-Item`** the work item its turn is charged to, as tracker and key (`native ENG-7`, `jira OPS-12`; the tracker alone for an item with no key), or `none` for a turn on no item (written rather than left out, so a rewritten commit keeps no other run's item). Each value is one word of printable characters: a key holding a space, newline or `%` is written as `%XX` and decodes back.
- **`Crewlet-Run`** is the turn the run belongs to, the one its dashboard page is addressed by (Live › Executors), so every launch of one turn names the same run.

On unless `providers.sandbox.commit_attribution` is `false`, which turns all four off for every run launched from then on: a company wanting no Crewlet credit wants no trailer either. The trailers are a convention, never a check; nothing in the engine reads them, and on Gitlet a push's record is the provenance ([Commit trailers](#commit-trailers)).

**Git adds the credit, not the model.** Each run's box is given a `prepare-commit-msg` hook, and the run's environment points git at it: a `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` item setting `core.hooksPath`, appended to any the box already sets after its login profile is read. Git reads that variable after every `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` entry, so a harness whose shell appends entries emptying `core.hooksPath` (Gemini CLI's does) still runs the hook, and so do plain `git`, git by its full path and `--no-verify`. No git configuration file is written, so your setup recipe's `git config --global` and the repository's settings stay. Git runs `prepare-commit-msg` on every commit, including with `--no-verify`, so the credit does not depend on the agent remembering. A harness may add its own line too, such as Claude Code's `Co-Authored-By: Claude`; the two sit side by side.

**The repository's own hooks still run.** The run's hooks directory stands in for the repository's, and every hook in it hands on to the repository's hook of the same name, from `.git/hooks` or the repository's own `core.hooksPath` (husky's, say), setting aside a harness's empty `core.hooksPath` entry when it looks. A repository hook that refuses a commit still refuses it.

**Only the run's own commits.** A commit is credited only when its author is the identity the run commits as. A person's commit the run amends, rewords, cherry-picks or rebases keeps its author and gets no credit. A commit of the run's own that it amends, rebases or cherry-picks carries **one of each** Crewlet trailer, naming the run that rewrote it, never a second set; the co-author line is added only where not already there, so a person already credited stays credited. A message git would refuse as empty, an untouched template, and a message given whole whose every line starts with the comment character (`git commit -m '#42 fix'`) are left to git and carry none.

**What it does not reach:**

- A commit made through a code host's API, such as a GitHub tool that writes a file, runs no git in the box.
- A command run with `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` removed from its environment (`env -u GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS git commit`) is not pointed at the hook.
- A hook the repository keeps under a name git did not have when this build shipped is not handed on while the run's entry stands.

The credit never stops a commit: a failed hook lookup hands nothing on and credits nothing, and a credit that cannot be written lets the commit through with a one-line warning.

---

## Credentials and the run environment

The engine assembles each job's run env at launch (`internal/engine/sandbox.go`), and `internal/sandbox/launch.go` adds the telemetry variables. The engine contributes **no credential** of a tool's but the agent's own at an integration it is on at ([below](#an-agents-own-integration-credentials)), only these facts and settings. For Gitlet, a run launched where it is served gets **access to that surface**: its run's credential and git configuration, reaching exactly the repositories it checks out, as every run gets the tool bridge's endpoint: a credential the box acts as, scoped to the run and dying with it (see [Repositories on Gitlet](#repositories-on-gitlet)). Every other host's credential is the operator's to declare:

- **The model's entry**, the role's resolved `providers.llm` entry (the chain above), whose own harness is the seat's runner (a launch passes over an entry whose harness has none): its whole `env`, as every call the entry makes on the engine host gets it, and whatever authenticates that harness: the headless token in the profile's own variable (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`) under `subscription`, the entry's key in the profile's `api_key_env` (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` for Claude Code) under `api-key`, the variables `inherit-env` forwards, and for `opencode` the credential-named `env` keys of the provider its model names. So a gateway's `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and the `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` it takes, a `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` or `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX` switch and its region, or a proxy reach the executor's run in every cell, remote included. They are the values the entry's own calls use, `${VAR}` references resolved through the secret store and environment at apply, with what its `auth.mode` removes from those calls removed here too (a `subscription` entry's `api_key_env`, an `api-key` entry's `token_env`); a value that resolved to nothing is left out. What tunes a call on the engine host stays there: the host's allowlisted variables, the seat home's isolation (`HOME`, XDG directories, the harness's configuration directory and switches; a box sets its own) and the profile's fixed `env`. Its login (credential files, or OpenCode's exported login) travels only to a [local](#local-sandboxes) box, never a remote one.
  **A seat that signs Claude Code in itself gets the entry's `env` without its sign-in.** Claude Code has several sign-ins under different names and ranks them (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` above a plan's `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, and a platform switch above both), so the by-name precedence below cannot see a seat is already signed in. When `role.sandbox.env` or a setup step carries any of `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` or a platform switch (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK`, `_VERTEX`, `_FOUNDRY`, `_ANTHROPIC_AWS`, `_ANTHROPIC_GOOGLE_CLOUD`, `_MANTLE` or `_GATEWAY`), a Claude Code run carries that and none of the entry's sign-in: none of those names, not the profile's token or key variable, and no [credential-named](llm-backends.md#6-a-provider-key-in-env-opencode-hermes-pi) variable of the entry's `env` (a cloud's own key, such as `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`), so a seat on its own plan is never moved onto the company's metered key or cloud. The rest of the entry's `env` still lies beneath the seat's: a base URL or region says where requests go, not whom they are made as, so a seat on its own token still reaches its model through the company's gateway, and a seat meant to bypass it names `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` itself. OpenCode reads one key per model provider, so there a variable the seat names simply wins over the entry's of the same name.
  **An entry's `env` and its key sit in every box run on that entry**, readable by the harness, which runs with every permission. Redaction of what the run reports back matches known credential **shapes** (vendors' `sk-…` prefixes and the like), not values: a key of no recognisable shape that the agent prints into its report or transcript is carried into the phase record as printed. Give a box a key scoped to the work (a provider project with a spend limit, a gateway token of its own), not the company's broadest.
  **The commands the model runs hold the sign-in, and none of the variables that lead to the run's bridge.** A run loads what a person's session of its harness loads, so each shell command its model runs inherits the run environment as a person's commands do: the harness's sign-in, the seat's own `role.sandbox.env` (an operator's own `OTEL_*` exporter settings included, untouched), its agent identity and Gitlet's variables. A runner's own variables that lead to the run's bridge stay out, so that a tool the model runs does not pick one up by accident: Codex's app-server is started with its [note helper](#codexs-notes) routes, `CREWLET_NOTES_URL` and `CREWLET_SKILLS_URL`, in `shell_environment_policy.exclude`, and OpenCode calls a plugin's `create.before` shell hook, which removes `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` and `CREWLET_STEER_SESSION` from the command's copy of its environment. This is no protection, and is not meant as one: the box has one user, and a run's model can read its own run's bridge token in its harness's configuration (its MCP servers' settings, Claude Code's `--mcp-config` file, Codex's `config.toml`); that token is scoped to the run, its tools and notes, and ends with it. Gitlet's credential is in a file `CREWLET_GIT_ACCESS_FILE` names, never a variable's value. An MCP server the run starts in its box is handed the run's environment.

  **Crewlet's telemetry is handed only to a run whose harness exports by it.** The run's OTLP endpoint (its token in the path), `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL`, an empty `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` (the turn and the seat) and `TRACEPARENT` are added at the job's start for GitHub Copilot CLI and OpenCode, which export to that endpoint whenever it is set, and hand their environment to the model's shell, so the shell holds them too ([Copilot](#github-copilot-cli), [OpenCode](#opencode)). Every other runner is handed none of them: Claude Code exports only under `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY`, Codex only under its configuration's `otel`, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code and Muse Code only with their telemetry setting on, which a run never turns on, Kimi Code and pi read no `OTEL_*` variable, and the engine reads no span of Grok Build's or Hermes Agent's. A seat that turns a harness's own export on in `role.sandbox.env` names its own collector there.
- **Agent identity**: `CREWLET_AGENT_HANDLE` and `CREWLET_AGENT_EMAIL`, the per-launch facts static config cannot know, which setup recipes map into tool shape (git commit identity above).
- **The agent's own integration credentials**, for an integration it is on at: see [An agent's own integration credentials](#an-agents-own-integration-credentials).
- **An integration's box defaults**, the non-secret settings a CLI in the box reads beside the seat's credentials (Scaleway's organization and default project, Google Cloud's default project), for a seat with one of that integration's lanes on. They are the lowest layer of the box's environment: a setup step's `env`, the seat's `sandbox.env`, the agent identity and the model entry's `env` each replace one. None counts as the harness's sign-in, and one named like a sign-in variable of the run's harness (a Claude Code cloud toggle, say) never reaches the box, so a cloud CLI's region or token file cannot switch, strip or stand in for it. A default whose reference does not resolve is left out and said, as an identity fact is, and never holds the run.
- **An integration's box files**, for the same seats: each a file at a path under the box's home holding one `${VAR}` reference whole (a token a CLI reads from a file), or literal text written as is (a CLI's configuration). The launch writes them, resolved through the seat's own resolution (so a credential issued at use is issued for it), in a setup step of their own ahead of every other, never into the environment, so none counts as a sign-in; a path a setup step writes is that step's, and a file whose reference does not resolve is left out and said, never holding the run. A file the integration marks as rewritten is kept current by the completion poll, as a [token file](../integrations/github.md#acting-as-the-app-the-seats-token) is, for as long as the launch runs. A file may also name the variable its CLI finds it through: the job is handed that variable set to the file's absolute path in its box (joined onto the home of the box it runs in; a `direct` box's home is minted per box, so no configured value could name it), as the lowest layer of the job's environment, beneath even the box defaults, so a seat's own line for the name wins. It never counts as a sign-in, and is set only for a file the box holds: one the launch writes, or a rewritten one the poll writes once its credential is issued. The value each file is launched with is taken out of the run's kept sessions by value, as everything a launch hands its box from a credential position is ([What is scrubbed](#each-launchs-session-kept)), and so is each value the poll writes since, which it records beside the run's record before writing the file. Any of them in what else the run hands back (report, transcript, live output) is taken out only where it has a shape redaction knows ([Security model](#security-model)). AWS writes its CLI profile and session file this way, Google Cloud its token file, GitHub the agent's app token file. A file holding a reference is a credential file, the integration's: a setup step's file at its path is dropped for it, as a line under one of the agent's credential variables is. A file of literal text, such as AWS's profile, is a setting, and a setup step's file at its path wins.

Everything else tool-specific comes from config: external-service tokens (registry tokens, a test `DATABASE_URL`, a personal access token for a seat off at its code host, …) are declared in `role.sandbox.env` or a setup step's `env` and merely `${VAR}`-resolved; the engine never extracts, names or special-cases them. One variable is the engine's to answer rather than the store's: a seat's own `${GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_<HANDLE>}`, its GitHub App's installation token, issued for this seat's run alone and good for at least 50 minutes from launch ([Acting as the app](../integrations/github.md#acting-as-the-app-the-seats-token)). Precedence, later wins: the model's entry (its `env` and sign-in), agent identity, setup-step env, `role.sandbox.env`, the agent's own integration credentials, non-secret OTel values; and over every one of them, every launch on a node that serves Gitlet gets the engine's access to it, before the run has checked anything out, whose names configuration reserves, with git's configuration appended after any of your own `GIT_CONFIG_*` entries rather than replacing them.

**A seat's own integration credential in its box is a tool's, never the harness's sign-in.** A line whose value references one of the agent's own credentials (its sealed `${<KIND>_<FIELD>_<HANDLE>}` names, or the variable its `mcp_env` block or role credential field names for an integration), such as doctl's `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN: "${DIGITALOCEAN_TOKEN_SRE}"`, reaches the box like the rest of the seat's `env` and never counts as the run's sign-in. It may not sit under a name a member of the seat's executor chain signs in by: its token or key variable, a `sign_in_env` name (Claude Code's, or Copilot's `GH_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_TOKEN`), or for `opencode` a credential-named variable of the entry's `env`. In one box the harness would make its model calls with the agent's tool credential, so such a line is refused on submit and a warning on a stored document. Reach that tool through its MCP server instead, or run the seat's executor on an entry that signs in by another name.

**A reference that resolves to nothing is left out, and said.** A `${VAR}` reference that resolves to nothing, whole (`"${TOKEN}"`) or embedded (`"Bearer ${TOKEN}"`), unset or empty, is never handed to the box as an empty string, by the rule every tool server is held to ([Tools & MCP](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#shared-vs-per-role-servers)): its key is left out of the run environment whole. The run is **not refused**: it is the seat's turn itself, and refusing would fail every message the seat could answer over its tool bridge for a token a pass may mint in a minute. It starts without what is missing, and its start logs **`sandbox_env_unresolved`** naming the keys, files and variables (never a value or body), because a run handed no code-host token clones and pushes nothing, and that line is how an operator finds out why. The line says why the value is missing: at info while a [provisioning pass](integration-reconcile.md) is minting it for the seat (the same `${VAR}` an `mcp_env` code-host credential points at; a run launched once its seal reaches the node is given it), or while the seat's GitHub App is not yet created or installed (for its own `${GITHUB_APP_TOKEN_<HANDLE>}`, whose token file a running job gets from the first poll after the app can issue one); and as a warning, with the remedy, where nothing will mint it: that pass cannot until somebody acts, or GitHub didn't issue the seat's token ([each story](#failure-modes) is told under its own field). Where that pass cannot say whether it holds the seat up (`unsure`), the line is at info while this node is only still reading its findings, and a warning otherwise. The engine's own identity facts never refuse a run: each is contributed when it has a value, and a seat `email:` naming a variable nothing sets is left out of `CREWLET_AGENT_EMAIL` and said on the same line, so a setup step's `git config user.email` reading it empty has a reason beside it.

A setting a run can go without (a test `DATABASE_URL`, a proxy) is declared by its **key** under `optional_keys`, beside the `env` that writes it: on `role.sandbox`, or on a setup step, where a file's path may be listed too. Such a key whose value does not resolve is left out whole, never half-substituted, as any other is, but quietly, since its absence is expected, so the line names only the gaps that are not:

```yaml
roles:
  - name: Backend
    sandbox:
      env:
        GITLAB_TOKEN: "${SWE_GITLAB_TOKEN}"            # expected: a run started without it has no code-host
                                                       #   identity, and sandbox_env_unresolved names it
        DATABASE_URL: "postgres://${TEST_DB_HOST}/app"
      optional_keys: [DATABASE_URL]                    # left out when TEST_DB_HOST resolves to nothing
```

The declaration that counts is the one beside the value that won: a key in `role.sandbox.env` replacing a setup step's is judged by `role.sandbox.optional_keys`, never the step's. A value a provisioning pass is still minting for the seat, or the seat's GitHub App token before its app can issue one, is said at info whatever the declaration says (it is on its way, not expected absent), and the run starts without it; a run launched after its seal reaches this node, or after the app is installed, is given it. An entry that leaves nothing out (a key or path its block does not write, a variable's name where its key belongs, or a key whose values reference nothing) is refused on the write that adds it (an [admission rule](configuration.md#what-a-stored-revision-is-held-to)), because the key it was meant for stays expected. Resolved values are injected only into that sandbox's process env and die with it; the DB stores only the `${VAR}` references. Shared infrastructure secrets, above all the OTLP backend's ingest token, never enter the sandbox at all (see below).

### An agent's own integration credentials

An integration that gives an agent a credential puts it in that agent's box itself, with no line in the company document, for as long as the agent is on at it:

| Integration | In the box | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| Expo | `EXPO_TOKEN`, the robot's sealed token | the EAS CLI |
| DigitalOcean | `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN`, the sealed token | doctl |
| Scaleway | `SCW_SECRET_KEY` and `SCW_ACCESS_KEY`, the sealed key | scw |
| GitHub | `GITHUB_TOKEN`, the app's installation token, and the same token in `~/.config/crewlet/github-token`, which the completion poll keeps current; a box whose executor runs Copilot gets the file alone ([Copilot](#github-copilot-cli)) | git's credential helper and gh |
| GitLab | `GITLAB_TOKEN`, the service account's sealed token | git's credential helper and glab |
| Google Cloud | `~/.config/crewlet/gcloud-token`, named by `CLOUDSDK_AUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN_FILE` and kept current | gcloud |
| AWS | `~/.aws/crewlet-credentials.json`, read by the `crewlet` profile in `~/.aws/config` and kept current | the AWS CLI |

Sealed credentials are put there where Crewlet provisions the integration and so seals them; where the agents' accounts are made outside Crewlet, the seat's own settings name the variable that holds one. GitHub's token is issued by the engine either way, while the company runs GitHub.

- **Only the agent's own.** Each value is resolved through the seat's own resolution, so it names that agent's credential and no other seat's, and is taken out of the run's kept session by value, as every credential the launch hands the box is ([Each launch's session, kept](#each-launchs-session-kept)), and out of everything else the run hands back where it has a shape redaction knows ([Security model](#security-model)). It never counts as the harness's sign-in. Under a name a member of the seat's executor chain signs in by (OpenCode on DigitalOcean's models reads `DIGITALOCEAN_ACCESS_TOKEN`), Crewlet withholds it from the box rather than sign the agent's model calls in with its tool token, logs `sandbox_credential_withheld` at each launch, and reports an advisory at the seat's `integrations` block.
- **On and off.** An agent turned on is given it from its next run; one turned off is given none from its next run, and its sealed credential is cleared or its token no longer issued. While a sealed credential is not there yet (a token nobody has pasted), a run starts without it and `sandbox_env_unresolved` says, at info, that the integration is minting it. Where that integration cannot say whether it holds the seat up (`unsure` under [Failure modes](#failure-modes)), the line is at info while this node is only still reading its findings, and a warning otherwise. A file whose credential is issued at use is written by the first poll after it can be.
- **A line of your own under the same name is ignored.** A `role.sandbox.env` line, a setup step's `env` key (the seat's or provider-wide) or a setup file at one of these paths is dropped for an agent on at the integration, and `crewlet validate`, a configuration write and every node applying the revision report an advisory at that line. The integration's wins, never the line, because the integration's state is the one authority on which identity the box acts as: a line that won could hand the box a broader credential (Expo's provisioner token holds Admin on the account, beyond every level an agent may hold) or one that outlives turning the agent off, while the Agents tab reports the level the agent's own credential holds. A line identical to the integration's changes nothing; remove it. The settings beside a credential (Scaleway's default project, the AWS profile) are the other way round: a line of your own wins.

---

## MCP inside the sandbox

The harness is itself an MCP client, so the engine renders the seat's scoped servers into the box, beside the [tool bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box) every box gets as the server `crewlet` (`internal/sandbox/mcprender.go` → Claude Code's `mcp.json` in the run's work directory, via `--mcp-config`, or the [configuration an OpenCode run is handed](#opencode)). Scoping is at the **server level only**: `role.sandbox.mcp.servers` names which of the role's `mcp_servers` run in the box, and the harness gets **every tool those servers expose**.

- A server named there is the box's; the [bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box) serves every other server the seat holds, never this one, so no server runs twice under one name. Name a server here when it must run where the checkout is (one that reads the box's files); otherwise leave it to the bridge, which records every call as the seat's and holds it to required skills.
- An entry naming a server the company does not declare, or one the seat is not [granted](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#choosing-which-agents-get-a-server), is refused when the document is written (a stored revision carrying one gives the box nothing for it and logs `sandbox_mcp_server_not_granted`). Removing a server takes it out of every list ([Tools & MCP](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#removing-a-server)).
- There is no per-tool allowlist in a box: OpenCode has no allowlist flag and Claude Code runs `bypassPermissions` headless, so a list couldn't be enforced uniformly. So a server whose every tool is not certain to run at `allow` ([Setting each tool's level](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#setting-each-tools-level): an entry saying `default: allow` and holding no tool back) is never given to a box, which could neither leave a blocked tool out nor ask a person before an `approve` call. Listing one is refused when the document is written, a level written on a server a box lists is refused at that box's entry, and a stored revision carrying one gives the box nothing for it and logs `sandbox_mcp_server_levelled`. A server with no `tools` is such a server (each tool starts at its hints' level, most at `approve`). The seat reaches its tools over the bridge, where levels hold.

**Beside them, the harness starts its own.** The servers the harness's own configuration declares start too: the box's user- and local-scope servers (an image's, or an earlier run's in the same box), the repository's `.mcp.json` (which a print-mode Claude Code run connects without an approval prompt), a plugin's, and the claude.ai connectors of the signed-in account. OpenCode adds together every configuration document it reads. The engine renders none of these and its bridge sees none of their calls: they act with their own configuration's credentials, and the cell bounds what they reach (`container` keeps them off the engine host's files). A server that does not start holds up the run's first step for at most Claude Code's `MCP_TIMEOUT` (30 s unless the run's environment sets it), then the run goes on without it. Keep the name `crewlet` for the engine: Claude Code does not document which of two same-named servers it keeps, so a repository's own `crewlet` could take the bridge's place, and a run with no bridge cannot submit its work.

Credentials from `role.mcp_env` are resolved into the rendered specs (HTTP servers get them as headers, stdio servers as env), so in-box servers authenticate as the seat. So is every `${VAR}` in the server's own `env`, `headers` and `url`, resolved through the secret store and the engine's environment as for the server's child on the engine host. A `${VAR}` reference is never written into the box: OpenCode does not read that syntax, and Claude Code would read it from the run environment, which holds a company secret only where the seat's `sandbox.env` or a setup step repeats it. OpenCode is handed the resolved value, in a file of its own its configuration names ([OpenCode](#opencode)). A reference one of those sources does not answer is not answered by a value the run environment happens to carry. The connected server names are listed in the harness's environment brief.

A server any of whose values does **not** resolve (the seat's or its own, under a key the server does not [declare optional](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#a-key-that-may-go-without-its-value)) is not rendered, by the rule the server's own child follows ([Tools & MCP](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#shared-vs-per-role-servers)): given an empty token it would refuse to start or act as nobody, costing the agent a round. A key declared optional is left out. The run logs `sandbox_mcp_server_withheld` naming the variables: at info while the integration that mints them is minting them (a run launched once the seal reaches the node, or, for the agent's GitHub App token, once its installation is recorded, is given the server), and as a warning where they are unset, where that integration cannot mint them until somebody acts, or where GitHub didn't issue the seat's token. Where that integration cannot say whether it holds the seat up ([Tools & MCP](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#shared-vs-per-role-servers)), it is at info while this node is only still reading its findings, and a warning otherwise.

A named server the company's `mcp_servers` does not carry is **skipped** with a warning, not rendered empty. So is one whose `transport` is neither `stdio` nor `http`. A skipped entry does not cost the seat the rest of its surface.

Two practical caveats:

- **stdio servers must exist in the box.** A stdio spec is *spawned inside* the sandbox, so its command must be in the box: on the host for `direct`, in the image for `container`, or installed by a setup step.
- **A container box reaches the engine host by name.** An HTTP server the engine host serves on loopback is handed to a `container` box under the runtime's name for that host ([Local sandboxes](#local-sandboxes)), so a server reached at `http://localhost:3000` by the engine's child is reached from the box too, on Linux as long as it listens beyond loopback.

---

## The tool bridge — a seat's own tools, from inside a box

Every run is its seat's executor ([LLM Backends](llm-backends.md#the-executors-run-in-a-box)). Beside the servers above, it needs the seat's *whole* tool surface, including the engine's builtins and the delivery tools the turn is judged on. Those cannot be shipped in: most are MCP children holding the **seat's** credentials, several are engine control, and a box is given only the credentials the seat acts as.

So the box is also given the engine: its own tools as one MCP server, `crewlet`, at the job's endpoint, and **each MCP server the seat holds as a server of its own** beneath it (`/mcp/{token}/server/{server}`), under the company's name for it, listing that server's tools alone, with the server's `description` as its MCP instructions. Every call on every one of them comes back out:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    BOX["The run's harness, in its box"] -->|"MCP over streamable HTTP: POST /mcp/{token}"| SURF["The seat's live tools.Surface: grant, skill guard, recording"]
```

**The dispatch is the seat's own.** A bridged call goes through the same `tools.Surface` a phase on this host calls, so the grant, the [required-skill guard](tool-skills.md), the failure shape and the recording are the ones operators know. `internal/api/mcpbridge` has no second idea of whether a tool is allowed. The MCP server behind each route is the one a run on this host reaches over its unix socket (`internal/toolsession`), kept in step with the seat's live tool set.

**Apart, because a harness keeps tools out of its requests by the server.** A run holds all its seat's tools from launch (50 to 150 MCP tools among them) and lists none in its prompt. Claude Code defers every MCP server's tools behind its tool search and keeps the one marked `alwaysLoad` in front of its model on every request; OpenCode offers a server through Code Mode unless declared `codemode: false` (so a continued OpenCode session is told a call made through Code Mode again, by design: the session holds the program, never the call). So `crewlet` (needed on every request) is always loaded and offered directly, and every other server is left to the harness ([Claude Code](#claude-code), [OpenCode](#opencode); Hermes's tool search exempts no server, so a [Hermes run](#hermes-agent) offers every tool directly): a seat's MCP tools need no `list_mcp_server_tools` or `activate_tool` rounds, and a run never has to search for the call that ends it. The servers a run is handed are fixed at launch, from what its surface offers; a server the seat runs in its box (`role.sandbox.mcp.servers`) is reached there, under the same name, and is not served here.

**A box reaches the bridge directly, past any proxy.** The run's harness starts with the hosts of Crewlet's own routes (the bridge, its notes route and its skill route) added to `NO_PROXY` and `no_proxy`, after the login profile, each spelling holding the other's entries too, so the operator's `role.sandbox.env`, the image's and the profile's own entries stay beside them. A proxy the run's environment, the image, the profile or the harness's own settings name (Copilot's `proxyUrl`, Pi's `httpProxy`) otherwise carried the bridge's calls, and one that could not reach the engine host left the run without its tools (measured on Copilot 1.0.114 and Pi 1.6.0); a seat's other servers and the model's own calls go through the proxy as they would in a person's session. Every harness honours a host-only entry in either spelling for its MCP connection (measured with each one's own client against a dead proxy). OpenCode 2.3.2, Kimi Code 2.7.2 and Hermes Agent 0.23.3 also reach loopback directly whatever the variables say. Claude Code assigns a settings file's `env` over the process's key by key and reads `no_proxy` first, so where the home's, the project's or the local settings set either spelling, the run's own settings (which rank above all three) set both to one list made as Claude Code starts: the process's entries, then every settings file's, then the bridge's host, in order and without repeats (measured: with both spellings there the bridge opened, with one it did not). A managed settings file's `env` (`/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json`, `managed-settings.d/*.json`) ranks above the run's own and replaces its list (measured on 2.1.330: a managed `NO_PROXY` without the bridge's host left it unreached behind a proxy), so where a proxy is set and a managed file's `NO_PROXY` or `no_proxy` leaves out a host of the run's own routes, the run does not start, naming the file, the key and the value. Hermes Agent loads its home's `.env` over the process's environment, so its run states the list in the managed `.env` it loads last ([Hermes Agent](#hermes-agent)).

**Every call is held to the run, as a phase holds its own.** The bridge adds what a detached run's calls are owed:

- The **seat's fence**, before and after each call: once this node stops holding the seat, or a person asks it to stop, that call and every later one are refused and written on the run's record as refused.
- The **order the calls arrived in**, fixed as each is admitted (`Surface.Admit`), not as it returns, so calls made at once read the same call log a re-run would.
- The **run's context, never the request's**: a box that disconnects mid-call abandons only the answer, never a tool half-way through a write.
- A **panic contained**: the call answered as failed, logged with its stack, the run's tools closed to it.
- A **run that is over refuses**: a call reaching a session after its run ended, or a relaunch replaced it, is answered and not run.
- A call whose arguments did not parse is answered with the words a phase on this host uses, never run on an empty object. No record reads a box's harness, so an object the harness made of what its model wrote (Claude Code's of an array) reaches the tool as sent, and the tool's own validation judges it.

It adds no tool loop (rounds, a terminator, a per-request budget): an executor run's loop is its harness's own, its turn is parked while it runs, and those settle when the run is collected and its turn resumes (a person's notes reach the run over the bridge too, between its steps: [Notes to a running run](#notes-to-a-running-run)). Where the launch continued a session, the bridge holds the run to the session its box started, read off which of the job's two tokens the box dials, before the first call ([Which session the box started](#which-session-the-box-started)).

**A call's answer starts at once and keeps going.** Streamable HTTP writes nothing on a response until its first event, and Claude Code gives up an HTTP response whose first byte has not come within a minute where the server's entry sets no timeout, telling its model the call timed out and cancelling nothing while the call runs on (measured on 2.1.310: a 90-second call given up at 60 seconds, run to its end by the bridge). So the bridge starts every call's answer the moment its tool starts, with a progress notification on the call's own progress token (one ahead of the answer however soon the tool returns), then another every 20 seconds until the tool returns, on every server it serves the run. Each is one small event (116 bytes, measured). That also answers Claude Code's other checks (read from its 2.1.310 bundle):

- It gives up a call that has sent nothing for five minutes, or for the server's own timeout where the box's settings give one ([below](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box)).
- Every 30 seconds it gives up a call 90 seconds after its transport was marked lost unless a progress has cleared the mark. The mark is routine: Claude Code loses the session's standing GET stream 360 seconds after opening it, whatever the server's timeout, marking every call then in flight, so each call running past that leans on the progress within 20 seconds. Measured with the bridge's bound in the server's entry: a 540-second call through that loss was answered whole; the same call with no progress token was given up at 449.9 seconds, cancelling nothing.

A call that lands while no node can answer waits (below) with nothing written, and its answer starts once it reaches the node that runs it. Both harnesses put a progress token on every call (measured on Claude Code 2.1.310 and OpenCode 2.3.2); a call answered without running (refused once the run's tools have closed, or for unparsed arguments) gets its answer alone, and so does a request with no token. A progress the bridge can no longer write means the harness hung up, and the call is recorded as [one nobody waited for](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session).

**A box waits for a call as long as the bridge can take to answer it.** The box is told that bound as each bridged server's own timeout (Claude Code's per-server `timeout`, OpenCode's `timeout.execution`). Past it the harness gives the call up and cancels it, whatever progress flows (measured on Claude Code 2.1.310, and on OpenCode 2.3.2 with none flowing), and the bridge records it as one nobody waited for. Unset, a hung call would hold its run for the harness's default: Claude Code's 1e8 ms, OpenCode's twelve hours. The bridge's bound, added up as the box is launched:

- the two seat-lease lifetimes a call may wait for a node that can answer (90 seconds at the default `coordination.lease_ttl_seconds`, as below);
- plus the longest bound the run's tools declare:
  - an MCP server's `request_timeout_seconds` after the wait for its restart: a call made while the server is replaced waits for the calls in flight (its request timeout again), the old process's stop (seven seconds) and the new one's start (its `startup_timeout_seconds` twice), 847 seconds at the defaults ([A restart into a new spec drops no call](../guides/tools-and-mcp.md#a-server-that-dies-or-will-not-start));
  - `delegate`'s `turn_engine.delegation.call_timeout_seconds`, never under the engine's one-call ceiling of 300 seconds;
- plus a minute for the bridge's own work around a call.

At the defaults: 1050 seconds on a seat that can `delegate`, 997 with an MCP server that cannot, 450 with neither. The bridge cuts nothing itself: a call past every bound is a defect or a hang, and a tool half-way through a write is the run's. A call still running as its job's session ends waits for none of it: the end answers it at once (below).

**A call longer than its harness waits parks the run on it.** A harness can give a call up at a clock no setting moves, so each runner states its harness's ceiling for one bridged call, or that it has none, and the launch names it with the job. A call still running near the ceiling is answered, by the clock a phase on this host uses (a tenth of the ceiling ahead of it, at least five seconds), as a phase answers it: "This call is still running, longer than your harness waits for one call. END YOUR TURN NOW: you will be resumed with its result. Do not make the call again." Not a failure. Before that answer the job is parked on the call on the run's row, as [`wait_for_run`](#a-seats-runs-see-each-other) parks one on a run: put to nobody, so no reply answers it and its conversation's mail waits aside. The call runs on and is recorded as one nobody waited for. Its run's collection waits for it (below), the job parks, and the node holding the seat carries the run on at once, from its row and never as an answer: in its own session, told that its call returned and what it returned, as the run's log keeps it (within the log's share of one call), as a held call's result is told. No note channel is needed, so a harness that takes no note mid-run can state a ceiling. A model that works on instead is served its other calls, refused `submit_work` while parked, and handed no item of the call as it lands, so its relaunch tells it once. Every call answered with that promise is parked the same way, whatever the job asked before it: a second long call is added to the calls the job waits on, and one after a question to a person or a `wait_for_run` is added beside that ask, which still decides who answers. Whichever carries the run on, the person's answer, the waited run's account or the engine's word that the calls returned, its brief tells each parked call with what it returned, or, where the round's record holds it still in flight, that its outcome is not known, once: no list of the round's calls repeats it. Where the job cannot be parked (its row refused the write), the call is answered still running alone, and its result reaches the run only as a call nobody waited for.
