The run's end removes the record, then the log; the store writes a log only beside a record, so a call landing as the run ends leaves nothing, and a log left between the two removals is taken by the [marker sweep](coordination.md#removal-markers-are-swept).

Every flip of the run is a compare-and-set of the record **whole**, and every listing of the fleet's runs reads every record whole: the completion poll, the pause reaper, the live panel's reconcile, Live › Executors, every git request a coding box makes (read first) and every ref answer past the box's floor (which writes it). None moves the log, the sealed secrets or the leads.

Every write of the record also states its **standing** in the same message: the run's seat, its handle's SHA-256 and the lease epoch stamped on it. The boot's epoch floor and the executor sessions' retention, which asks only which turns still have a record, read the standing alone, and a seat's busy check, its recovery and a mailbox retirement read it and then only that seat's records whole, so a node across a leaf's link boots beside runs at their bound by moving a few hundred bytes a run, not megabytes. A record that states none, written by an older version during a rolling upgrade, is read whole and judged on what it holds until a newer node writes it.

Measured on three members, every bucket at three replicas, from a member not leading the runs' bucket, for a job parked with a 32 KiB frozen context and a full log, its launch numbered on the record and no capture stamped yet:

- The record is 38 008 bytes once its box's attach has said which brief the job was handed (`"brief":"fresh"`, 16 bytes; a job whose launch continues no session records no `session_start`) and its launch the run its leads are kept for (`"leads_run"` and the launch's id, 51 bytes). A box's read takes 0.38 ms and a raise of its floor 0.90 ms at the median (0.61 and 2.40 at the 99th percentile, on the benchmark's record of 37 941 bytes, which names no box).
- The 478 374-byte log is moved only by its readers and an append: 10.6 ms (15.6), or 10.8 ms (15.3) for a call that moved the job's spend and so writes the record's total too.
- The sealed secrets are about 0.7 KiB for a launch handed a model key, two MCP servers' tokens and its own telemetry and Gitlet tokens (computed from its encoding), read only by a capture and the next launch's opening.
- With the log on the record it was 516 173 bytes, 5.8 ms and 11.1 ms (7.9 and 26.0), for every one of those requests ([Gitlet → Coding boxes](gitlet.md#coding-boxes)).
### What a run's record and its log keep

A run's record and its tool log are each **one value** in the coordination store, read and written whole by every write that touches it, and the store holds one key to **6,290,346 bytes** (`coord.MaxValueBytes`): the largest value whose read a node without `data` takes back across its leaf link, where the stream leader's reply carries it base64-encoded, a third larger, under the transport's 8 MiB. The store refuses a write past it before sending anything. So each is held to that byte budget (`sandbox.RowBytes`), and every field it carries has a share of it, counted in the bytes the store's JSON encoder writes, escapes included (a `<` is six bytes, a control byte six, a quote two):

| Value | Share | Bytes | Held by |
|---|---|---|---|
| The tool log | Its calls: `calls`, `elided`, `elided_calls`, `absorbed_calls` | 3,473,408 (3.3125 MiB) | each call's own share, two hundred calls, and the identities of the calls the log counts without listing them |
| The tool log | Its calls in flight: `in_flight` | 1,048,576 (1 MiB) | 256 entries, each its call's identity and the id its harness gave it, at most 4 KiB |
| The tool log | Everything else: the tool names of the turn's earlier rounds, the records the run wrote (128 at most), the log's own fields, and room for what a later version adds | 1,768,362 (1.69 MiB) | each field's own bound |
| The record | The parked turn's state (`execute_state`) | 2,097,152 (2 MiB) | the park, which condenses it to fit and refuses it past that |
| The record | Everything else, the turn's wake items within 100 KiB, and 156 KiB for fields a later version adds | 4,193,194 (4 MiB less 1,110 bytes) | each field's own bound, held by the write that puts it on the record |

The sealed set of secrets beside them is the third value, a fraction of the same budget: at most 64 KiB before sealing. The turn's leads beside them are the fourth: at most 512 KiB of them and at most 2,048, the oldest dropped first and counted, beside a few fields of their own, within the same budget.

**A change of the record across a slow link is given the record's crossing.** Every change of the record reads it whole and writes it whole, and a node without `data`, or any node on an external broker, reads and sends it across a link the engine allows to carry as little as a mebibyte in thirty seconds both ways: the read's reply carries the record base64-encoded, a third larger, and is heard only once its last byte is in — four minutes for a record at its bound there — and the store's acknowledgement of the write waits on its last byte too — three minutes a send, up to three sends. The store gives the read the time its reply takes to cross the node's connection, beyond the read term and beyond the thirty seconds a read is otherwise ever asked for — none on a member, where a read dropped across an election is asked again at two seconds — and a write whose caller set no deadline the crossing of what it carries, and keeps a caller's own deadline as it is ([Coordination](coordination.md#a-compare-and-set-waits-for-the-leader-to-decide)). So where the engine bounds a change of the record for a reason of its own, it bounds it by that reason and the crossing of a change of a record at its bound at the node's own pace: thirteen minutes across a link at the slowest pace allowed, and none on a member, whose store is in its own process. The reasons are a store's slow moment, five seconds, for a resumed turn's record of what it does with its round, for which session a job's box started and for a job's first pull of a person's notes; a leader's election outlasted, thirty seconds for every attempt at a capture's stamp together and ten for each attempt at settling a take of a person's notes; a teardown's grace, thirty seconds, for a claim handed back, a box let go, how a collected job's harness ended, a turn's owed end and each call an ending makes of the store on the record — its decision, a read of the record or of its log, an answer let go of, the copies it hands back cleared, a stop's collection, the turn's end owed and cleared, the delete — each call its own grace and crossing, a read's its reply's alone, and each run a person's stop ends its own; and a box's poll or the waiters' duty, for the reaper's release of a box past its pause and for the launch-node watch's release of a box, or its verdict on a job, whose launch node is gone. A capture's own budget counts its stamp of what came of it at the slowest node's crossing, since any node may read its age, and so does a read standing by for it, for its stamp of the place after it. A read of the record alone is bounded by its reason and its reply's crossing, four minutes there, never a change's, since it sends no write: a take's read of the record it places its capture by, a takeover's read of it back, a standby's last read, a turn's end's last read, a save's reads of the record and of what its box was handed, and an ending's reads of the record and its log. Held to the reason alone, a record of megabytes was cut while its bytes were still crossing and read as a store that did not answer. **A stopping node gives no change its crossing**: once the sandbox coordinator stops, a write of the record it still makes — a keep's stamp of what came of a capture it cut, a standby withdrawn, a retry's teardown — is held to its reason alone from then on, and everything a retry still running makes on a context of its own — its writes, its stamps, its box's kill — to one grace from the stop, all of it, so the stop is never held for a record still crossing, nor for a retry's teardowns one after another, past the grace a pod is given; a stamp so left begun is settled by a peer once the node's taker lease is gone. The stop's last attempts at settling takes of a person's notes keep their own five-second window for the same reason. A box read gives each change of the record its host's read makes — the reservation of a capture's place, the stamp of what came of the take, how the job's harness ended and the pause's record — its crossing on the host's own connection, and its asker counts the slowest node's for each (*How long a read waits*, above). One bound keeps its own time: a write on a harness's own request, held to what the harness gives that request — a bridged call's entry, a hook's take of a person's notes and its plugin's confirmation of them, a notes poll's serve ([#1150](https://github.com/crewlet/crewlet/issues/1150)).

**A call's share.** Each call keeps up to **16 KiB**: its arguments up to **8 KiB** as the log holds them, its answer up to **4 KiB**, its name up to 256 bytes, the id its harness gave it up to 64 bytes, and room for what a later version adds to a call. Past its share, a call's arguments **keep their shape**: their largest values are left out one by one, so the short ones (the ids, paths and names that say what the call was about) stay, each value left out replaced by a marker such as `(1.0 MiB not kept on the run's record, digest 1a2b3c4d)` naming its size and four bytes of its digest, so a commit keeps its repository, branch and file paths beside the file contents it leaves out. Its answer keeps its opening, cut on a character boundary, ending in `…` and `(60 KiB of 64 KiB not kept on the run's record)`. And the call states the size of what it sent and answered (`args_bytes`, `output_bytes`) wherever the log keeps less, which is what every reader decides by: the [executors board](../reference/api-endpoints.md#get-executors) draws such a call **partly kept**, and the reviewer and the prior-work ledger read a left-out value as the marker it is, never a fragment as the whole.

**The run's submission is kept whole.** The collection replays the run's newest successful `submit_work` from the log as the round's outcome, so that one call keeps its arguments up to **64 KiB**; the moment a newer one lands, the one before it is held to the ordinary 8 KiB. A submission past **32 KiB** (as the log would hold it) is refused while the run makes it, naming its size, so the run shortens it rather than being collected as a round that said nothing; and a submission its log still did not keep whole is never replayed: the round is rescued as one with no submission, never reported with a marker as its summary.

**A long run's middle is kept as identities.** Past two hundred calls the middle is dropped, and each dropped call is tallied by its tool and the digest of its arguments, with how many calls had each and how many failed (`elided_calls`, up to 64 KiB). A resumed segment counts them as the calls they were, and every delivery check reads a reply among them as delivered; the reviewer, the board, the execute phase's record (`calls_elided`, `elided_calls`), the next round's prior-work ledger and a session a relaunch continues after its save — how many of the dropped calls came after the save, beside the tally ([What a continued session is told](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)) — are told what was dropped, by tool. Past its own share the tally gives up an identity's digest (counted as calls to its tool asking for something new), and past that its tool (counted against every later call): an over-count, which makes a repeat after the resume a fresh write, and never an under-count, which would answer a new write with an earlier one's operation. The tallies are the round's, as the log is: a new round's log starts without them, and calls a version without them dropped, with no identity, are read as calls whose tool is not known.

**Every call the run made is counted when it resumes.** A segment that resumes the run — its collection, its continuation after a person's answer, its reopening on a node that took the seat over — starts its count of the run's calls from its log: the calls it lists, by the identity each was admitted under, never by the arguments it kept; the ones it counts without listing, by their tallies; and the calls a bridged `delegate`'s workers made, which the run counted between its own and the log lists nowhere, tallied apart (`absorbed_calls`, up to 64 KiB) and read by nothing but that count, since a worker's call is no reply of the turn's. A call held for a person's approval, and the call they approved, keep neither their arguments nor a digest of them in the clear — the arguments ride the record sealed, and a digest beside the tool's name would confirm a guess at them — so each is counted as a call of its tool whose arguments are not known: an over-count, of a tool no write's operation is derived from. And a call still running elsewhere is counted too, by its entry on the log (below), so a later call that asks for something else never derives its operation id.

**A call is on the log before it runs.** The bridge writes each call's entry on the run's log ahead of it — its tool, its place among the run's calls, when the bridge took it, the digest it was admitted under (none for a tool that may ask a person first, so a held call's digest is never in the clear), the node process running it and the instant past which nobody waits for it (`in_flight`), beside the id its harness gave it — and runs the call only once the log has taken it. **Only then is the call counted in the run's call log** (the count every operation id a write derives carries, so a write that asks for something else is a new operation): a call refused at its entry is in no call log, as it is in no record, so a segment that resumes the run counts exactly what this one counted, and calls made side by side are still counted in the order they arrived, each waiting for the entries of the calls that arrived before it. The call's one update, as it finishes, takes the entry out and lists the call in its place, in the same write, so the log never holds two records of one call; the update finds its entry by the call's place, the instant the bridge took it and its tool, never by the id its harness gave it. A segment that resumes the run, on any node, counts a call still in flight by its entry's identity — as a call of its tool whose arguments are not known, where the entry carries no digest — and numbers its next call after it. **An entry the store does not take within five seconds**, four attempts included, **is a call not run**: its box is told `This call was not run: it could not be recorded. Call it again if it is still needed.`, failed, so its harness makes it again, and the engine's log names it (`bridge_call_not_recorded`); a log holding 256 calls in flight refuses the next one the same way, and a log that takes no more calls of the job tells the call its run has ended. A call whose entry was written and that is then not run — its job's session ended while the entry was written, its seat's fence closed meanwhile — has the entry withdrawn in the same step; one the call log counted that its tool then could not run at all is recorded as a call that was not run, failed, by the identity the log counted. **An update the store does not take** after four attempts over 1.75 seconds, which outlast a stream leader's re-election, leaves the entry, the call's identity on the record, and is asked for again once the call's answer is out — so its box waits for none of it — every one to five seconds, until it lands or the call's own bound passes (`mcp_bridge_call_update_owed`): a submission or a work item whose update met an outage lands as soon as the store takes it, and a collection waiting for the call ends on it. Past the call's bound its entry stays: what it answered, cost and committed is lost (`mcp_bridge_call_update_unrecorded`), every later reader of the run reading it as a call whose outcome is unknown. One the store takes after a relaunch that carried the round on is listed as a late call of the round ([A relaunch continues the turn's session](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)), and it is counted as any call is. **What it costs**: one coordination-store write before every bridged call runs, 11.89 ms at the median and 17.04 ms at the 99th percentile over a thousand writes (the update after it 13.62 ms and 18.96 ms, where an append before was 12.14 ms and 17.13 ms), on the engine's own broker of three members from a member that does not lead the runs' bucket, with the log at its full count of calls ([Gitlet](gitlet.md)); the update after it is the write the call made before. A call made beside others waits, to be counted, for the entries of the calls that arrived before it, each written at the same time as its own. And a coordination store in an outage refuses the calls it used to let run off the record, and is asked for each refused update about once every seven seconds until it is back or the call's bound passes.

**A parked state past its share is condensed, and refused only for the turn's own context.** The state grows with the turn's closed rounds — up to two hundred calls each, and as many rounds as `max_iterations` allows — and a closed round carries no successful call's answer, which nothing reads again, so past 2 MiB the park gives up, in order, the closed rounds' arguments and errors, tier by tier, then their produced text past its opening, then the intent each round set out with past its opening, then the digests in their tallies of dropped calls, each tool's calls folded into one count; then the closed rounds' calls themselves, each folded into its round's tally — by identity first, so a resumed count is still exact, then by tool — which the prior-work ledger then says by tool rather than call by call, the names of the round's read-only tools, which only a listed call is drawn with, going with them; then their reviewer's prose past its opening; then whole rounds from the middle — the first round and as many of the newest as fit are kept, and the rounds between are folded into one entry standing for them, as few as fit — and last every round into one such entry. An entry standing for dropped rounds keeps their calls, counted by tool with their outcomes, so a reply one of them posted still counts as the turn's and a resumed count still includes their calls, and the artifact hash of the last of them for the [stall guard](turn-engine.md#the-review); what the rounds set out to do, produced and were told is gone, and the prior-work ledger says so (`### Iterations 2–40`) rather than drawing rounds that did nothing. Each tier cuts a payload as its round was parked, never what the tier before kept of it, so the marker a cut ends with says how much of the whole is not kept, and the park's log line (`sandbox_suspension_condensed`) counts each round and each call it cut once, and the rounds it dropped (`rounds_dropped`). Every call keeps its tool and its outcome however far it is condensed, and its identity until the last fold of its tool; a call whose outcome nobody knows, still in flight when its round's calls were read, is counted apart from the failures in its tally, so the prior-work ledger still says it may have taken effect and is to be checked before it is made again, and the turn's end still reads a reply it may have been as one whose delivery is unknown. A state still past its share is refused, and its park fails as `sandbox_suspension_too_large` rather than as a record the store refuses: what does not fit is the turn's own context — what it was asked, its trigger's words, its turn-start blocks, and how its conversation's earlier turns ended (up to 24,000 bytes as the state holds them) — which no condensing touches, beside one count of calls per tool, and never its closed rounds, however many it ran. A run's task description and label, and a colleague's question its turn answers, are a trigger's own words too, and the record keeps each to 16 KiB, as its opening with the cut said, the description and label redacted and never cut inside a marker, the question as asked and never cut inside a credential: only the answer, which echoes it to the asking seat, reads it so, and every other read of the record, its JSON included, shows it redacted. The turn's own record keeps the whole.

**What a person, a tool or a box puts on the record is held too.** A person's reply recorded as a parked run's answer — sealed, and with every message it was made of — keeps to **512 KiB**, and so do the copies a let-go answer owes back to the seat; a reply past that is not recorded as the answer at all: its **refusal** is, as the question's outcome, with its figures and none of its words, and the run is resumed told the reply was too large to reach it, so it asks again for less or carries on ([above](#mid-run-clarification-ask_and_wait), `sandbox_answer_refused`). The bound is not lowered for it: a log or a configuration pasted whole, the answer a coding run's question typically gets, is taken whole. The refusal is recorded as `executor_answered` with the outcome `too_large`, naming what the reply weighed and what an answer may and none of its words. An answer by turn is held far under it, to a page, by `answer_executor`. A call held for approval carries its arguments sealed, up to **256 KiB** of them as the record holds them — about 190 KiB in plain text: a call past it is refused when it is made, naming its size, so the run splits or shortens it. An executor's ask to open a change keeps its title to **256 bytes**, Gitlet's own bound on a change's title, on each repository the record grants it. A person's note keeps to **16 KiB** sealed, a [wake](#notes-to-a-running-run) item to **8 KiB** of seals, and a question is put to at most **256** seats — a `team` question to the unit's lead and then its members in the chart's order — so in a unit larger than that, a member past the 256th who holds no other reach into the asking seat is not shown the question on the board or asked it in their list, though who may answer it is unchanged. What a box says of its session — the release of the harness that wrote it, read off a file the run's own agent can write — is held to the bounds the executor log holds it to: a release longer than 64 bytes is read as none, and a capture's stamp past any of its bounds is refused before it reaches the record.
**The completion poll is THE completion signal.** The box's waiter — its launching node's (below) — attaches to each running box every 15 s (`DefaultPollInterval`) and asks the runner whether the job finished; a run's `submit_work` nudges an immediate poll, and the 15 s tick is the fallback. Nothing from inside the box replaces it: only a poll can see a job that died before its last step, and the tick has to run anyway because it **doubles as the box keepalive** (the stamp that keeps a running box from being reaped as an orphan).

**A waiter on every node, and one watch over the fleet.** A box is a process tree or a container on the host of the node that launched it — the run's record names that node, `launch_node` — and no other node can reach it: polled from another node, it reads as gone. So **every node runs a waiter of its own** for the boxes on its own host, whatever roles it has: it polls those runs, keeps their boxes alive and reaps their pauses, and no other waiter touches them. Each pass, a waiter on a `workers` node also claims the fleet's [singleton duty](seat-ownership.md#singleton-duties) `launch-node-watch`, and only while it holds the claim does it end the runs of a launch node gone for good ([below](#durability-completion-and-observability)). Its own polls, sweep and reaper never wait on the claim. Without a coordination store there is no claim, and no node is judged gone for good.

**A finished job is announced once, and again on a schedule.** The first poll that finds a job over announces its completion at once: on the event stream, as the record that the job finished, and on its seat's control topic, for the seat's holder to collect it and resume its turn. A job its holder does not resume then (its admission refused it, a condition held its resume on that node, or its collection was handed back to be asked again) stays running on its record, and its waiter announces it again, to the seat's control topic alone, for as long as the record is running and no hold is written on it: each announcement a fresh message, each waiting twice as long as the one before, from one poll interval to twenty, so five minutes apart at the default 15 s. A condition that clears with nothing to signal it resumes its job within five minutes, and a job held for a day is announced a few hundred times; announced on every poll, one finished job held for a model's weekly limit was announced 6280 times in 27 hours.

**A run that submits is polled at once.** When a run's `submit_work` is recorded on its row over the [tool bridge](#the-tool-bridge--a-seats-own-tools-from-inside-a-box), the node serving the run's session tells the waiter that drives it — on whichever node that is — to poll it now, and again 1, 3 and 7 s later while its harness makes its closing model call and exits; the schedule doubles its gaps and stays inside one poll interval, past which the ordinary poll is as soon. The run's completion is found within seconds of its exit instead of up to 15 s after it, and the 15 s poll stays the fallback for a run that ends any other way — one that died, was cut off at its turn's cap, or never submitted. The nudge is a hint on an ephemeral broadcast, never an instruction: the waiter it reaches reads the run's row and does what its own poll would, so a nudge that is lost costs one interval, never the run.

**No box waits on another.** Each tick of a node's waiter lists the runs it launched and hands every box that needs work — a poll, or the reclaim of a pause past its TTL — to a task of its own, at most **16 at once** across every tick in flight (`sandbox.MaxConcurrentPolls`: a `container` poll forks up to two runtime CLI processes against one daemon, so a wedged runtime holds at most about 32, and 16 slots still serve hundreds of boxes in a 15 s pass). The tick does not wait for its tasks: the next one comes on schedule, polling every box whose last poll has finished, and passes over a box whose poll is still running, so one box is never polled by two polls at once. A box's completion is announced the moment its own poll finds it. Free slots go first to the boxes whose last poll ended longest ago, so a box that held one goes to the back of the line after its turn. Each poll — reaching the box, its keepalive and asking its runner — is bounded by **60 s** (`sandbox.ConnectGiveUp`), the window after which an unreachable box is given up: a poll unfinished within it is a box not answering. Such a box costs its own poll (counted against reaching it, where it was reaching it) and a slot, never anybody's tick: with N boxes held at the bound, a healthy box waits at most N/16 bounds, rounded up, for a slot.

Two signals cover every way a job can end:

1. **The done-marker** — the wrapper shell wrote the exit code after the agent process returned (clean finish or crash; the marker is non-empty by construction so it can't be confused with "not yet").
2. **Process liveness**: the box is asked whether the detached wrapper is still running. **A read that fails never skips this probe**: the probe still runs, a dead wrapper is still a finished job, and the read's error is reported beside a "not done". A container box answers with `kill -0` on the wrapper's pid inside its own process namespace; a `direct` box answers from the job's recorded identity (the pid and its start time, see [Local sandboxes](#local-sandboxes)), because on the engine host a pid the kernel has handed to another process would otherwise read as the job and hold a dead run open. A dead wrapper with no marker means the whole process group was killed (SIGKILL / OOM); the run completes and `collect` surfaces the partial output and exit code instead of stalling forever — unless nothing saw it die: a job on the engine host whose last witness, the engine process that last saw it running, is gone too was **lost** with that process rather than ended, and is not collected as a result (below).

Both harnesses this build drives exit when their work is done, so nothing is read off the end of a stream to decide it. OpenCode 1.x did not — it finished and held its process open — and was once polled for a terminal event at its stream's end; OpenCode 2 exits when its session does, and its run's script exits after it.

**A reader never wakes a box.** The poll and the live view reach a box with `Provider.Attach`, which never resumes it: a paused container is refused, since its liveness probe is an exec it cannot take; a `direct` box is read as it is, stopped or not, since its files and its probe are the host's. Only the collection and a follow-up run reconnect with `Connect`, which resumes. This closes a race: the poll's list of running runs is a moment old, and a collection claims a run, reads its box and pauses it — a poll that woke the box after that pause would set the parked job working again under nobody's claim. A paused box sends the poll to the run's record instead. A record still running the same job in the same box whose job a collection already read back — the collection paused the box and its resume then handed the claim back, held by the node that met a model's limit or to be tried again — has the job announced again and its box left asleep, neither woken nor kept alive: the job is over, and the collection that next claims it wakes the box to read it. A poll that woke it kept a running box alive at every tick for as long as the hold lasted, up to the hour a vendor's window is sat out. Only a box under a job no collection has read back is woken, kept alive and polled, since only the poll can say whether that job finished, and no finished job is left that way for a condition of its seat's: a completion is refused for its seat's budget or a limit its models know only after it is collected.

**A box is the node's that launched it** ([ADR-0065](../../adr/0065-a-local-box-is-driven-by-the-node-that-launched-it.md)). The seat a run belongs to can move while its job works — a rebalance, a drain — and the run's tool calls follow the seat over the bridge, but a `direct` or `container` box stays where it is, so every touch of that box is made on its host. The seat's new holder collects the run by asking the host to read its box back, over a channel the fleet signs (`sandbox.box_read`), with how long its asker waits, which the host counts from the request's arrival on its own clock — a host whose clock stands up to two hours from the asker's still takes it — and a host already making sixty-four reads of its boxes with sixty-four waiting answers at once that it is busy, handled as a host that did not answer; the asker fits the result itself; the host makes the read only where the run's own record licenses it, and a host that does not answer, restarting or stopping as it reads (which its reply says, rather than passing the cut read off as the box's failure), has the claim handed back uncounted (`sandbox_collect_host_silent`) and announces the completion again from its own poll once it is back, unless the seat's holder last heard from that host that its coordination store did not answer it: its poll reads the run's record through that store, so the completion is then asked again on the queue's backoff and renewed, as below (`store_silent` on the line). A host whose coordination store does not answer its read of the run's record is no failure of the box either: the claim is handed back uncounted and the completion retried until the store answers (`sandbox_collect_unsettled`), for as long as a silent host is waited for where the store answers the seat's holder: the box and its host are up, but only that host can read the box, and one that cannot for `host_grace_seconds` since it first said so is as good as away, as a node that left the fleet is: the seat's holder then records the run's job lost with that node, on its own claim (`launch_node_store_silent`, `sandbox_collect_lost_with_host`), and carries its round on in a box of its own, as for any lost job (below), a job that had finished included, whose turn is never ended as an unreachable box's; and a job already lost has its round carried on without its read. Nothing else announces such a job meanwhile: the host's own waiter reads the run's record through the store that does not answer it, and the broker carries a failing message for about ten minutes before its dead letter, never under eight, less than the bound. So while it keeps that clock the seat's holder **renews the completion**, whatever hands it back: the host's answer that its store did not answer, a claim of the job its own store did not answer, or that it refused itself while it still owes the release of its last claim, a host that did not answer the read at all, a record of the job's loss its own store did not take, a carry of the job's round that failed after its loss was recorded (the clock is kept until the run settles, never dropped at the recorded loss), a refusal of the node's admission (kept for its condition's signal besides), an answer that settled nothing (a claim another attempt holds, a resume its record holds for the seat's budget), and any other step that failed: no delivery of the completion is acknowledged while that clock runs unless the run settled, which drops the clock. Once the delivery in hand has five or fewer deliveries left after it, it announces the completion afresh on the seat's control topic and only then acknowledges that delivery, so one announcement is in flight however long the wait (`sandbox_completion_renewed`); a renewal the broker does not take leaves the delivery to come back and try again (`sandbox_completion_renew_failed`). Where the store does not answer the seat's holder either, no claim of the job lands, so nothing is given up for as long as that lasts. A person's stop of such a run is decided and its tool-bridge session closed at once on the seat's holder, and that node's own retry asks the host to end the job and read what it had spent, off the frame the pause reached it on — the host ends the job, as the only node that can, and only where the run's record says it is stopped: a host that does not answer is asked again rather than having the run's spend written off (`sandbox_stop_read_waits`), until it answers, or has been silent for `host_grace_seconds` by that node's own clock since it first asked it — the bound after which the fleet takes a silent launch node for gone, counted again by the seat's next holder as the launch-node watch counts again when its duty moves — or the stop is that long and two hours old by its clock, the most two machines' clocks may stand apart; a host that answers it is busy is there, and its silence starts again — and only then is the run ended with nothing read (`sandbox_stop_unread`, logged once the stop's record of that lands, never before it). A host whose coordination store does not answer its read of the run's record is waited for the same way, up to the same bound, while the store answers the seat's holder: the box and its host are up, but only that host can read the box, and one that cannot for that long is as good as away (`sandbox_stop_read_waits`, its `waits_for` the store; `sandbox_stop_unread` past the bound, its `store_silent` set). Where the store does not answer the seat's holder either, nothing the stop's ending writes would land, so the stop is kept for as long as that lasts, whatever the bound, and never logged as ended (`sandbox_stop_read_waits` with `shared` set). The collection of a run claimed past its turn's wall-clock cap is read on the host the same way, and the host ends a job still working past that cap — the cap as its own clock reads the row's deadline, or as the run's record says an earlier collection of the job found it — before it takes the session. A relaunch on the new holder starts in a fresh box of its own, from the pushed branch, rather than continuing in one it cannot reach. A box no run names any more — its run ended, stopped or relaunched elsewhere — is reclaimed by its host: each box records the run it was made for, every pass of the host's own waiter kills the box whose run no longer names it (`sandbox_host_box_reclaimed`), and the node that left the box there tells the host to look at once. A box whose run ended while its host was stopped is reclaimed the same way on the host's first pass. The run's [live output](#watching-a-run-live) is read on the host too, and a `from_sandbox` publish on another node is refused rather than reading a box it cannot reach.

**A node that never comes back.** If the node a box is on leaves the fleet and does not return — its presence lease lapsed and stayed lapsed for `host_grace_seconds` (15 min) — the holder of the `launch-node-watch` duty records on each of that node's running jobs that it was lost with the node (`sandbox_launch_node_gone`) and announces their completion, and the seat's holder carries each job's round on in a box of its own, as for any lost job (below). A run of that node parked on a question has its box released and waits for its answer without it, resuming from its pushed branch. A node that is merely restarting — a drain gives its presence up at its first step — is back inside that bound, and its own waiter picks its runs up again; the bound is measured from when the duty's holder first found the node away, while it held the claim throughout: a waiter that loses the claim, or cannot confirm it, forgets every absence it was timing, so an absence nobody watched whole is never counted, and a move of the duty can only make a verdict later. Raise `host_grace_seconds` for a deployment whose nodes are routinely away longer than that.

**A vanished sandbox can't orphan a run.** If reconnecting fails on several consecutive ticks (~1 min at defaults), the waiter gives the box up and fires completion anyway. A box its backend says is **gone** — a box root that did not outlive its node (a pod recreated with its scratch volume) — took its job with it: the waiter records it lost (`box_gone`), and its round is carried on (below). A box that is only **unreachable** — a network partition — may still hold a working job, so the coordinator's collection asks again for its own minute of retries, which a partition that heals in that minute survives (see [Failure modes](#failure-modes)), and only then frees the agent, ends the run and announces it as `executor_failed` with reason `collect_unreachable`, rather than polling a dead box forever.

**A job lost with its host is carried on, not collected.** A job can go without ending: a `direct` box's job is a process tree of the engine host, detached into a session of its own so that it outlives the engine process — and it does, when only that process dies — but a container restart takes every process in the container, a systemd unit stopped or restarted kills every process in its control group (the default `KillMode`), and a host reboot takes a `container` box's job as well. Each kills the job mid-step, before its wrapper writes the marker that says how it ended, which is exactly what a job that crashed on its own leaves; read that way, the turn resumed on a truncated run as though the run had failed, or — once its box was gone too — the run ended the turn, which the park had already acknowledged, so nothing would ever start it again. So each box records its job's **witness**: the engine process that last saw the job running — the one that started it, and then whichever process of the engine first finds it still running after a restart — by its pid and the start time the kernel gives it, which together do not repeat. A job that is not running ended in its witness's sight while that process is still there, and is collected as before, a crash included; a job whose witness is gone too went with it, or after it, before any engine could see it end, and is **lost** (`sandbox_run_lost`, cause `engine_restarted`). A box with no witness record is read as ended. A `container` box's runtime is asked whether the container is up before the job is (a listing it answers, absence included), so a daemon that is briefly away is no answer at all rather than a job that ended.

The waiter that drives the box records the loss on the run's row before it announces the completion — `engine_restarted`, `box_gone`, or `launch_node_gone` for a node that left (above) — and the seat's holder, claiming it, never collects it as a result. The seat's holder records one loss itself, on the claim it collects under: `launch_node_store_silent`, for a job whose box only its node can read and that node has not been able to read the run's record off the coordination store for `host_grace_seconds` (above), and it carries that round on at once. Where the box is still there it reads what the job did up to then off it, charges what it spent once and publishes it as the job's own record, noted *cut off* rather than failed; a box that does not answer is asked again like any collection, and one that has not answered for the give-up window is left behind, its spend uncharged (`sandbox_lost_run_unread`); a coordination store that does not answer a step of that read is no box that did not answer, and the round is not carried on without the read for it (`sandbox_collect_unsettled`), unless only the box's host has found the store silent, for the host grace (above). Then the turn resumes and **carries the round on** (`sandbox_run_lost_carried_on`): the same round relaunched, its calls so far kept and counted — in the lost job's box where the relaunch runs on that box's host with the same harness, its working tree as the job left it, and in a fresh box from whatever the job pushed otherwise. That line says, in whole seconds to the instant the loss was found, how long the job ran from its launch (`ran_s`) and how long since the newest capture of its own launch that was kept, final or not (`since_save_s`): what the loss cost, and the work a relaunch continuing that capture does again. Each is left out where its instant is not known: a launch recorded with no start, or a turn whose only kept capture is an earlier job's, which says nothing of this one. They are read off three clocks, those of the node that found the loss, of the node whose write launched the job and of the capture's taker, so each is an estimate, good to within twice the hour a clock may stand from the fleet's before [`clock_skew`](../reference/alarms.md) is raised; one those clocks would put below zero, or a final capture kept after the loss was found, is `0`. It **continues the lost job's own session** where it can ([A relaunch continues the turn's session](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)) — the capture taken when the loss was found, where the engine's restart left its box behind, never the box's copy as it stands; and, where the box went with its host, or that capture was refused, the newest capture of that job that was kept (its newest [save](#a-running-jobs-session-saved-as-it-works), taken as it worked or as its node drained, where one landed), past a newer one still being kept when the relaunch's wait ran out — told that it was cut off and why, every call it made through the seat's tools since the save point of the capture it continues, some of which its session may already hold, and that its session may end mid-call; otherwise — a job that kept no capture, and an earlier job's holds none of what this one was told — and always after a second loss in the round, it starts a fresh harness session told that a run before it was cut off, why, where to look for its work, and that what it did through the seat's tools did happen. Two exceptions: a job whose round's calls already hold its `submit_work` finished its work and was lost on its way out, so the round is collected; and a job that had asked a person before it went is parked on its question, as one that finished asking is. **A round is carried on after at most two lost jobs** (`sandbox.MaxRoundLosses`): one loss is routine — a deploy, a drained node, a patched host — and two in one round is a long run that saw a deploy and its rollback, but a third is a run taking its own host down (exhausting the memory its container is held to kills every process in the container on a cgroup-v2 Kubernetes node), and each further relaunch would take the node's other seats down with it. The next loss ends the round's executor phase, and with it the turn, saying how often the round was lost.

**Per-run OTel, without handing the sandbox a secret.** The harness's telemetry exports to an **engine-fronted OTLP receiver**, enabled for a box that does not share its node's loopback (a `container` box) by setting `CREWLET_SANDBOX_OTEL_RECEIVER_URL` to the engine API base the sandbox can reach — the public listener's address when Tier A sets `api.public.port`, since an `ingress` node serves `/otlp/` there and nowhere else. A value that is not an absolute `http://` or `https://` URL a box can use — a host a URL parser accepts (a name, or an address with no zone: an unfilled `<host>` placeholder or a mistyped IPv4 address such as `10.0.0.300` is refused), a port from 1 to 65535 if it names one, and no user information, query or fragment — refuses the node's boot, naming the variable and never repeating the value, rather than handing every box an endpoint its exporter cannot use and losing the run's telemetry without a word. Plain `http://` is accepted, and what that costs is in [Security model](#security-model). A `direct` box needs no address: on a node that forwards — `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` set, which the engine's own spans read too — and binds `api.port`, it exports to that node's own listener on loopback, by the tool bridge's rule (above), whether or not the variable is set. A node that forwards nothing hands its own boxes no endpoint of its own, since it would drop what they sent, and a box with no address that reaches it gets no telemetry endpoint at all. Each run gets a **per-run, trace-scoped, expiring token embedded in the endpoint path** (`POST /otlp/{token}/v1/{signal}`), so `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` — the backend's ingest credential — never enters the box; the receiver validates the token and forwards upstream, adding the real auth outside the sandbox. That variable is set **empty** in the box rather than left unset, because an exporter reads it from its ambient environment otherwise — and while a box inherits nothing of the engine's own environment, its image may export a value of its own, and so may a `-e` in `local.run_args`. The empty value is what makes the endpoint's token the only credential the run's exporter presents.

The token is **signed and self-describing** rather than a key into a store, because minting and verifying can happen on different nodes: the node running the seat mints when it launches a run, and whichever node the box exports to verifies. Every node derives its signing keys from the Tier A keyring, so a fleet agrees without sharing state. There is no per-process fallback: every node holds a keyring (a node without one does not start), and a keyring that cannot sign for the fleet is refused by name when the receiver is built, because a key of one process's own would validate at the node that minted and nowhere else. Expiry rides in the token, so nothing is reaped and a restart does not invalidate a live run's endpoint. The token also **names the key that signed it**, so a keyring rotation does not invalidate a run already in flight: the key stays on the ring until the operator drops it, and a token naming a key a node no longer holds is refused rather than retried against the active one. The runbook is in [Secret store](secret-store.md).

The receiver **accepts and drops** when no upstream is configured: the engine's own per-turn span still carries the trace, and a deployment with no backend should not have every export fail. A failing backend is never reported to the box either — an exporter that gets a 5xx retries, and retries against a backend that is down turn one outage into two. The run env also carries non-secret resource attributes (`crewlet.turn_id`, `crewlet.agent_handle`) and a `TRACEPARENT`, so a harness's spans file under the turn. Only a run whose harness exports by this environment is handed it ([Credentials and the run environment](#credentials-and-the-run-environment)): GitHub Copilot CLI exports its traces and metrics to the endpoint (measured on 1.0.114), and OpenCode its traces and logs (2.3.2).

**A run keeps the work item its turn is on.** The launch writes the turn's `work_item` onto the run's record and onto `executor_launched`, and a question the run parks on carries it on `executor_asked`. The record is where the resumed turn reads its item from — the event that resumes it, a box's completion or a person's chat answer, names none — so the second half of the turn is charged to the same work as the first, under the basis `resume` (see [Which work a turn is on](turn-engine.md#which-work-a-turn-is-on)). What the turn had written before it parked travels on its parked state (`execstate`, `Written`) for the same reason. **A record keeps every key it cannot read**: each status flip, claim and release rewrites the whole record, and a node running an older build writes back the keys a newer one added rather than dropping them, so a rolling upgrade cannot strip the item, or anything added after it, off a parked run.

**Dashboard.** The live-state projection keeps the set of runs in flight, and it builds that set from two sources, because neither is enough alone.

- **The lifecycle events keep the set current.** `executor_launched` adds a run. `executor_asked` moves the run to `awaiting_clarification`. `executor_finished`, `executor_failed` or `executor_stopped` removes it. A failure used to be read by nothing, so a lost run stayed on the panel as running; a stop is read the same way, so a run a person stopped leaves the panel the moment its stop is announced rather than at the next reconcile.
- **The durable run record decides which runs exist.** The record is read once when the node starts, before the node serves (before its listener is handed the API surface), and then every 30 seconds (`livestate.ReconcileInterval`). What the record holds replaces what the events built. A process that starts while runs are in flight never saw their starts, and a completion that never arrived would otherwise leave a finished run on the panel with nothing to remove it. Two cases keep the event's version. A run whose event arrived after the read began is newer than the read. A run whose end the events already reported is not put back, because the record lags the end by the collection the end starts. A completion names the job it finished, and a failure is compared with the record's last write.

This replaced a twelve-hour age-out, which was wrong in both directions. A finished run whose completion was lost stayed on the panel as running for twelve hours. A run parked on a question for longer than twelve hours disappeared from the panel, and a run waiting on a person is the one the panel most needs to show.

Each entry is `{turn_id, role, agent_handle, agent_id, harness, provider_key, model, sandbox_id, task, status, started_at, question, audience, body_withheld, work_item, owner, paused_at, launch_id, held_call}` — `provider_key` and `model` the `providers.llm` entry the launch picked and its model. `launch_id` is the job the run is on, which an answer to its question names, and `held_call` (`{id, server, tool, raw, digest, held_at}`) the tool call its question is about where it asks to make one, answered through [`POST /mcp-approvals/{id}`](../reference/api-endpoints.md#post-mcp-approvalsid) rather than `answer_executor`, so a surface reading the live set offers the answer the engine takes without reading the board first. The entry is the company's configuration, sent to an admin alone, as it is on the [`executors`](../reference/api-endpoints.md#get-executors) board; every other reader, a seat's lead included, is sent the model the run runs under.

- `body_withheld` is set for a reader who may not read the launching seat's body, which only an administrator and the seat's lead may: `task` is then empty, and so are `question` and `held_call` unless the question is put to that reader ([A status reader never receives a transcript](../reference/api-endpoints.md#a-status-reader-never-receives-a-transcript)). A reader without Worklet is sent no `work_item`.
- `status` uses the record's own vocabulary: `launching`, `running`, `awaiting_clarification`, `reseed` or `answered` (a reply is recorded and the engine is resuming the run with it). A `resumed` run is over, because its turn has already taken back the result, so it is not listed. The panel used to write `awaiting_input`, a status the record cannot hold, so the dashboard never saw a live run as waiting on a person.
- `owner` is the node driving the run.
- `paused_at` is the pause reaper's own reading of when the box began being held.

Every node reads the same fleet-wide record, so every node's panel shows the fleet's runs. The dashboard's **Executors** screen reads the record directly (`executors`). A run whose box has already been reclaimed is therefore still listed there, with the row's own facts that the panel does not carry.

### Watching a run live

Nothing a running job writes leaves its box until the run is collected, when its transcript (held to the record's bound, its start and its end) rides the launch's own `executor_collected` record. While it runs, its live output is a **question**, asked only while somebody looks: `executor_tail{turn_id, launch_id}` (`GET /executors/{turn_id}/tail?launch_id=…`). There is no event and no row behind it.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Dashboard
    participant A as API node
    participant O as Launching node
    participant B as Box
    D->>A: executor_tail{turn_id, launch_id, epoch, after, digest}
    A->>A: read the run's record (launching? not running? which node launched it?)
    A->>O: ask on crewlet.observe.executor_tail, with the asker's budget
    alt the reading was read in the last 2 s
        O-->>A: the text after `after`, from the shared reading
    else
        O->>B: attach without waking, then read what each stream grew
        B-->>O: new complete lines
        O->>O: decode, settle and redact, then append to the reading
        O-->>A: the text after `after` — or a reset carrying the last 256 KiB
    end
    A-->>D: {outcome: tail, output: {text, start, end, epoch, digest, reset, held}}
    D->>D: append (or replace on a reset), then trim the front past 256 KiB
```

- **It names the job, not only the run.** A turn can launch several jobs, so `executor_launched` carries the job's `launch_id` (the one the run's record holds and its `executor_collected` record repeats) and the instant the store recorded the launch (`started_at`); a request naming only the turn would show whichever job the record holds now.
- **The node that hosts the run's box answers it, from one reading per job.** Every node serves `crewlet.observe.executor_tail`. The asker reads the run's record; the node that launched the box (`launch_node`, the one node that can reach it whoever holds the seat) re-reads the record and answers from its **reading** of the job (`Runner.Follow`): the transcript the harness's decoder builds from the event stream, or the error stream while the event stream has said nothing yet (a harness that failed to start), read through a box attached without waking it (`Provider.Attach`). A reading begins at the start of each stream's last mebibyte, on a line, and every later read takes only what was written since (a ranged read of the stream's end sized to its growth). When that mebibyte holds no line break at all (a line longer than the window, `\r`-only progress, a minified blob), the reading DROPS the rest of that line, up to the first break after it, as a partial first line always is, and begins from there; showing it as a whole redacted line could put the tail of a credential straddling the window's edge on screen. Those bytes are not counted as held, since nothing will show them; the reading says instead that it began after the stream's start (`front`). The error stream's reading also reads the **386.5 KiB before** where it begins (`redact.LookBack`), with that dropped line's rest after them, and never shows them: they give its first text the cross-line context redaction needs (a private key whose BEGIN came before the reading, a password's key above its first line), and the reading shows only what they settle, from the line after anything they decide. Nothing in the box is written, signalled or cleared.
- **What it shows is settled.** A line is shown only once nothing written after it can change how it redacts (`redact.Settled`):
  - A line still being written waits for its line break.
  - A private key's BEGIN and the lines under it wait while what comes next could still be the key's body or END; a mere mention of the armour line waits only for the next line.
  - A line that reads like a key's body (base64 as wide as a key's line, in upper and lower case both) waits until two lines in a row that cannot be one follow it, with two more lines after them: four such lines in a row most often, five for a run exactly as wide as a key's line (64, 70 or 76 characters), which an END can read back to across two lines, counted again above a line that could be OpenPGP's checksum, which an END reads back from as from itself.
  - A password key waits for the line that decides its value: the value's own, past the wrapping's blank lines, or the next one holding a key or not ending as the key's line did. It does not wait where that line only confirms what the key's line gave on its own, so a run of `password:"` lines is shown as written, not held whole. A key followed on its line by punctuation and more (`msg="Enter password:" level=info`, whose quote may be a wrapping's) waits for the next line, as does a key a quote closes whose separator ends its line (`case "password":`): one line.
  - A hash in hex or a path in lower case is in one case and is shown at once. A Go test's name, a CamelCase identifier or a mixed-case path as wide as a key's line is in both cases, with or without a digit, and waits like a key's line, so a verbose test run's output can arrive in bursts, held as far back as 64 KiB until lines that are no key's release it.
  - A line holding a run that reads like a piece of a key anywhere on it (eight characters or more in both cases with a digit, which an END written next could read back to as a line a cut wrote into) waits until four lines that hold none follow it. On `go test -v` output of Crewlet's own packages fed a line at a time, a few hundred bytes wait on average and at most about 4 KiB.

  So what a viewer sees, read by read, is exactly the whole text redacted, never a key's body that its END line, a moment later, would have hidden. What is held back is counted (`held`), so the screen can say why a line has not appeared. Once the job is done nothing is held back, and a transcript's reading writes each entry as a line trimmed to its words.
- **One read of the box answers everybody watching.** The host reads a job's box at most once every two seconds (`sandbox.LiveReuse`), however many people have the run open; requests arriving while a read is in flight wait for it. Each answer waits for the box at most three quarters of its asker's budget (the request carries it), so a request the asker gave up on frees its answer slot; the read itself goes on, under its own budget of one completion-poll interval, and the next request is answered from what it found, or, if the box is still being read, from the last read there was, stamped with when it was taken. A reading nobody has asked about for 30 seconds is dropped by the host's own sweep, every ten seconds, whether or not anything asks again. In a fleet nothing does once a run stops: the node serving the dashboard reads the run's record, answers `not_running` itself and never asks the host again, and a viewer who closes the page asks nobody.
- **A viewer is sent only what it lacks.** Every request says what the asker holds: the reading's `epoch`, the byte offset it holds through (`after`) and the `digest` the host gave it there, all three absent on a first request. The answer is the text after that offset, with its `start` and `end` offsets beside it, always both, `0` included (a run that has settled nothing yet is answered at `0` and followed from it). Anything else is a **reset** carrying the last 256 KiB in whole lines (the most a viewer holds, the record's own bound): an epoch naming another reading (the host restarted, the reading began again further on, the account switched from the error stream to the transcript), a digest that does not match the window the asker holds (a node on a build that derives the stream differently), or a viewer more than 256 KiB behind. A box is read on the node that launched it whoever holds the seat, so its run is followed across a move of the seat with no reset, and a launching node that does not answer is `host_silent`, naming that node.
- **Six outcomes, never an empty answer standing in for another.**
  - `tail` is the output (possibly empty: a run that has written nothing yet says so).
  - `launching` is a job whose box is still being made and provisioned, not a run that stopped; a screen keeps asking.
  - `not_running` names the record's own status: parked on a question, `replaced` by a later job on the same run, or no record at all because the run was collected.
  - `host_silent{node}` is the node that launched the run's box, held or not, not answering inside the two-second fleet read budget (a draining node or one whose heartbeat lapsed is asked like any other, and its silence is this); it names that node.
  - `box_paused` is a running record whose box is paused where its backend cannot read it without waking it (the moment between a collection pausing the box and the record moving on); the box is left paused.
  - `box_gone` is a running record whose box its backend says is gone for good: its root didn't outlive its node. Nothing more is read from it, its waiter records its job lost, so its round is carried on in a fresh run (see *A job lost with its host* under [Durability](#durability-completion-and-observability)), and a screen keeps asking until the record says so.

  A box the host couldn't read is an error, and only its class crosses from the host, never its text. The host logs the failure (`sandbox_tail_failed`, the class as `failure`, at warn for a fault and for a class no wait clears, at debug otherwise), whether answering a peer or the person directly, and the asker answers the class. The surface that answers the person writes its own debug line, because the failure is in the host's log already; a host on a newer build that names a class this one doesn't know is answered as a fault, and the asker logs `sandbox_tail_failure_unknown` naming it. A runtime that didn't answer, and a host that couldn't answer just now (the node stopping, its coordination store not answering), are `unavailable` with a `Retry-After`; a sandbox setup somebody has to fix is `unavailable` with none, by the [classes a launch is told by](#when-a-run-does-not-start); a fault of the host's own is `query_failed`, whose detail is in the host's log.
- **The dashboard asks every three seconds, and only while somebody is looking**: while a running run's span is open on the turn trace, or while the run's own page (Live › Executors, `#/live/executors/{turn_id}`) is open on a running job. Each request is chained after the last answer, so one open view has one request in flight. Closing the view or the run ending stops the poll, and so does a failed read the engine says no wait clears (a sandbox setup somebody has to fix), until the socket reconnects or the view is opened again. The run's page asks by the `launch_id` the run board names (`executors` serves it), so it shows the job the row holds now, and when a later job replaces it the page reads the board again and follows the new one.
- **After collection the record is the turn's.** A collected run's row is deleted, and its page reads the turn instead: every `executor_collected` the turn's launches published (what each job reported, delivered, its tokens and its transcript) under the task its `executor_launched` carried. A link to a finished run still lands on what it did.
### Reading a seat's sessions

**A run's session is kept after it, and read back as its transcript.** Every
capture a collection takes — the archive the run packed when its harness
exited ([Claude Code](#a-claude-code-runs-session),
[OpenCode](#an-opencode-runs-session)) — is sealed into the fleet's
[object store](object-store.md) and named by its turn's row of the `executor`
log
([ADR-0073](https://github.com/crewlet/crewlet/blob/main/adr/0073-a-seats-executor-session-is-a-sealed-object-its-turns-row-names.md),
and [Conversation Sessions](conversation-sessions.md#configuration) for how
long and how much is kept). That archive is the whole record of what the run
read, called and wrote, and a seat's **Sessions** (under the Memory section of
its page's Activity tab on the dashboard, [A seat's profile](../reference/dashboard-design.md#a-seats-profile),
or [`GET /agents/{id}/sessions`](../reference/api-endpoints.md#get-agentsidsessions))
list them, the latest begun first: how each turn ended (the engine's own
account, which the transcript cannot know), what it was asked, and whether its
session is still kept. **A row begins at its turn's first launch** where the
turn read its conversation — its `begin`, which names the session that launch
was handed (`base_turn`) — and at its first capture otherwise. **And a row goes
with the turn that was handed it**: once a later turn of its conversation that
was handed its session, and that kept a session of its own, ends, its end
absorbs the turns its read handed out, and their rows are gone from the list —
as are rows past the retention, and a removed seat's. A session read by its turn
after its row went is `404 not_found`, saying it may have gone any of these ways.
**Reading a session holds nothing**, so a session can go while it is read, and
is said as released rather than as a loss: see below.

**A row that keeps no session says why**, one of four: nothing of the turn's
session was captured (yet, while it runs); its newest capture was not kept, and
none before it was — its end said so, with the reason the store or the log gave,
redacted; an end an earlier version of the engine recorded took an older capture
off the row too, where one of this version keeps it and says the turn
[went on past it](turn-engine.md#how-a-turn-ends-on-the-executor-log);
a run [ran out of context](conversation-sessions.md#a-session-that-ran-out-of-context-is-retired)
in its session, which retired it; or the seat's session budget released it to
make room for newer ones — a session its turn went on past included, which only
the budget takes off, said with the newer capture that was not kept beside it.

**A live turn's row that names a session is in progress** (`in_progress`): the
newest session its runs have kept — a job's final capture as its collection
took it, while the turn goes on to its review or waits on a person's answer, or
one a loss left its box to take — which its run may have gone on past, and
whose last call may have no result yet. It is read as the turn's session, never
as an ended turn's, and a relaunch continues it only where its `continuable`
says so: a relaunch continues the newest kept capture of the job it follows,
and a live turn's row often names an earlier job's. Every reader is told so in
one sentence of the engine's (`in_progress_note`), its words alone: "This turn
has not ended: this is the newest session its runs have kept, captured at
`<captured_at>`; its run may have gone on past it, and its last call may have
no result yet." **A row kept up to a session its turn went on past says so**
(`kept_note`): that the session was taken while the turn still worked and that
what the turn did after is not in it — or, of a turn that was lost, that it may
not hold the last of what the turn did — with the newer capture that was not
kept and why, redacted, where its end names one; that reason quotes what
refused the capture, so a seat reads the note fenced, as it reads the row's
other words. A row that holds its turn's last word says neither, unless its
turn was lost, which every lost turn's row says. Both are read off the row
alone: nothing on the log says what kind of capture landed a row, and no reader
of it reads the turn's run record.

**Each says which launch would continue it** (`continued_by`), **whether it
would** (`continuable`), where (`continues_in`), and where not, why
(`not_continuable`), each decided by the one decision that launch takes, over
what that launch reads, and of the member of the seat's executor chain it would
be launched on now — the first not sitting out its plan — with the cell its run
lands in and its runner:

- **A live turn's session, by a relaunch of it** (`relaunch`): the decision a
  relaunch takes ([above](#a-relaunch-continues-the-turns-session)), over the
  turn's row of the executor log as a relaunch reads it, the turn's run record
  in the coordination store and the job that record names as the one a relaunch
  would follow. `any_box` where the turn is live and not ending, the newest
  capture of that job was kept, states its save point and is the one the row
  names, and that runner restores its harness, format and release; a round
  whose job was lost a second time is carried on in a session of its own,
  which a reader is told cannot be said where a review of the work it
  submitted may yet continue it. `parked_box`
  where that is not so but a person's answer would still carry the turn's
  parked run on in the box it parked in — the run still holds the box, the box
  ran the row's own session (not one it started in that one's place, and not
  one whose job's box never said which of the two it ran), the member is of the
  box's harness in its cell, and a box on the engine host is on the host of the
  node holding the seat, which alone can continue in it — which continues the
  session that box holds there and nowhere else, for as long as the box is
  held; `not_continuable` then says why no other box would. A box that cannot
  be continued in says why, beside why the kept capture is not continued. **A
  turn that has kept no session of its own** — its first job lost with its box
  before anything of it was kept — says so, and where its row still holds the
  session its first launch was handed and the member restores it, that a
  relaunch in a box of its own continues that session instead
  ([A conversation's next turn continues its last turn's
  session](#a-conversations-next-turn-continues-its-last-turns-session)).
- **An ended turn's session, by its conversation's next turn** (`next_turn`):
  the decision that turn's first launch takes of the head its dispatch reads.
  Only the conversation's **head** is continued — of its ended turns whose rows
  still name a session, the one that read the conversation last ([A
  conversation's next turn continues its last turn's
  session](#a-conversations-next-turn-continues-its-last-turns-session)), which
  the read that answered the row names from
  the same snapshot, so a row's standing is the one its page's `read_level`
  states — `any_box`, where the member restores it, and in a box of the next
  turn's own. A row that is not the head names the turn whose session the next
  turn is handed instead; one that names no session says why; and one whose
  company keeps no session says so. A turn whose run is over, or whose ending is
  decided, and whose end is not on the log as the row was read is the next
  turn's too, and `null` until its end lands. A turn that served no
  conversation — a colleague's ask, a generic source's wake — is continued by
  no launch: it sends no `continued_by`, and `continuable` is `false`.
- **An ended fire's session, by its schedule's next fire** (`next_fire`): the
  same decision as `next_turn`, for a row of a schedule's conversation — a
  schedule is a conversation of each seat that runs it
  ([above](#a-conversations-next-turn-continues-its-last-turns-session)) — told
  in the schedule's words: a fire that is not its schedule's head names the
  fire whose session the next fire is handed instead. A live fire's row is a
  relaunch's like any other's, and where its turn has kept nothing it names the
  last fire a relaunch in a box of its own would continue.

**The member is the one the node holding the seat would pick**, off the chain
of the company revision the launch runs on: which members sit out a spent plan
is what that node's own calls have met, which company revision says sessions are
kept is the revision it runs, a resumed segment of the turn running there
relaunches — its reviewer's send-back, the round it carries on — on the revision
it was admitted under, whatever an apply has put live since, and a
conversation's next turn is admitted under the revision live when it comes. So
the node answering asks it — itself where it holds the seat, and otherwise the
node the seat's lease names, once a page — and is answered, session by session,
with that node's pick and whether that member's runner restores the session: a
live turn's by its turn, and a conversation's head by none, so a segment of the
ended turn still pinned in the moments before it returns answers for no
revision the next turn runs on. As far as the engine can know before a box is
chosen, and no further: whether the box a launch gets runs a harness release
that can take the session up, whether it is a box of the launch's own, and
whether the seat's budget can carry its context, are the launch's to find out,
and no row says them.

**An unknown is never a no**: `continuable` is null, with its reason, where the
run record or the row at the relaunch's level could not be read, and where the
launch would not decide now either — the job a relaunch would follow still
working, or a claim on it whose read is still under way, one that has neither
taken the job's final capture nor begun its turn; that job's capture still being
kept; what the launch is launched on not to be said (every member of the seat's
chain sitting out its plan, no node holding the seat, the node holding it not
answering within two seconds); a relaunch only the resume of a collected job
decides, until its turn begins — whether its round is carried on in its box,
which it is where the job's sign-in was replaced while it ran, and whether a
round lost a second time is carried on in a session of its own or reviewed from
the work it submitted; and a turn whose end is not on the log yet. **A resumed
turn says what it does with the round as it begins**, on the job's record —
collects the job, or carries the round on — and from then on, its review
included, the claim is decided on that, whether or not its read took any
capture: a turn that collects its job is reviewed, and its send-back continues
nothing in the job's box; one that carries the round on in that box continues it
there. A claim of a person's answer reads no box, and is decided whatever its
job kept.

**What a page costs.** A page reads the coordination store once for its runs,
one listing of the seat's live runs — and one turn's record alone for a live row
the listing does not hold, a record of a status this build does not know or one
it could not decode — and none where every row on it has ended; and once more
for the seat's lease, to find the node holding the seat, wherever a row asks it
— a live row whose run is neither over nor ending, or a conversation's head —
that node's own pages included. Where the store does not answer, a live turn's
row says so, and the page is answered all the same. **A live row is read again
at the relaunch's level** (`linearizable`) only where the page was read below
it and the row names another capture than the one its run's record keeps, or
the record keeps none — a copy of the log behind the record, which would read a
capture a relaunch continues as one the log no longer names: a read at that
level costs a barrier on the executor log, and a row naming the kept capture
decides as one read there would. An ended row is decided on its page's own
snapshot, its conversation's head read in the same transaction as the rows: one
seek of the conversation's line index for each conversation the page names. A
transcript's later pages (read with a `cursor`) leave `continuable` null: its
first page says it.

**One session opens as its transcript**
([`GET /agents/{id}/sessions/{turn_id}`](../reference/api-endpoints.md#get-agentsidsessionsturn_id)):
its object is streamed out of the store and opened under its own associated
data, and the archive is read by the runner that packs it, which alone knows
its layout — Claude Code's transcript, one record a line, then each subagent's
own from its sidecar; OpenCode's export, in one pass that holds no message,
each read by the kind OpenCode 2 gives it. The entries are what the run was briefed, the notes a
person sent it while it worked, the late calls the engine handed it while it
worked (a call of the work that finished after the run that made it had stopped
waiting for it), what its model wrote, every tool call and what
answered it, and the compaction summaries the harness wrote in place of what
came before them; the model's thinking and the harness's bookkeeping are none —
OpenCode's own messages included: its notices in the person's turn, an update
of the run's instructions, a skill or a shell command a person ran in the
session, an execution's end, and a switch of the session's agent, model or
directory. An OpenCode message of a kind this build does not know is said where
it was, as a record of no shape the read knows is. A note or a late call is
known by the heading the engine opens each with, wherever the harness filed it
— OpenCode as a person's message, Claude Code as a hook's context in a record
of its own — where the heading starts its line or follows only the harness's
framing, so a tool's words the engine quotes on a line never head an entry. The
line the run's own hook prints as it hands them over is an entry too: a late
call where it names late calls alone, a note otherwise. It is
read a page at a time and bounded — 200 entries and 1 MiB of text a page,
16 KiB an entry, 2^20 lines of the record and the blocks and parts in them a
read, and 256 MiB a read of the archive as it inflates and, apart, of what a
tar's members hand out, so an archive a box packed to inflate without end, or
with a sparse member that declares more than it holds, stops there; a line of
any length is read, a value in it held to 2 MiB and past it streamed through
the redaction into its entry, never held —
and every entry's text is **redacted at this read before it is cut**, whatever
the capture did, and is always an opening of what its whole text redacts to:
